rules.description: Reports a block comment that follows an opening token on its line and ends the line (`if (a) { /* note */`). The tokens are the option `after` (default `{`). A line comment there, and a block comment with code after it on the line, are not reported.

options.description: The tokens a block comment must not follow on their line.
options.name: after

rules.why:
The style keeps a block comment from ending the line of an opening brace. A comment on a line of its own above the first statement says clearly which statement it describes.

To fix, move the comment to its own line.

rules.description: Reports a line comment whose text starts right after the marker (`//text`, `#text`). Not reported: a comment with nothing after the marker, a repeated marker (`////`, `##`), a `--` separator line and a `#!` shebang on the first line. With the option `block` it also checks block comments (`/*a*/`: text right after the opening or before the closing delimiter). The fix inserts the space.

options.description: Check line comments (`// a`). Off, only block comments are checked (with `block`).
options.name: line

options.description: Also check block comments: text right after the opening or before the closing delimiter is reported (`/*a*/`). Exempt: an empty comment, and a delimiter repeated (`/**`, `/***/`). The fix inserts the space.
options.name: block

upstream.note: Line comments only.

rules.why:
One space after the marker is the common way to write comments, and it separates the text from the marker so that the comment reads as text and not as a disabled piece of code. A comment without it is also hard to tell from commented-out code (`//foo();`).

To fix, add the space; the fix does it.

rules.description: Reports the body of an `if`, `else`, loop or `when` entry that is one statement without braces (`if (a) b();`, `else c();`, `for (;;) d();`, `while (x) y();`). `else if` is not reported. Style `always` (default) wants braces on every body; style `chain` wants them on the branches of a chain only where one branch has braces, spans lines or passes the line width, and on a loop body that stands on its own line. The language's `curly_style` option overrides the style when the formatter runs the rule. The fix adds the braces.

options.description: `always`: every body; `chain`: see the rule. The `style` row of the language's `curly_style` option overrides it in the formatter.
options.name: style

upstream.note: No option for single-line bodies.

rules.why:
Without braces a second line added later to the body looks as if it belongs to the `if` or loop, but it runs every time. That is how the 2014 Apple `goto fail` bug happened, and braces make the extent of the body visible.

To fix, add the braces; the fix does it.

rules.description: Reports a name that a command declares when it does not match the pattern of its class, for languages whose files are a flat list of commands (CMake). The option `names` says which argument of which command is a name and of which class (`command:position:class`), `markers` and `scopes` settle the class of a variable (a marker word among the arguments, or the innermost listed block it is set in), and `patterns` gives each class a regex that the name must match from its start. A class without a pattern is not checked. `reference_start` and `reference_end` cut references such as `${...}` out of a name first, and `ignore_pattern` leaves matching names out.

example.input:
set(lower 1)
set(UPPER 1)
set(lc "" CACHE STRING "x")
set(_OK "" CACHE INTERNAL "x")
set(lc2 "" CACHE STRING INTERNAL)
set(ENV{any} 1)
set(${x} 1)
set(${x}_a 1)
list(LENGTH UPPER out)
foreach(Item a b)
endforeach()
function(F_n Arg)
  set(Local 1)
  set(local 1)
  set(xy 1 PARENT_SCOPE)
endfunction()
macro(m)
  set(xy 1)
  set(XY 1)
endmacro()

options.description: Rows `command:position:class` (`command` may be `command FIRST-ARGUMENT`): the argument at the position (`0`, `-1` for the last, or `1+` for the rest) are names of the class; the class `variable` is told by `markers` and `scopes`.
options.name: names

options.description: Rows `WORD:class`: a command with the argument WORD (or the arguments `WORD WORD`, in a row) declares a variable of the class; the last row that fits wins.
options.name: markers

options.description: Rows `block:class`: a variable set inside the block that starts with the command `block` (the innermost listed one) has the class; the row with no block is the class outside them. An empty class is not checked.
options.name: scopes

options.description: Rows `class:regex`: the regex a name of the class must match from its start.
options.name: patterns

options.description: Where a reference to another name starts inside a name (`${` in CMake); the references, up to the matching `reference_end`, are cut out before the name is matched, and a name that is only references is left out.
options.name: reference_start

options.description: Where a reference ends (`}` in CMake).
options.name: reference_end

options.description: A regex; a name that matches is left out.
options.name: ignore_pattern

rules.why:
A naming convention is only useful when it holds everywhere: with it, a reader can tell from the name what kind of thing it is, and a search finds all of one kind. Without the option rows the rule checks nothing.

To fix, rename the variable or function.

rules.description: Reports a command listed in the option `commands` (for example `function` and `macro` in CMake, compared ignoring case) that has no comment on the line right before it, or whose comment has no text (`#` alone). A comment further up with a blank line between, or code in between, does not count. The option `doc_kinds` limits which comment kinds document (all by default); a comment of another kind counts as an empty one.

example.input:
# Does a thing.
function(a)
endfunction()

# Detached.

function(b)
endfunction()
#
macro(c)
endmacro()
set(d 1)
#[[ block ]]
function(e)
endfunction()
# Text.
#
function(f)
endfunction()

options.description: The commands that need a comment (case ignored).
options.name: commands

options.description: The kinds of comment token that document (none listed: every comment does); a comment of another kind counts as one with no text.
options.name: doc_kinds

rules.why:
A function or macro is called from other files, so a reader meets the name far from its definition. A comment right above it is the place where tools and readers look for what it takes and does.

To fix, write the comment on the line before the definition.

rules.description: Reports a heading written in another style than the document's: `#` before the text (ATX) or the text over a line of `=` or `-` (setext). The option `style` is `atx`, `setext` or `consistent` (the style of the first heading, the default). The fix rewrites a one-line heading of level 1 or 2.

example.fixed:
# Title

  # Section

  ## Sub

## Atx

  Two
  lines
  ---
example.input:
# Title

  Section
  =======

  Sub
  ---

## Atx

  Two
  lines
  ---

options.description: `atx`, `setext`, or `consistent` (the first heading's style).
options.name: style

options.description: The name of the grammar kind of a heading node.
options.name: kind

upstream.note: `consistent` only (the first heading's style); the fix writes a setext heading of one line as atx, the other way is not fixed. No `setext_with_atx` styles.

rules.why:
Two heading styles in one document make it look edited by different hands, and tools that search for headings (outlines, scripts) must know both. Only level 1 and 2 have a setext form, so ATX is the one style that works for every level.

To fix, use the style of the document; the fix does it for level 1 and 2.

rules.description: Reports a key that does not follow one of the allowed naming conventions of the option `allowed` (default `camelCase`; also `PascalCase`, `snake_case`, `kebab-case`, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE`). A key with punctuation or white space never matches; `camelCase` also rejects `_` and `-`, and `snake_case` and `kebab-case` reject capitals. Keys that match one of the `ignored_keys` regexes, and a YAML merge key (`<<`), are not checked. There is no fix, because renaming a key changes the data.

example.config:
key-name-casing:
  level: warn
  options:
    allowed: [snake_case, kebab-case]
    ignored_keys: ["^P"]
example.input: {"camelCase": 1, "snake_case": 2, "kebab-case": 3, "PascalCase": 4, "SCREAMING_SNAKE": 5, "a b": 6}

options.description: Accepted conventions: `camelCase`, `PascalCase`, `snake_case`, `kebab-case`, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE`. A key is fine when it matches one.
options.name: allowed

options.description: Regular expressions; matching keys stay where they are and are not compared.
options.name: ignored_keys

rules.why:
Configuration and data files are read by programs and people, and one casing for all keys lets both guess a key's name without looking it up. A key in another casing is often a typo or a copy from another file with other conventions.

To fix, rename the key and every place that reads it.

rules.description: Reports a line longer than `max` characters (default 120). With `allow_non_breakable_words` (default on) a line that has no space after its indentation, a leading `#` run or `- ` is not reported (a long URL); `allow_non_breakable_inline_mappings` also allows a YAML `key: value` line whose value has no space.

options.description: Longest allowed line, in characters.
options.name: max

options.description: Do not report a line that has no space after its indentation (and after a leading `#` run or `- `), such as a long URL.
options.name: allow_non_breakable_words

options.description: With `allow_non_breakable_words`, also do not report a `key: value` line whose value has no space. Only in languages that have such lines (YAML).
options.name: allow_non_breakable_inline_mappings

upstream.note: No ignore pattern for `package` and `import` lines.
ktlint_official allows 140 columns (the `max` option defaults to 120); no exemption for package, import and raw-string lines.
No exemptions for code blocks, tables and headings (`code_blocks`, `tables`, `headings`), no `strict`, `stern` or `line_length` per-language defaults.
no allow_non_breakable_words

rules.why:
Long lines do not fit next to each other in a diff or a code review, wrap unpredictably in narrow windows, and hide the end of the line when a view scrolls sideways. The limit is a convention of the project, set with `max`.

To fix, break the line at a natural place.

rules.description: Reports the modifiers of a declaration (`public`, `static`, `final`, `override`, ...) that are not in the order the style of the language wants: for Java the order of the Java Language Specification (`public protected private abstract default static sealed non-sealed final transient volatile synchronized native strictfp`), for Kotlin the order of the Kotlin coding conventions. Annotations and unknown keywords keep their place. The finding sits on the keyword that is out of place, or on the first modifier with the option `report: list`. The fix reorders the keywords.

options.description: Where a finding is reported: on the keyword that is out of place, or on the first token of the modifier list.
options.name: report

upstream.note: Annotations are not checked against the modifiers.
The shared rule over the `#modifiers` node; ktlint's order, annotations stay in place

rules.why:
Modifiers in a fixed order are easier to scan: the access level is always first, so a reader and a search for `public static` find every declaration alike. The order carries no meaning for the compiler, so no behaviour changes.

To fix, reorder the modifiers; the fix does it.

rules.description: Reports a key that a mapping has twice, after decoding escapes and quotes (`{"a": 1, "\u0061": 2}` has `a` twice). It reads the mappings of the language's grammar: JSON and JSONC objects, YAML and TOML mappings, JavaScript object literals, and similar entries of other languages. A YAML merge key (`<<`) may repeat, and the option `merge_keys: forbid` reports a second one too. The second key is reported, the first is shown as related.

options.description: Languages with a merge key (YAML `<<`) only. `allow` skips merge keys, which may repeat; `forbid` reports a second one like any other duplicate key.
options.name: merge_keys

upstream.note: partial
repeated `v-on` handlers and slots are allowed, and `class` next to `:class` is not a repeat

rules.why:
Parsers disagree on what a duplicate means: many keep the last value, some the first, some reject the file. The value that is lost is silent, so a file can mean something different in two tools, and the second entry is often a copy that was meant to have another name.

To fix, remove one of the keys, or give it its own name.

rules.description: Reports a section that has the same name as an earlier section of the file (INI and EditorConfig: the section header, for EditorConfig the glob).

example.input:
[*.cs]
indent_size = 4

[*.vb]
indent_size = 2

[*.cs]
tab_width = 4
[*.CS]
tab_width = 4

rules.why:
Readers of the format handle repeated sections in different ways: some merge them, some keep only the last, so the settings of one of them may be lost or applied in an order that is hard to see.

To fix, merge the two sections into one.

rules.description: Reports a comment with no text. An empty block comment (`/**/`) is reported wherever it is. An empty line comment is reported only when it begins or ends a run of comment lines, because a bare `//` between two comment lines separates paragraphs; the option `separators` reports those too.

options.description: Also report an empty line comment between two comments.
options.name: separators

rules.why:
An empty comment says nothing: it is a leftover of a deleted comment or of an unfinished one, and a reader stops to look for the meaning that is not there.

To fix, write the text or delete the comment.

rules.description: Reports a key that is empty or only white space after decoding escapes (`"": 4`).
rules.why:
A property with no name cannot be reached the usual ways: a dotted path, a command line option or an environment variable has no spelling for it, and some consumers fail on it. It is nearly always a missing name.

To fix, give the key a name.

rules.description: Reports a tab character in a line; a run of tabs is one report. The option `ignore_kinds` lists token kinds whose tabs are not reported (for example the code of a Markdown fence), and `indentation_only` reports only the tabs in the white space that starts a line.

example.input:
if(A)
  	set(x 1)
  set(y	2)
endif()

options.description: Kinds of tokens whose tabs are not reported (for example the code of a fence).
options.name: ignore_kinds

options.description: Report only the tabs in the whitespace that starts a line.
options.name: indentation_only

upstream.note: Reported on the tab run, as markdownlint does; no `spaces_per_tab` fix, no `ignore_code_languages`; `code_blocks` off is the option `ignore_kinds` naming the code tokens.

rules.why:
A tab is as wide as each reader's editor and tool makes it, so text that is aligned with tabs looks different in a diff, in a review and on the web. Spaces look the same everywhere. Some formats (YAML indentation) do not accept tabs at all.

To fix, replace the tab with spaces.

rules.description: Reports a block comment that fits on one line and ends its line (`/* text */`): it is written as a line comment. Documentation comments (`/**`), empty comments, comments with code after them on the same line and languages without a line comment marker are not reported. The fix turns it into a line comment.
rules.why:
A line comment is the plain form for a short note. A block comment on one line is usually left over from a longer comment, and the next edit adds a second line inside it.

To fix, use `// text`; the fix does it.

rules.description: Reports spaces or tabs at the end of a line, from the first one to the line break. Every language is checked the same way, so Markdown's two-space line break is reported too.

example.input:
text

fine

upstream.note: also reported inside pre and raw text
Also reports inside block scalars, where the content is data and the formatter keeps it.

rules.why:
Trailing white space cannot be seen, adds nothing, and many editors strip it, so a later edit shows a change on a line the author did not touch and makes diffs and blame noisy.

To fix, delete it.

rules.description: Removes a return type that the language gives every function with a block body anyway (`fun f(): Unit { }` in Kotlin; the types come from the option `redundant_return_types`). The functions are those with a block body, the type is the one after the colon that follows the parameters. The rule works in the formatter, which applies it when it is on (Kotlin has it on); `sudsy lint` makes no report for it.
rules.why:
The type says nothing the reader does not already know, and it makes the signature longer. `Unit` is what a block body returns when it has no `return` of a value.

To fix, delete the colon and the type; the formatter does it.

rules.description: Reports the items of a sequence that are not in order, for sequences of only strings or only numbers (ascending by default; numbers compare as numbers). A sequence of other or mixed items is skipped. The fewest items that would have to move are reported, and the first report carries the fix. The fix is unsafe: the order of a sequence can be data. Options: `direction`, `compare` (`ordinal`, `case_insensitive`, `natural`), `min_values` (default 2), `blank_line_groups` and `path_patterns` (only the sequences whose key path matches one).

example.config:
sorted-array-values:
  level: warn
  options:
    direction: desc

options.description: `asc` or `desc`.
options.name: direction

options.description: `ordinal` (code points), `case_insensitive`, or `natural` (digit runs compare as numbers: `a2` before `a10`).
options.name: compare

options.description: Sequences with fewer items are not checked.
options.name: min_values

options.description: Sort each run of entries between blank lines on its own.
options.name: blank_line_groups

options.description: Regular expressions; only mappings (sequences) whose key path matches one are checked. The path is `a.b[0].c` (`["odd key"]` for keys that are not identifiers), empty for the root; none listed means everywhere. A TOML table counts as its header key and an array table is not indexed.
options.name: path_patterns

upstream.note: one ordering per rule configuration (ESLint takes a list of {pathPattern, order} entries with different orders per path; use `overrides` per file instead); no `key` (sort objects by a property), no explicit value lists or `valuePattern`, mixed or non-scalar arrays are skipped, report positions when several equally short moves exist
Taplo sorts only values not separated by blank lines; the rule sorts the whole array.

rules.why:
A list that is kept sorted is easy to scan and to merge: new entries go to one place, and two branches that add different entries rarely conflict. The rule only makes sense where the order is not data, so it is off by default.

To fix, sort the items, or turn the rule off for that list with `path_patterns`.

rules.description: Reports the keys of a mapping that are not in order (alphabetical by default). By default the fewest keys that would have to move are reported (`report: moved`), `misplaced` reports every key that sorts before one above it. The first report carries the fix. Comments on lines of their own stay where they are and a comment after an entry moves with it. Options: `order` (keys that come first), `direction`, `compare` (`ordinal`, `case_insensitive`, `natural`), `ignored_keys`, `min_keys` (default 2), `blank_line_groups`, `path_patterns` and `has_properties` (only mappings that have all of these keys). The fix is unsafe: moving a YAML anchor below its alias breaks the document.

example.config:
sorted-keys:
  level: warn
  options:
    blank_line_groups: true

options.description: Keys that come first, in this order; the rest follow in the configured order.
options.name: order

options.description: `asc` or `desc`.
options.name: direction

options.description: `ordinal` (code points), `case_insensitive`, or `natural` (digit runs compare as numbers: `a2` before `a10`).
options.name: compare

options.description: Regular expressions; matching keys stay where they are and are not compared.
options.name: ignored_keys

options.description: Mappings with fewer keys are not checked.
options.name: min_keys

options.description: Sort each run of entries between blank lines on its own.
options.name: blank_line_groups

options.description: Regular expressions; only mappings (sequences) whose key path matches one are checked. The path is `a.b[0].c` (`["odd key"]` for keys that are not identifiers), empty for the root; none listed means everywhere. A TOML table counts as its header key and an array table is not indexed.
options.name: path_patterns

options.description: Only mappings that have all of these keys are checked.
options.name: has_properties

options.description: Which keys are reported. `moved`: the fewest keys that would have to move (eslint-plugin-jsonc). `misplaced`: every key that sorts before one above it (yamllint).
options.name: report

upstream.note: no groupByNesting; natural order is not guaranteed identical to Biome's for non-ASCII keys (unverified)

one ordering per rule configuration (ESLint's list of entries with different orders per path: use `overrides` per file); no per-key `keyPattern` orders and no `ignore` order type (`ignored_keys` is the closest); report positions when several equally short moves exist
Upstream picks the kinds to sort (fields, values, selections, variables, arguments, definitions) and a `groups` order; sorted-keys has no per-kind switch and does not sort definitions.
Taplo sorts only keys not separated by blank lines; the rule sorts the whole table.
A lint rule, not a formatter option.
no locale collation: yamllint's global `locale` uses the C library's collation; Sudsy offers `compare: ordinal | case_insensitive | natural` instead

rules.why:
Keys in a fixed order are quick to look up, and two branches that add different keys to a sorted file rarely conflict. The order of a mapping is usually not data, but where a tool reads it (a build order, a dependency list that is applied top down) the rule should be limited with `path_patterns` or turned off.

To fix, sort the keys; the fix does it.

rules.description: Reports more than `max` blank lines (default 1) right before a top-level statement (a direct child of the file that starts its line). The first statement of a file may have one more. Block arms and closers of the language (`else`, `endif`) are not checked. A line with only white space counts as blank. The finding is on the first token of the statement.

options.description: The longest run of blank lines allowed before a statement.
options.name: max

rules.why:
A run of blank lines is a visual gap that separates parts of a file. One blank line separates statements well, and more leave holes that make the file look as if something is missing.

To fix, delete the extra blank lines.

rules.description: Reports a statement, the closing parenthesis of a multi-line statement or a comment between statements that is not at the column that its block depth gives (depth times `size`, default 2) in a language whose files are a flat list of commands with block words such as `if` and `endif` (CMake). With `allow_unindented` a token in column 0 is accepted at any depth. A comment between statements may sit at the depth of the statement before or after it. The fix rewrites the white space before the token.

options.description: Columns per block depth.
options.name: size

options.description: Accept a token at column 0 whatever its depth.
options.name: allow_unindented

rules.why:
In a flat list of commands the indentation is the only sign of the blocks, because nothing but the block words delimit them. When it is wrong the reader sees a different nesting than the one that runs.

To fix, indent to the block depth; the fix does it.

rules.description: Reports a comment that disables rules of another tool (`# rubocop:disable Foo/Bar`) by a `Group/Name` whose group the tool does not have, for example the group of an extension that is not installed. A name inside a known group is not checked (the groups are listed in the grammar's `suppress directive-group` rows).

example.input:
x = :true
y = :ok
z = 'a #{b}'
"a #{1} #{x} #{[:a]}"
/(?<a>x)(y)/
/(?<a>x)(?:y)/
a = a
@b ||= @b
c = d
f == 0.1
f == 0
begin
  x
end while y
case x
when 1
when 2 then z
end
begin
  1
rescue Exception
end
begin
  1
rescue
end
# rubocop:disable Foo/Bar
h = { true: 1 }

upstream.note: only the unknown department of a cop name; not the other malformed directives or an unknown cop of a known department

rules.why:
A directive with a group the tool does not have does not suppress what the author expects, so the finding stays or the directive is ignored. It is usually a typo in the group name or an extension that is missing in the project.

To fix, correct the name, or install the extension.

rules.description: Reports a number that a double-precision parser (JavaScript and most JSON libraries) cannot hold exactly: an integer beyond 2^53 - 1, a value that overflows to infinity, or one that underflows to zero or is subnormal.

upstream.note: lone UTF-16 surrogates in strings are not reported

rules.why:
JSON allows any number of digits, but most parsers read numbers as 64-bit floating point. A large integer such as an id then changes silently (`12345678901234567890` becomes `12345678901234567000`), and `1e999` becomes infinity, so the receiver sees a different value from the one that was written.

To fix, write the value as a string.

rules.description: Reports the alpha value of `rgb()`, `hsl()`, `hwb()`, `lab()`, `lch()`, `oklab()`, `oklch()` or `color()` written as a number (`/ 0.5`), also the fourth argument of the comma form of `rgba()` and `hsla()`, on the function name. A percentage is not reported.
rules.why:
An alpha value can be a number or a percentage, and a file that mixes both makes the reader convert in the head: `0.5` and `50%` are the same. The rule keeps one notation, the percentage, which reads as a share of opacity and matches how the channels of `hsl()` are written.

To fix, write `/ 50%` instead of `/ 0.5`.

rules.description: Reports an `@extend` of anything but a placeholder selector (`%name`); a selector with interpolation is not reported.
rules.why:
Extending a class or an element rewrites every selector that mentions it, so one `@extend` can add many selectors to the output and change the cascade of rules that are far from it. A placeholder exists only to be extended, so the effect is local.

To fix, extend a placeholder, or use a mixin.

rules.description: Reports a `@function` whose name does not match the `pattern` option (a regex). An empty pattern allows everything.

options.description: The regex a function name must match.
options.name: pattern

rules.why: A naming convention for Sass functions keeps them predictable, so one can be guessed and searched for. The rule is a policy: with no `pattern` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports an `@if` that compares with `null` (`== null`, `!= null`).
rules.why:
In Sass `null` and `false` are falsy and everything else is truthy, so `$a == null` is written more directly as `not $a`, and `$a != null` as `$a`. The shorter form also treats `false` the way a condition does.

To fix, use `@if not $a` or `@if $a`.

rules.description: Reports an `@include` of a mixin with empty parentheses (`@include foo()`). A `using (...)` clause after them is not reported.
rules.why:
Sass allows `@include foo` and `@include foo()` for a mixin without arguments. Empty parentheses add noise and suggest arguments that are not there.

To fix, delete the `()`.

rules.description: Reports a `@mixin` whose name does not match the `pattern` option (a regex). An empty pattern allows everything.

options.description: The regex a mixin name must match.
options.name: pattern

rules.why: A naming convention for mixins keeps them predictable, so one can be guessed and searched for. The rule is a policy: with no `pattern` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports an at-rule that is not in the `list` option (a vendor prefix is left out of the name). An empty list allows everything.

options.description: The allowed at-rules, without `@`: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can limit the at-rules of its stylesheets, for example to keep `@import` out of a bundle. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports the condition of an `@if`, `@else if` or `@while` that is written in parentheses (`@if ($a == 1)`).
rules.why:
In Sass the condition ends at the block, so the parentheses do nothing; they come from the languages where they are needed, and they add noise.

To fix, delete the parentheses.

rules.description: Reports an at-rule that is in the `list` option (a vendor prefix is left out of the name).

options.description: The disallowed at-rules, without `@`: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can forbid an at-rule, such as `@import`, that costs a request per file or that its build does not support. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports an at-rule with no empty line before it. The first at-rule of a block, one right after a comment, and a blockless at-rule right after a blockless one of the same name (a run of `@import` lines) need none. `@else` is not checked.
rules.why: Blank lines separate the blocks of a stylesheet, so an `@media` or `@include` that follows a declaration or a rule stays visible as its own unit. A run of `@import` or `@use` lines is one list and stays together.

rules.description: Reports a deprecated at-rule (`@document`, `@nest`, `@viewport`).

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

rules.why:
A deprecated at-rule was removed or is being removed from browsers, so a stylesheet that depends on it stops working there. A replacement exists or the feature was dropped.

To fix, use the replacement named in the specification, for example `&` nesting for `@nest`.

rules.description: Reports an at-rule that no CSS specification lists. Vendor-prefixed ones are not reported; SCSS has its own (`@include`, `@mixin`, ...) and Less at-rules are not checked. Tailwind's are left out by default; the `ignore` option lists more.

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

upstream.note: Less at-rules are not told apart (detached ruleset calls look like at-rules), so none is reported in Less.
Less at-rules are not told apart (detached ruleset calls look like at-rules), so none is reported in Less.

rules.why:
An unknown at-rule is a typo or a rule that the browser does not implement, and the browser skips the whole block it opens, so a large part of the stylesheet can be dropped.

To fix, correct the name.

rules.description: Reports a vendor-prefixed at-rule that has a standard one (`@-webkit-keyframes`).

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

rules.why:
A prefixed at-rule was a way to try a feature before it was standardised. Browsers support the standard name now, so the prefixed one repeats the whole block for nothing.

To fix, use the standard at-rule.

rules.description: Reports a rule or at-rule block with nothing in it, comments included.
rules.why:
An empty block does nothing. It is a leftover of a deleted declaration or a placeholder that was never filled, and it adds bytes and noise to the file.

To fix, delete the rule, or put the declarations in it.

rules.description: Reports `rgba()` and `hsla()`, the legacy names of `rgb()` and `hsl()`, on the function name.
rules.why:
Since Color Level 4 `rgb()` and `hsl()` take an optional alpha value, so the `a` names are aliases that exist only for old code. Two names for one function make a stylesheet read as two styles.

To fix, write `rgb(0 0 0 / 50%)` instead of `rgba(0 0 0 / 50%)`.

rules.description: Reports `rgb()`, `rgba()`, `hsl()` or `hsla()` with the legacy comma-separated arguments (`rgb(0, 0, 0)`), also when one argument is a call such as `var()`. The space-separated form (`rgb(0 0 0)`) is not reported.
rules.why:
The modern notation separates the channels with spaces and the alpha value with `/`, the way every other color function of Color Level 4 (`lab()`, `oklch()`, `color()`) does, so one rule of writing covers them all. The comma form is kept only for old browsers.

To fix, replace the commas with spaces and put `/` before the alpha value.

rules.description: Reports a hex color that can be written with three or four digits (`#aabbcc`). With the `style` option set to `long`, a color written short is reported instead.

options.description: `short` reports colors that can be shortened, `long` those that are short.
options.name: style

rules.why:
One length for hex colors keeps a file uniform, and the short form is the usual one: it is half the bytes and still unambiguous.

To fix, shorten each pair of equal digits to one.

rules.description: Reports a hex color (`#fff`).
rules.why:
Some projects use named colors or functions only, so a color can be told by its name or channels, not by a code that has to be decoded. The rule is a policy for those; it is off by default.

To fix, write the color as a name or with `rgb()`, `hsl()` or another function.

rules.description: Reports a hex color that does not have 3, 4, 6 or 8 digits (`#ab`).
rules.why:
CSS accepts only those lengths, so the declaration is invalid and the browser drops it, and the element is left with the inherited or default color.

To fix, correct the number of digits.

rules.description: Reports a `/* */` comment on a line of its own with no empty line before it. One that is first in its block, on the line of code, or a directive comment is not reported. A `//` comment is another rule's.

upstream.note: `//` comments are left to double-slash-comment-empty-line-before, as stylelint ignores them

rules.why: A comment describes what follows, and an empty line before it ties it to the next rule rather than to the end of the previous one.

rules.description: Reports a `@container` name that does not match the `pattern` option (a regex). An empty pattern allows everything.

options.description: The regex a container name must match.
options.name: pattern

rules.why: Container names are global to the page, so a convention keeps them predictable and lowers the risk of two components using one name. The rule is a policy: with no `pattern` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a `@custom-media` name, without its `--`, that does not match the `pattern` option (a regex). An empty pattern allows everything.

options.description: The regex a custom media name, without its `--`, must match.
options.name: pattern

rules.why: A naming convention for custom media queries keeps the breakpoints of a project predictable. The rule is a policy: with no `pattern` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a custom property declaration with no empty line before it. One that is first in its block, right after a comment or another custom property, or in a single-line block is not reported.

example.config:
dollar-variable-empty-line-before: warn
custom-property-empty-line-before: warn
double-slash-comment-empty-line-before: warn
no-empty-comment: { level: warn, options: { separators: true } }

rules.why: Custom properties are the variables of a block, and a gap before the first of them sets them off from the ordinary declarations, so a reader finds the values a block defines.

rules.description: Reports a custom property that the file declares, used in a value without `var()` (`calc(--x * 2)`), on the property name. Properties that take names (`transition`, `will-change`, ...) are not reported.
rules.why:
`--x` in a value is a plain identifier, not the value of the custom property, so the declaration is invalid or means something else.

To fix, write `var(--x)`.

rules.description: Reports a custom property whose name, without the `--`, does not match the `pattern` option (a regex), where it is declared, used in `var()` or named by `@property`. An empty pattern allows everything.

options.description: The regex a custom property name, without its `--`, must match.
options.name: pattern

rules.why: A naming convention for custom properties makes the variables of a design system predictable, so a name can be guessed and searched for. The rule is a policy: with no `pattern` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a custom property declared twice in one block (names are case sensitive), on the repeat.
rules.why:
The later declaration of a custom property wins and the earlier one is lost, so the value that a reader sees first is not the value `var()` returns. It is almost always a copy and paste mistake.

To fix, delete one of the declarations or rename it.

rules.description: Reports a property declared twice in one block, on the earlier declaration (on the later one when only the earlier one is `!important`). `src` and custom properties are not reported. With `ignore_consecutive_different_values` a repeat right after the same property with another value is left alone.

options.description: Leave a repeat right after the same property with another value alone (`display: -webkit-box; display: flex`).
options.name: ignore_consecutive_different_values

rules.why:
The later declaration replaces the earlier one, so the earlier one does nothing. Most often it is a copy and paste mistake or a leftover of an edit, and the author reads the wrong value as the one in force.

To fix, delete the declaration that is not meant to apply. A deliberate fallback for old browsers (`display: -webkit-box; display: flex`) can stay with `ignore_consecutive_different_values`.

rules.description: Reports a shorthand property declared after one of its longhands in the same block (`margin-top: 1px; margin: 0`), on the longhand.
rules.why:
The shorthand sets every longhand it stands for, so it overwrites the earlier longhand. The longhand does nothing, and the author probably meant it to apply on top of the shorthand.

To fix, put the longhand after the shorthand.

rules.description: Reports a block written on one line that has more declarations than the `max` option.

options.description: The most declarations a single-line block may have.
options.name: max

upstream.note: differs from stylelint on single-line @font-face blocks

rules.why: A single-line block is easy to scan only while it is short; with many declarations the line becomes long, and a diff shows the whole line as changed. A limit (often 1) moves the rest to separate lines.

rules.description: Reports a declaration that follows a rule or at-rule and has no empty line before it. A declaration after another declaration, one first in its block, one right after a comment, one in a single-line block, and custom properties and variables are not reported.
rules.why: Declarations that come after a nested rule belong to the parent again, and without a gap they read as part of the nested block. An empty line shows the return to the parent.

rules.description: Reports a declaration that ends in `!important`.
rules.why:
`!important` breaks the cascade: only another `!important` with higher specificity can override it, so each use makes the next override harder and the stylesheet drifts into an arms race. Specificity and source order should decide.

To fix, raise the specificity of the selector that should win, or reorder the rules.

rules.description: Reports a `$variable` declaration with no empty line before it. One that is first in its block, right after a comment or another `$` variable, or in a single-line block is not reported.

example.config:
dollar-variable-empty-line-before: warn
custom-property-empty-line-before: warn
double-slash-comment-empty-line-before: warn
no-empty-comment: { level: warn, options: { separators: true } }

rules.why: A group of Sass variables is the settings of a block, and a gap before it sets it off from the rules and declarations around, so the settings are easy to find.

rules.description: Reports a `$name` declaration whose name, without the `$`, does not match the `pattern` option (a regex). An empty pattern allows everything.

options.description: The regex a variable name, without its `$`, must match.
options.name: pattern

rules.why: A naming convention for Sass variables keeps the variables of a project predictable. The rule is a policy: with no `pattern` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a `//` comment on a line of its own with no empty line before it. One that is first in its block, right after another comment, on the line of code, or a directive comment is not reported.

example.config:
dollar-variable-empty-line-before: warn
custom-property-empty-line-before: warn
double-slash-comment-empty-line-before: warn
no-empty-comment: { level: warn, options: { separators: true } }

rules.why: A comment describes what follows, and an empty line before it ties it to the next rule rather than to the end of the previous one.

rules.description: Reports a quoted font family name that is also valid without quotes (`"Arial"`, `"Open Sans"`).

upstream.note: does not report a name that is missing a quote it needs (`always-where-required`)

rules.why:
A family name that is a sequence of identifiers (`Open Sans`) needs no quotes, and quoted and unquoted names then mean the same. Quotes stay for the names that are not identifiers, such as one that starts with a digit.

To fix, delete the quotes.

rules.description: Reports a family that appears twice in one `font-family` list, on the repeat.
rules.why:
The second entry is never reached: the browser has already tried that font. It is a copy and paste mistake that hides the fallback order.

To fix, delete the repeat.

rules.description: Reports a `font-family` (or `font`) list that has no generic family (`serif`, `sans-serif`, `monospace`, ...). `@font-face` is not checked.
rules.why:
When none of the named fonts is installed, the browser uses its default font, which can be a serif face on a page designed for sans-serif. A generic family at the end tells it which kind of face to fall back on.

To fix, end the list with the generic family that fits the first font.

rules.description: Reports a function that is not in the `list` option. An empty list allows everything.

options.description: The allowed functions: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can limit the functions its stylesheets call to the ones its browsers support or its design system allows. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports `+` and `-` inside `calc()` that lack whitespace on one or both sides (`calc(1px+2px)`), on the operator.
rules.why:
CSS requires whitespace around `+` and `-` in `calc()`; `1px+2px` is read as a number with a sign, not as a sum, so the whole declaration is invalid and the browser drops it. `*` and `/` do not need the space.

To fix, put a space on each side of the operator.

rules.description: Reports a function that is in the `list` option.

options.description: The disallowed functions: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can forbid a function that its browsers do not support or that its design system replaces. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a `linear-gradient()` that starts with a side keyword (`top`, `left bottom`) instead of `to top` or an angle.
rules.why:
Before the standard, prefixed gradients named the side the gradient starts from. The standard names the side it goes to, so `top` and `to top` mean opposite directions. Code copied from the old notation draws the gradient reversed or is dropped.

To fix, write `to bottom` for a gradient that starts at the top, or use an angle.

rules.description: Reports a function name with capitals (`RGB()`). Names such as `translateX` that are written in camel case in the specification keep theirs.
rules.why: CSS reads function names without regard to case, so capitals add spellings of the same name. A file that writes them in lowercase only is easier to search and read.

rules.description: Reports a function in a declaration value that no CSS specification lists. SCSS and Less are not checked, because their built-in functions are not in the table. The `ignore` option lists names to leave out.

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

upstream.note: SCSS and Less built-in functions are not in the table, so none is reported there.
SCSS and Less built-in functions are not in the table, so none is reported there.

rules.why:
An unknown function is a typo or a function that the browser does not implement, and the declaration is dropped without an error.

To fix, correct the name.

rules.description: Reports an unquoted `url(...)`.

upstream.note: differs from stylelint on url() inside image-set()

rules.why:
An unquoted url has to escape spaces, parentheses and quotes, and a file name that has one of these breaks the declaration. A quoted url can hold any character, so the habit of quoting never breaks.

To fix, wrap the argument in quotes.

rules.description: Reports the hue of `hsl()`, `hsla()`, `hwb()`, `lch()` or `oklch()` written as a bare number (`120`), on the function name. A hue with a unit (`120deg`) is not reported.
rules.why:
A hue is an angle, and without a unit `120` does not say if it is degrees, radians or turns; CSS reads it as degrees, but the next reader has to know that. Writing `120deg` makes the value self-describing and matches the other angle properties.

To fix, add `deg` to the number.

rules.description: Reports an `@import` written in the notation the `url` option does not ask for: by default a string, so `url(...)` is reported; with `url: true`, `url(...)`, so a string is reported.

options.description: Ask for url() instead of a string.
options.name: url

rules.why: One notation for imports keeps the file uniform and easy to search. The string form is shorter; the `url()` form is the one that the older tools and bundlers read.

rules.description: Reports a selector that is used twice in one `@keyframes` rule (`from` and `FROM` count as the same, names are compared in lowercase).
rules.why:
Keyframes with the same offset are merged by the browser in order, and the later declarations win for the same property. The animation then differs from what the first block says.

To fix, merge the two blocks.

rules.description: Reports `!important` in a declaration of a `@keyframes` rule.
rules.why:
A declaration with `!important` in a keyframe is ignored, so the property does not animate, and no error tells you.

To fix, delete the `!important`.

rules.description: Reports `from` and `to` in a `@keyframes` that also uses percentages. A block with nothing but keywords is not reported.
rules.why:
`from` is `0%` and `to` is `100%`, so mixing the forms in one animation makes the reader translate. With percentages the animation reads as a timeline.

To fix, write `0%` and `100%`.

rules.description: Reports a `@keyframes` name that does not match the `pattern` option (a regex). An empty pattern allows everything.

options.description: The regex a keyframes name must match.
options.name: pattern

rules.why: Animation names are global to the page, so a convention (a prefix, kebab case) keeps them predictable and lowers the risk of two animations having the same name. The rule is a policy: with no `pattern` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a `@layer` name that does not match the `pattern` option (a regex). An empty pattern allows everything.

options.description: The regex a layer name must match.
options.name: pattern

rules.why: Layer names fix the order of the cascade across a project and its libraries, so a convention keeps them predictable and collisions rare. The rule is a policy: with no `pattern` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a zero length written with a unit (`0px`). Dimensions that are not lengths (`0s`, `0deg`), and anything inside a function, are not reported.
rules.why:
Zero is the same in every length unit, so the unit says nothing and costs bytes. Inside `calc()` and the like the unit may be needed, so those are left alone, as are times and angles, where a unit is required.

To fix, write `0`.

rules.description: Reports a `@use`, `@forward` or `@import` of a partial with a leading underscore (`@use 'a/_b'`). CSS imports are not reported.
rules.why:
Sass looks the partial up without the underscore, so the underscore is noise that makes a path look like a different file.

To fix, write the name without the underscore: `@use 'a/b'`.

rules.description: Reports a rule or at-rule nested inside more rules or at-rules than the `max` option.

options.description: How deep rules may nest.
options.name: max

rules.why: Nested rules multiply: three levels of nesting give a selector that is the product of three, with high specificity and tied to the markup. Deep nesting also makes the file hard to read. A limit keeps nesting shallow.

rules.description: Reports a media feature that is not in the `list` option. An empty list allows everything.

options.description: The allowed media features: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can limit the media features of its queries to the ones its design uses. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a media feature that is in the `list` option.

options.description: The disallowed media features: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can forbid media features that its browsers do not support or that its breakpoints replace. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a media feature name in `@media` that is not a CSS one; vendor-prefixed names are not reported.

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

rules.why:
An unknown media feature makes the query false, so the block is never applied, and no error tells you.

To fix, correct the name.

rules.description: Reports a vendor-prefixed `device-pixel-ratio` media feature (`-webkit-min-device-pixel-ratio`).

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

rules.why:
The standard media feature is `resolution`, and the prefixed names are supported only by old engines. The standard one works in every current browser.

To fix, use `min-resolution: 2dppx`.

rules.description: Reports a deprecated media type (`tv`, `handheld`, `projection`, ...) in `@media`.

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

rules.why:
Media Queries Level 4 deprecates these types, and browsers match them as never true, so a block that depends on one never applies.

To fix, use a media feature (`width`, `pointer`) that tells the same thing, or delete the block.

rules.description: Reports a `grid-template-areas` whose rows differ in length, are empty, or hold an area that is not a rectangle.
rules.why:
The browser drops the whole `grid-template-areas` declaration when its table is not a rectangle of named cells, and every item placed by area then falls into an automatic cell.

To fix, give every row the same number of cells and make each area a rectangle.

rules.description: Reports a rule whose selector ends in the same compound selector (not counting its pseudo-classes) as an earlier rule in the same at-rule, and has a lower specificity. Nested rules are not compared.
rules.why:
For the same element the rule with higher specificity wins, whatever its place. A later rule with lower specificity (`a:hover` before `a`) never applies to what the earlier one covers, which is almost never what the author meant.

To fix, move the rule with the lower specificity up, or raise its specificity.

rules.description: Reports an `@import` that repeats an earlier one in the same file (same url, same media list; `'a.css'` and `url(a.css)` are the same url).
rules.why:
The second import is wasted: the browser fetches the file once, and the stylesheet is still parsed twice in some engines. It also hides which of the two position in the cascade is meant.

To fix, delete the repeat.

rules.description: Reports a selector list that is already used by an earlier rule in the same block or file; the order of the selectors in the list does not matter (`b, a` repeats `a, b`).
rules.why:
Rules with the same selector are one rule written twice. The declarations end up apart, so a later change to one of them is easy to make in the wrong place, and the cascade between the two is hard to follow.

To fix, merge the declarations into the first rule.

rules.description: Reports a file with nothing but whitespace. A file with only comments is not empty.
rules.why: An empty stylesheet is a mistake: either the content was lost or the file is not needed. A build that imports it then loads a file that does nothing.

rules.description: Reports a call of a Sass global function that a module of the standard library replaces (`map-get` is `map.get`, `mix` is `color.mix`); calls written with their module are not reported.

options.description: `name=replacement` entries: a global function and the module function that replaces it.
options.name: list

rules.why:
Sass deprecates the global functions in favour of modules loaded with `@use`, and drops them in a later major version. A call of a module function says where it comes from and is not changed by a global of the same name.

To fix, `@use "sass:map"` and call `map.get`.

rules.description: Reports a rule or declaration that starts with `//`.
rules.why:
CSS has no line comments. The browser reads `// note` as part of the next statement, so the selector or the property name is wrong and the rule or declaration is dropped. The comment seems to work and breaks the line below it.

To fix, write the comment as `/* note */`. Sass and Less read `//` as a comment, so there it is not reported.

rules.description: Reports an `@import` that comes after a rule that is not `@charset`, `@layer` or another `@import`.

example.input:
.a { color: red }
@import "a";

rules.why:
CSS ignores an `@import` that is not at the top of the stylesheet, so the file it names is never loaded and the styles silently are missing. There is no error in the browser.

To fix, move the `@import` above every rule, behind `@charset` and `@layer`.

rules.description: Reports a declaration at the top of a file, or in an at-rule such as `@media` that is not inside a rule.
rules.why:
CSS has declarations only inside a rule. At the top of a file the declaration is a syntax error and the browser skips it and the text up to the next `}` or `;`, which may take the next rule with it.

To fix, put the declaration in a rule.

rules.description: Reports a number with more decimal places than the `max` option.

options.description: The most decimal places a number may have.
options.name: max

upstream.note: numbers in a Less variable declaration (an at-rule prelude) are not checked, named gap

rules.why:
Long decimals (`1.23456789px`) are almost always the output of a calculator, and a browser rounds lengths to a fraction of a pixel anyway, so the extra digits only add bytes and noise.

To fix, round the number to the precision that is needed.

rules.description: Reports a property that is not in the `list` option (names, or `/regex/`). Custom properties are not reported, and an empty list allows everything.

options.description: The allowed properties: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can limit the properties its styles use, for example to a design system's set, so a one-off property fails in review rather than later in the browser. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a property that is in the `list` option (names, or `/regex/`). Custom properties are not reported.

options.description: The disallowed properties: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can forbid properties that its browsers or its design system do not support, or that cause layout trouble (`float` in a flex design). The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a deprecated property (`clip`, `word-wrap`, `grid-gap`, the `box-*` properties of the old flexbox, ...).

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

upstream.note: `-webkit-box-orient` is not reported (stylelint reports it unless the value is `vertical`), and there is no fix.

rules.why:
A deprecated property is replaced by another one, and browsers keep it working only for old pages. New code should use the replacement, which gets the fixes and new values.

To fix, use the replacement: `overflow-wrap` for `word-wrap`, `gap` for `grid-gap`, `clip-path` for `clip`.

rules.description: Reports a property that no CSS specification lists. Vendor-prefixed and custom properties, descriptors of `@font-face` and the like, and names with interpolation or SCSS and Less variables are not reported. The option `ignore` lists names to leave out.

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

rules.why:
An unknown property is almost always a typo (`colour`) or a property that is not yet supported, and the browser drops the declaration without an error, so the style is silently missing.

To fix, correct the name.

rules.description: Reports a vendor-prefixed property that has a standard property (`-webkit-transition`). The `ignore` option lists names to leave out.

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

upstream.note: `-webkit-background-size` with several values is reported (stylelint skips it).

rules.why:
Prefixed properties were the way to try a feature before it was standardised. Browsers support the standard name now, so the prefixed one is dead weight, and tools that add prefixes where needed (autoprefixing in a build) do it better.

To fix, delete the prefixed property or use the standard one.

rules.description: Reports a rule whose block spans several lines and has no empty line before it. A rule that is first in its block, and one right after a comment, need none.
rules.why: An empty line between rules shows where one rule ends and the next starts, and keeps a long file scannable. A rule that opens a block has nothing to be separated from, and a comment belongs to the rule below it.

rules.description: Reports an `:nth-child()` and the like whose `An+B` can never match (`0`, `0n`, `-n`, `-2n-1`).
rules.why:
The selector matches no element, so the rule does nothing. It is a miscalculated formula, or a leftover of a larger one.

To fix, correct the formula; `-n+3` matches the first three.

rules.description: Reports an attribute selector whose name is in the `list` option.

options.description: The disallowed attribute names: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can forbid selecting on an attribute such as `style`, whose value is generated or changes without notice. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports an attribute selector operator that is not in the `list` option. An empty list allows everything.
rules.why: A project can limit the attribute operators of its selectors to the ones it understands, since `~=`, `|=` and `*=` match in ways that are easy to misread. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports an attribute selector operator that is in the `list` option.

example.input: ul.nav, a[x~=y], a[x=y], b > c {}

options.description: The disallowed operators (`=`, `~=`, `|=`, `^=`, `$=`, `*=`).
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can forbid an operator, such as `*=`, whose substring match is easy to misread or slow. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports an attribute selector whose value is not quoted (`[a=b]`).
rules.why:
An unquoted value must be a valid identifier, so a value with a space, a digit at the start or a punctuation mark makes the selector invalid and the rule is dropped. Always quoting avoids the trap.

To fix, wrap the value in quotes: `[a="b"]`.

rules.description: Reports a class selector whose name does not match the `pattern` option (a regex). An empty pattern allows everything.

options.description: The regex a class name must match.
options.name: pattern

rules.why: A naming convention for classes (kebab case, BEM) makes them predictable, so you can guess a class and search for it. The rule is a policy: with no `pattern` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a combinator (`>`, `+`, `~`, or a space for the descendant combinator) that is not in the `list` option. An empty list allows everything.

options.description: The allowed combinators.
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can limit which relations between elements its selectors may use, for example to keep selectors short and fast to match. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a combinator (`>`, `+`, `~`, or a space for the descendant combinator) that is in the `list` option.

options.description: The disallowed combinators.
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can forbid a combinator, for example the descendant combinator, which ties a rule to the depth of the markup. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a rule whose selector list, with whitespace collapsed, is in the `list` option (selectors, or `/regex/`).

example.input: ul.nav, a[x~=y], a[x=y], b > c {}

options.description: The disallowed selectors: text, or `/regex/`.
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can forbid selectors that cause trouble, such as `*` or a bare element, which restyle everything. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports an id selector whose name does not match the `pattern` option (a regex). An empty pattern allows everything.

options.description: The regex an id name must match.
options.name: pattern

rules.why: A naming convention for ids makes them predictable, so you can guess one and search for it. The rule is a policy: with no `pattern` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a selector with more attribute selectors than the `max` option.

options.description: The most attribute selectors a selector may have.
options.name: max

rules.why: Each attribute selector adds the specificity of a class and one more thing to match, so a limit keeps rules short and easy to override.

rules.description: Reports a selector with more class selectors than the `max` option; classes inside `:not()` and the like count.

options.description: The most classes a selector may have.
options.name: max

rules.why: Every class in a selector is one more thing that must match, so a rule with many classes has high specificity and is hard to override and tied to the markup. A limit keeps selectors short.

rules.description: Reports a selector with more combinators than the `max` option; a space between two compound selectors counts.

options.description: The most combinators a selector may have.
options.name: max

upstream.note: differs from stylelint on :nth-child(An+B of S) selector lists

rules.why: Every combinator ties the rule to one more level of the markup, so deep selectors break when the markup changes and are slow to read and match. A limit keeps selectors shallow.

rules.description: Reports a selector with more compound selectors (parts between combinators) than the `max` option.

options.description: The most compound selectors a selector may have.
options.name: max

rules.why: A selector with many compound parts describes a long path through the markup. It breaks when the markup changes and has to be matched from right to left on every element. A limit keeps it shallow.

rules.description: Reports a selector with more id selectors than the `max` option.

options.description: The most ids a selector may have.
options.name: max

rules.why: An id adds more specificity than any number of classes, so a rule with ids can only be overridden by another id or by `!important`. A limit (often 0) keeps the specificity of a project flat.

rules.description: Reports a selector with more pseudo-classes than the `max` option.

options.description: The most pseudo-classes a selector may have.
options.name: max

rules.why: Each pseudo-class adds the specificity of a class and a state that must hold, so a long chain such as `a:hover:focus:active` is hard to override and hard to read. A limit keeps selectors simple.

rules.description: Reports a selector with more type selectors than the `max` option.

options.description: The most type selectors a selector may have.
options.name: max

rules.why: A selector made of many element names (`div ul li a`) is tied to the markup and breaks when an element is wrapped or changed. A limit pushes the styling to classes.

rules.description: Reports a selector with more `*` than the `max` option.

options.description: The most universal selectors a selector may have.
options.name: max

rules.why: The universal selector matches everything, so each one widens the rule, and `* *` can cost time on large pages. A limit keeps such selectors rare.

rules.description: Reports a deprecated pseudo-class, pseudo-element or HTML or SVG element used as a type selector (`center {}`).

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

rules.why:
A deprecated selector targets something that the standard removed, so it matches less and less over time, and browsers may drop it.

To fix, use the replacement named in the specification.

rules.description: Reports a type selector in the same compound as a class, id or attribute selector (`ul.nav`).
rules.why:
The element name adds specificity and ties the rule to one element: changing `ul` to `ol` breaks the style, while `.nav` would have kept working.

To fix, delete the type selector.

rules.description: Reports a vendor-prefixed pseudo-class or pseudo-element that has a standard one (`::-moz-selection`).

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

rules.why:
A prefixed selector was a way to try a feature before it was standardised. Browsers support the standard name now, so the prefixed one is dead weight that a build step can add where it is needed.

To fix, use the standard selector.

rules.description: Reports a pseudo-class that is not in the `list` option. An empty list allows everything.

options.description: The allowed pseudo-classes, without `:`: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can limit the pseudo-classes of its selectors, for example to the ones its browsers support. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a pseudo-class that is in the `list` option.

options.description: The disallowed pseudo-classes, without `:`: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can forbid a pseudo-class that its browsers do not support or that is slow on large pages. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a pseudo-class that is not a CSS one. Vendor-prefixed ones are not reported, and the `-webkit-scrollbar` pseudo-classes count after those pseudo-elements.

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

rules.why:
A selector with an unknown pseudo-class is invalid, and the browser drops the whole rule, not only the pseudo-class. A typo (`:hovr`) therefore removes the style for every selector in the list.

To fix, correct the name.

rules.description: Reports a pseudo-element that is not in the `list` option. An empty list allows everything.

options.description: The allowed pseudo-elements, without colons: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can limit the pseudo-elements of its selectors, for example to the ones its browsers support. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports `:before`, `:after`, `:first-line` or `:first-letter` written with one colon.
rules.why:
CSS3 separated pseudo-elements from pseudo-classes with two colons so the reader can tell them apart. The single colon is kept only for old browsers, and a file that mixes both is inconsistent.

To fix, write `::before`.

rules.description: Reports a pseudo-element that is in the `list` option.

options.description: The disallowed pseudo-elements, without colons: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can forbid a pseudo-element that its browsers do not support or that its design avoids. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a pseudo-element that is not a CSS one. Vendor-prefixed ones are not reported.

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

rules.why:
A selector with an unknown pseudo-element is invalid, and the browser drops the whole rule.

To fix, correct the name.

rules.description: Reports a type selector with capitals (`A {}`).

upstream.note: differs from stylelint on camelCase SVG element names (clipPath)

rules.why:
HTML element names are matched without regard to case, so `A` and `a` select the same elements and capitals only add spellings. Lowercase is the convention and the one the markup uses.

To fix, write the selector in lowercase.

rules.description: Reports a type selector that is not an HTML, SVG or MathML element; custom elements are accepted. Keyframe selectors and the arguments of `:lang()`, `:nth-child()` and the like are not reported.

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

rules.why:
An unknown type selector never matches, so the rule does nothing. It is almost always a typo (`dvi`) or a class that lost its dot.

To fix, correct the name or add the missing `.` or `#`.

rules.description: Reports a `margin`, `padding`, `border-color`, `border-style`, `border-width` or `border-radius` with two, three or four values that repeat (`1px 1px` is `1px`).
rules.why:
CSS fills the missing values of these shorthands by repeating the others, so the longer form says the same as the shorter one. The short form is easier to read and cannot have one value changed by mistake.

To fix, delete the values that the shorthand repeats by itself.

rules.description: Reports a unit (`%` included) that is not in the `list` option, in values and at-rule preludes. An empty list allows everything.

options.description: The allowed units: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can fix the units its layout uses (`rem` and `%`, not `px`), so lengths scale the same way throughout. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a unit (`%` included) that is in the `list` option, in values and at-rule preludes.

options.description: The disallowed units: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: list

rules.why: A project can forbid a unit that does not fit its design, for example `px` where text has to follow the user's font size. The rule is a policy: with no `list` it reports nothing.

rules.description: Reports a unit that is not a CSS unit, in values and `@media` preludes. `x` is accepted only in `image-set()`, `image-resolution` and `resolution` media features. The `ignore` option lists more names.

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

rules.why:
An unknown unit (`1foo`, or `10pxx` by a typo) makes the declaration invalid, and the browser drops it without an error.

To fix, correct the unit.

rules.description: Reports a vendor-prefixed keyword or function that has a standard value (`-webkit-flex`).

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

rules.why:
A prefixed value was a way to try a feature before it was standardised. Browsers support the standard value now, so the prefixed one is dead weight that a build step can add where it is needed.

To fix, use the standard value.

rules.description: Reports an equality or inequality with a boolean literal on either side (`x == true`, `x !== false`, `true == x`, `x != False`). The option `literals` lists the texts that count as boolean literals, `not_operators` the operators that are not a comparison of value (Python `is`). Off by default.

example.input:
x = 1
x == True
x != False
True == x
x is True
x == 1

options.description: The texts that are boolean literals
options.name: literals

options.description: Equality operators that are not a comparison of value (Python `is`)
options.name: not_operators

upstream.note: Only a comparison with a boolean literal, not the double negation or the conditional forms.

rules.why:
Comparing a condition with `true` or `false` adds a token pair that says what the expression already says. `x == true` reads longer than `x`, and for values that are not strictly boolean (a number, a string) the comparison also means something other than the plain test.

To fix, use the expression itself, or `!` before it.

rules.description: Reports an assignment used as the condition of an `if`, a ternary or a loop (`if (a = b)`, `while (x = next())`) when it is not wrapped in parentheses of its own (`if ((a = b))` is accepted). Python's `:=` is left alone. Off by default.

upstream.note: only the default `except-parens` mode
`a && b = c` is the Ruby rule no-assignment-in-logical-condition; over several lines is reported at the first line of the condition, RuboCop reports the assignment line

rules.why:
An assignment in a condition is nearly always a typing error for `==`: the test then stores a value and branches on it, and the comparison the author meant never happens. A reader cannot tell the two intentions apart.

To fix, write `==` if a comparison was meant, or move the assignment out of the condition (or add the extra parentheses) if it was meant.

rules.description: Reports an equality or a comparison whose two sides are both literals (`1 === 2`, `"a" < "b"`). An operand that is an expression of literals (`1 + 1 === 2`) is not reported.

upstream.note: only two literals compared

rules.why:
The result of a comparison of two literals is fixed when the code is written, so one branch of the `if` never runs. It is usually a leftover of debugging, or of a value that was meant to be a variable.

To fix, compare the variable, or replace the test with its result.

rules.description: Reports the condition of an `if`, a ternary or a loop that is a literal (`if (true)`, `if (0)`, `x = true ? 1 : 2`, `while (false)`). The usual forms of an endless loop (`while (true)`, `while (1)`, `for (;true;)`, `do {} while (true)`) are left alone.

upstream.note: literals only (no object, function or `!` forms)

rules.why:
With a literal as the test one branch always runs and the other never does, so the test is either dead code or a switch that was left on while debugging.

To fix, remove the test and keep the branch that runs, or put the real condition in.

rules.description: Reports an arm of a `switch`, `match`, `when` or `case` whose test is the same as the test of an earlier arm of the same statement (`case 1:` twice). The second arm is reported, the first is shown as related.
rules.why:
Only the first arm with that test can run, so the second is dead code. It is usually a copy that should have had another value, and the case it was meant for is then unhandled.

To fix, change the test to the value it was meant for, or merge the two arms.

rules.description: Reports a block with no statement and no comment as the body of an `if`, `else`, loop, `try` or `finally` (`if (a) { }`, `for (;;) { }`). A comment inside counts as content. A bare `{ }` and a function body are not reported, and an empty `catch` is the rule `no-empty-catch`. With `comment_handles` off a comment does not count. With `waiting_loops` an empty loop whose condition is a call is a wait and is left alone, and so is a loop whose head matches `ignored_loop_heads`.

options.description: A comment in the block counts as content
options.name: comment_handles

options.description: Leave alone an empty loop whose condition is a call
options.name: waiting_loops

options.description: A regular expression for the condition or head of a loop whose empty body is left alone
options.name: ignored_loop_heads

upstream.note: the `allowEmptyCatch` option is not supported
a bare `{}` block statement and an empty `switch` body are not read

rules.why:
An empty block is usually a branch that was started and never filled in, or code that was deleted around it. The reader cannot tell whether the nothing is meant.

To fix, write the code, or say in a comment that nothing is intended.

rules.description: Reports a `catch`, `except` or `rescue` clause whose body has no statement and no comment (`catch (e) { }`; in Python a lone `pass` counts as no statement). With the option `comment_handles` off a comment does not count either. With `broad_only` only a clause that catches everything, or one of the exception types of the option `types`, is reported.

options.description: A comment in the body counts as handling the error
options.name: comment_handles

options.description: Report only a clause that catches everything or a broad type
options.name: broad_only

options.description: Types that count as broad
options.name: types

upstream.note: the `allowEmptyCatch` option is not supported

rules.why:
An empty handler swallows the error without a trace: the program goes on in a state it did not expect, and the failure shows up later far from its cause, with nothing in the logs.

To fix, handle the error, log it, or let it propagate; if ignoring it is right, say why in a comment.

rules.description: Reports an assignment whose two sides are the same tokens (`x = x`, `x.y = x.y`, `x[0] = x[0]`, `x ||= x`). The option `operators` lists the operators that store the right side as it is (`=`, `||=`, `&&=`, `??=`); `x += x` is not reported.

options.description: The assignment operators that store the right side as it is
options.name: operators

upstream.note: the `props` option is always on; only identifiers and static member chains are compared
not multiple assignment (`a, b = a, b`)

rules.why:
The assignment changes nothing, or only calls a getter and a setter for nothing. It is nearly always a typing error where the right side should have been another variable, such as a parameter with the same name as a field.

To fix, name the right variable, or delete the statement.

rules.description: Reports an equality or comparison whose two sides are the same tokens (`x === x`, `x < x`). `x != x` used as a test for NaN is reported too. Two calls (`f() === f()`) count as the same tokens and are reported.
rules.why:
For a value the result is the same every time (except for NaN), so the test is dead or a typing error: the author compared a variable with itself instead of with another one.

To fix, compare with the right value; to test for NaN, use `isNaN` or the language's own check.
