rules.description: Reports a statement that can never run: after `return`, `throw`, `break` or `continue`, after an `if`/`else` or `try` that always jumps, or after a loop that never ends. Only the first statement of such a run is reported. Where the language has a flow layer (C#) it also covers constant conditions and calls that do not return (`does_not_return` in `semantics:`, the option `non_returning_calls`). Hoisted declarations and empty statements are left out. Removing the statement is offered as an editor quick fix only, because unreachable code usually signals a bug.

options.description: With a flow layer, treat the code after a call that never returns (`[DoesNotReturn]`, `does_not_return` in `semantics:`) as unreachable. A compiler does not, so turn this off to report exactly what it reports.
options.name: non_returning_calls

upstream.note: the code after `panic`, `os.Exit`, `log.Fatal*` and `t.Fatal*` is not read as unreachable

rules.why:
Code that cannot run is either a leftover or a sign that an earlier `return` or `throw` is in the wrong place, in which case what the author expected to run does not.

To fix, delete the statement, or move the jump that makes it unreachable.

rules.description: Reports an `apk add` without the `--no-cache` flag. A `RUN` with a `--mount` of type `cache` or `tmpfs` on `/var/cache/apk` is not reported, since nothing is stored in the image there.

example.input:
FROM alpine:3
RUN apk add curl
RUN apk add --no-cache curl=8.5.0-r0
RUN apk add --no-cache --virtual .deps gcc=13.2.1-r0 musl-dev=1.2.4-r2
RUN apk add --no-cache ./pkg.apk
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apk apk add curl=8

rules.why:
Without `--no-cache`, `apk add` keeps the downloaded package index in `/var/cache/apk`. That copy is written into the layer and stays in the image, making it larger for data nobody reads at run time.

`--no-cache` fetches the index for this one command and stores nothing; it replaces the older pair `apk update` and `rm -rf /var/cache/apk/*`.

rules.description:
Reports an `apk add` that names a package without a version. A package is pinned when its name has `=`, `~`, `<` or `>` (`curl=8.5.0-r0`, `curl~8.5`) or when it is a local `.apk` file; a variable such as `$PKGS` counts as unpinned, because its content is unknown.

The values of options that take one (`--virtual NAME`, `-t NAME`, `--repository URL`, `-X URL`) are not taken for packages, and an `apk add` with no package is fine.

example.input:
FROM alpine:3
RUN apk add curl
RUN apk add --no-cache curl=8.5.0-r0
RUN apk add --no-cache --virtual .deps gcc=13.2.1-r0 musl-dev=1.2.4-r2
RUN apk add --no-cache ./pkg.apk
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apk apk add curl=8

rules.why:
Without a version, `apk add` installs whatever the Alpine repository holds on the day of the build. Rebuilding the same Dockerfile later can give an image with other package versions, and a new release that breaks your program arrives without any change on your side.

A pinned build is repeatable. The price is upkeep: when the repository replaces a version with a newer one, the build fails until you update the pin.

rules.description: Reports an `apt-get install` that also installs recommended packages. `--no-install-recommends` (or `-o APT::Install-Recommends=false`) stops that. Other `apt-get` commands are not checked.

example.input:
FROM debian:12
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install curl
RUN apt-get install -y curl=7.88 wget=1.21
RUN apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl
RUN apt-get install -qq -y -t stable curl=7.88
RUN apt-get -y install foo/stable
RUN apt-get install -yq ./a.deb
RUN apt-get install --yes \
    curl \
    git
RUN apt-get update

# a blank line or a comment before an instruction does not hide it
RUN apt-get install -y curl=7.88

rules.why:
By default `apt-get` also installs the packages that a package only recommends, which it does not need to run. In an image they add size and build time, and more software to patch and to be attacked through.

With the flag only the real dependencies are installed; name anything else you need yourself.

rules.description: Reports an `apt-get install` of a package without a version. A package is pinned when its name has `=` (`curl=7.88.1-10`) or `/` (`curl/stable`, a release), or when it is a `.deb` file. The value of `-t` or `--target-release` is not taken for a package. A variable such as `$PKGS` counts as unpinned.

example.input:
FROM debian:12
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install curl
RUN apt-get install -y curl=7.88 wget=1.21
RUN apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl
RUN apt-get install -qq -y -t stable curl=7.88
RUN apt-get -y install foo/stable
RUN apt-get install -yq ./a.deb
RUN apt-get install --yes \
    curl \
    git
RUN apt-get update

# a blank line or a comment before an instruction does not hide it
RUN apt-get install -y curl=7.88

rules.why:
An unpinned install takes the newest version the distribution offers on the day of the build. Two builds of one Dockerfile can then differ, and a new release can break the image without any change in your code.

Pinned versions make the build repeatable. Debian and Ubuntu remove old versions from their repositories, so a pin stops resolving after a while and needs updating.

rules.description: Reports an `apt-get install` that does not answer apt's prompts. The flags that do are `-y`, `--yes`, `--assume-yes` and `-qq` (also `-q=2` and `--quiet` twice), which implies yes; they may stand anywhere in the command (`apt-get -y install` is fine). Other `apt-get` commands are not checked.

example.input:
FROM debian:12
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install curl
RUN apt-get install -y curl=7.88 wget=1.21
RUN apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl
RUN apt-get install -qq -y -t stable curl=7.88
RUN apt-get -y install foo/stable
RUN apt-get install -yq ./a.deb
RUN apt-get install --yes \
    curl \
    git
RUN apt-get update

# a blank line or a comment before an instruction does not hide it
RUN apt-get install -y curl=7.88

rules.why: A build has no terminal to answer questions. When `apt-get` needs a confirmation, for example because the install pulls in additional packages, it prints `Do you want to continue? [Y/n] Abort.` and exits with an error, which fails the `RUN` and the build.

rules.description: Reports a `COPY --from` that names its own stage. That is `COPY --from=build` in the stage that `FROM alpine AS build` starts. Names are compared without regard to case.

example.input:
FROM alpine
FROM alpine:3 AS build
FROM build
FROM scratch
FROM alpine:3 AS build
FROM $BASE
FROM alpine:3 AS Build
FROM BUILD
FROM localhost:5000/img
FROM localhost:5000/img:1
FROM alpine@sha256:abc
USER root
USER app
USER 0:0
COPY --from=build /a /b
COPY --from=nope /a /b
COPY --from=BUILD /a /b
COPY --from=0 /a /b
COPY --from=99 /a /b
COPY --from=alpine:3 /a /b
CMD ["a"]
CMD ["b"]
ENTRYPOINT ["a"]
ENTRYPOINT ["b"]
HEALTHCHECK CMD a
HEALTHCHECK CMD b
FROM alpine:3 AS last
COPY --from=LAST /a /b
USER app
CMD ["a"]
USER root

rules.why: A stage cannot copy from itself: its content does not exist yet while it is built, and BuildKit stops with a circular dependency error. The source is usually an earlier stage, or the build context (then drop `--from`).

rules.description: Reports a `COPY --from=name` that names no stage defined earlier. Not reported: the number of an earlier stage (`--from=0`) and an image reference with a `:` (`--from=nginx:1`). A stage defined further down does not count. Names are compared without regard to case.

example.input:
FROM alpine
FROM alpine:3 AS build
FROM build
FROM scratch
FROM alpine:3 AS build
FROM $BASE
FROM alpine:3 AS Build
FROM BUILD
FROM localhost:5000/img
FROM localhost:5000/img:1
FROM alpine@sha256:abc
USER root
USER app
USER 0:0
COPY --from=build /a /b
COPY --from=nope /a /b
COPY --from=BUILD /a /b
COPY --from=0 /a /b
COPY --from=99 /a /b
COPY --from=alpine:3 /a /b
CMD ["a"]
CMD ["b"]
ENTRYPOINT ["a"]
ENTRYPOINT ["b"]
HEALTHCHECK CMD a
HEALTHCHECK CMD b
FROM alpine:3 AS last
COPY --from=LAST /a /b
USER app
CMD ["a"]
USER root

rules.why: Docker does not fail on an unknown name: it takes it for an image and pulls it from the registry. A typo in a stage name (`buidler`) or a reference to a stage defined further down copies files from whatever image has that name, or fails only when the pull fails.

rules.description: Reports an `ADD` that only copies. That is an `ADD` with no URL (`http://`, `https://`) and no archive (a name ending in `.tar`, `.gz`, `.tgz`, `.xz`, `.bz2` and the like) among its arguments.

example.input:
FROM alpine:latest
FROM --platform=linux/amd64 alpine:3
FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM alpine:3
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM alpine:3 AS scratch
FROM alpine:3@sha256:abc
WORKDIR app
WORKDIR /app
WORKDIR $HOME
EXPOSE 8080 70000
EXPOSE 80/tcp 443
CMD node server.js
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
ENTRYPOINT /run.sh
ONBUILD CMD echo hi
ONBUILD ONBUILD RUN x
ONBUILD MAINTAINER x
MAINTAINER a@b.c
COPY --from=0 / /
COPY a b /dest
COPY a b /dest/
COPY a /dest
ADD app.js /app/
ADD app.tar.gz /app/
ADD https://example.com/f /app/
USER app
USER 1000:1000
USER $UID
ENV DB_PASSWORD=x
ENV A=1 NPM_TOKEN=y
ARG GITHUB_TOKEN
ARG VERSION=1
ENV AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=x

upstream.note: Reports an ADD with no URL and no archive among its arguments; hadolint reports one source that is neither.

rules.why:
`ADD` does more than copy: it unpacks local tar archives and downloads URLs. For a plain file or folder that is a surprise, since an archive you meant to copy is extracted and a value that turns out to be a URL starts a download. `COPY` only copies, so the instruction says what happens.

Keep `ADD` for unpacking an archive into the image.

rules.description: Reports a `COPY` with several sources whose destination does not end with `/` (`COPY a b /app`). The JSON form, a single source and a heredoc (`<<`) are not checked.

rules.description: Reports a `RUN` that updates the apt package lists and does not delete them. It runs `apt-get update` or `apt update` and has no `rm` of `/var/lib/apt/lists` after it in the same `RUN`. `apt-get clean` does not count, it empties another directory. A `RUN` with a `--mount` of type `cache` or `tmpfs` on `/var/lib/apt/lists` is not reported.

example.input:
FROM debian:12
RUN a
RUN b
# a comment between does not matter
RUN c
ENV A=1
RUN d
RUN e && f
RUN g
RUN h $(i)
RUN j
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/x k
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/x l
RUN m
RUN ["n", "o"]
RUN ["p"]

RUN a | b
RUN a || b
RUN ["a", "b"]
SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"]
RUN a | b
FROM debian:12
RUN a | b
RUN apt-get update
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y a
RUN apt update
RUN apt-get update && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y a && rm -fr "/var/lib/apt/lists"
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/lib/apt/lists apt-get update
RUN apt-get install -y a

upstream.note: Only the RUN that runs `apt-get update` is checked, and any `rm` of a path under /var/lib/apt/lists in it counts, as hadolint does.

rules.why:
`apt-get update` downloads the package index files into `/var/lib/apt/lists`, often tens of megabytes that no program needs at run time. They are written into the layer of that `RUN`, and deleting them in a later `RUN` hides them but does not make the image smaller, because the earlier layer still holds the files.

To fix, remove them in the same `RUN`: `apt-get update && apt-get install -y ... && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*`.

rules.description: Reports a `RUN` that installs with dnf and does not clean the cache. It runs `dnf install`, `upgrade` or `reinstall` (also `microdnf`, and the short forms `in`, `up`, `rei`) and has no `dnf clean all` or `microdnf clean all` after it in the same `RUN`. An `rm -rf /var/cache/libdnf5*` written exactly so is accepted as well.

example.input:
FROM fedora:40
RUN yum install curl
RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && yum clean all
RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && rm -rf /var/cache/yum/*
RUN yum install -y nginx-1.2 && yum clean all
RUN dnf install curl
RUN dnf install -y curl-7.0
RUN dnf install -y curl-7.0 && dnf clean all
RUN microdnf install -y curl-7.0
RUN dnf install -y ./a.rpm && dnf clean all
RUN zypper install curl
RUN zypper install -y curl=7.0 && zypper clean
RUN zypper install -y curl
RUN zypper dist-upgrade
RUN zypper -n in curl=1 && zypper cc

rules.why:
`dnf` stores the metadata and packages it downloaded under `/var/cache`. That cache is written into the layer and stays in the image, adding size that nothing uses at run time.

Clean it in the same `RUN`: a later `RUN` cannot shrink a layer that was already written.

rules.description: Reports a `dnf install`, `dnf groupinstall` or `dnf localinstall` (also with `microdnf`) without `-y` or `--assumeyes`.

example.input:
FROM fedora:40
RUN yum install curl
RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && yum clean all

rules.description: Reports a stage name that an earlier stage already uses, as in `FROM a AS app` followed by `FROM b AS app`. Names are compared without regard to case, as Docker does.

example.input:

FROM alpine:3 AS build
FROM build
FROM scratch

CMD ["b"]

ENTRYPOINT ["b"]
HEALTHCHECK CMD a
HEALTHCHECK CMD b
FROM alpine:3 AS last
COPY --from=LAST /a /b
USER app
CMD ["a"]
USER root

rules.description: Reports an `EXPOSE` with a port number above 65535. Several ports, `/tcp` and `/udp` suffixes and ranges (`8000-70000`) are all checked; a variable is not.

rules.description: Reports an instruction other than `ARG` before the first `FROM`. Comments, parser directives and blank lines are allowed there.

example.input:
ARG V=1
RUN echo hi
FROM alpine:3
RUN echo ok

rules.why: Every instruction works on a build stage, and a stage starts with `FROM`. Only `ARG` may come first, because its value can be used in the `FROM` line (`ARG VERSION=3` then `FROM alpine:${VERSION}`). Any other instruction first makes the Dockerfile invalid, and Docker rejects it.

rules.description: Reports a `gem install` (or `gem i`) of a gem without a version: `rails` instead of `rails:7.1.3`. `-v` or `--version` pins as well. The values of options that take one (`--source URL`, `-i DIR`, `--platform NAME`) are not taken for gems.

example.input:

RUN pip install flask
RUN pip install flask==2.0 "requests>=2"
RUN pip3 install -r requirements.txt
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -i https://x/simple flask==1
RUN pip install .
RUN pip install git+https://github.com/a/b
RUN pip install git+https://github.com/a/b@v1
RUN npm install
RUN npm install express
RUN npm install express@4 @scope/pkg@1
RUN npm install --loglevel verbose express@4
RUN npm install ./local
RUN npm i express
RUN npm add express@4
RUN gem install rails
RUN gem install --no-document rails
RUN gem install --source https://rubygems.org rails:7.0
RUN gem install rails:7.0
RUN gem install rails -v 7.0
RUN go install example.com/x
RUN go install example.com/x@v1
RUN go install example.com/x@latest

rules.why: Without a version `gem install` takes the newest release on the day of the build, and so a major release of a gem can break the image, and two builds of one Dockerfile give different results.

rules.description: Reports a `go install` or `go get` of a package without a version, or at `latest` or `none` (`example.com/tool@latest`). `example.com/tool@v1.4.0` is pinned. A path that starts with `.` or `/` (a package of the current module) is not reported.

example.input:
FROM node:20
RUN pip install flask
RUN pip install flask==2.0 "requests>=2"
RUN pip3 install -r requirements.txt
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -i https://x/simple flask==1
RUN pip install .
RUN pip install git+https://github.com/a/b
RUN pip install git+https://github.com/a/b@v1
RUN npm install
RUN npm install express
RUN npm install express@4 @scope/pkg@1
RUN npm install --loglevel verbose express@4
RUN npm install ./local
RUN npm i express
RUN npm add express@4
RUN gem install rails
RUN gem install --no-document rails
RUN gem install --source https://rubygems.org rails:7.0
RUN gem install rails:7.0
RUN gem install rails -v 7.0
RUN go install example.com/x
RUN go install example.com/x@v1
RUN go install example.com/x@latest

upstream.note: `go install` and `go get`; `go run` is not checked.

rules.why:
`@latest` builds whatever release is newest on the day of the build, so the tool in the image changes between builds and a new release can fail or behave differently. Without any version, `go install` uses the version in the `go.mod` of the working directory (and fails when there is none), and `go get` moves it to the latest release. In both cases the Dockerfile does not say which version ends up in the image.

Write the version: `go install example.com/tool@v1.4.0`.

rules.description: Reports a `CMD`, `ENTRYPOINT` or `HEALTHCHECK CMD` in shell form. That is `CMD node server.js` instead of the JSON array form `CMD ["node", "server.js"]`. The same instruction after `ONBUILD` is not reported.

example.input:
FROM alpine:latest
FROM --platform=linux/amd64 alpine:3
FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM alpine:3
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM alpine:3 AS scratch
FROM alpine:3@sha256:abc
WORKDIR app
WORKDIR /app
WORKDIR $HOME
EXPOSE 8080 70000
EXPOSE 80/tcp 443
CMD node server.js
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
ENTRYPOINT /run.sh
ONBUILD CMD echo hi
ONBUILD ONBUILD RUN x
ONBUILD MAINTAINER x
MAINTAINER a@b.c
COPY --from=0 / /
COPY a b /dest
COPY a b /dest/
COPY a /dest
ADD app.js /app/
ADD app.tar.gz /app/
ADD https://example.com/f /app/
USER app
USER 1000:1000
USER $UID
ENV DB_PASSWORD=x
ENV A=1 NPM_TOKEN=y
ARG GITHUB_TOKEN
ARG VERSION=1
ENV AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=x

rules.why:
The shell form runs the command as `/bin/sh -c "..."`, so the shell, not your program, is the main process of the container. `docker stop` sends SIGTERM to that shell, which usually does not pass it on; after the timeout (10 seconds by default) Docker kills the container with SIGKILL, and the program gets no chance to shut down cleanly. With an `ENTRYPOINT` in shell form, the arguments of `CMD` and of `docker run` are ignored as well.

The JSON form starts the program directly. If you need a shell, write `["sh", "-c", "exec node server.js"]`.

rules.description: Reports a stage whose last `USER` is root, on that `USER`. That is `root` or `0`, also `root:group` and `0:group`. Every stage is checked, build stages too. A stage with no `USER` instruction is not reported.

example.input:
FROM alpine
FROM alpine:3 AS build
FROM build
FROM scratch
FROM alpine:3 AS build
FROM $BASE
FROM alpine:3 AS Build
FROM BUILD
FROM localhost:5000/img
FROM localhost:5000/img:1
FROM alpine@sha256:abc
USER root
USER app
USER 0:0
COPY --from=build /a /b
COPY --from=nope /a /b
COPY --from=BUILD /a /b
COPY --from=0 /a /b
COPY --from=99 /a /b
COPY --from=alpine:3 /a /b
CMD ["a"]
CMD ["b"]
ENTRYPOINT ["a"]
ENTRYPOINT ["b"]
HEALTHCHECK CMD a
HEALTHCHECK CMD b
FROM alpine:3 AS last
COPY --from=LAST /a /b
USER app
CMD ["a"]
USER root

The container's main process runs as the last user. If the application is compromised, the attacker is root inside the container, which makes it easier to damage mounted volumes or to break out of the container, and files the process writes to a volume are owned by root.

End the stage with an unprivileged `USER` (a numeric one, see `numeric-user-id`).

rules.description: Reports a `RUN` that could be merged into the `RUN` before it. Both are one simple command, with the same leading options (`--mount=...`). A comment between the two does not break the pair; any other instruction does. A `RUN` with `&&`, `;` or a pipe is neither reported nor part of a pair.

example.input:
FROM debian:12
RUN a
RUN b
# a comment between does not matter
RUN c
ENV A=1
RUN d
RUN e && f
RUN g
RUN h $(i)
RUN j
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/x k
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/x l
RUN m
RUN ["n", "o"]
RUN ["p"]

RUN a | b
RUN a || b
RUN ["a", "b"]
SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"]
RUN a | b
FROM debian:12
RUN a | b
RUN apt-get update
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y a
RUN apt update
RUN apt-get update && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y a && rm -fr "/var/lib/apt/lists"
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/lib/apt/lists apt-get update
RUN apt-get install -y a

upstream.note: Both RUNs must be a single command with the same flags.

rules.why:
Every `RUN` creates an image layer. Files that one `RUN` writes and the next one deletes (a download, a package cache) still sit in the earlier layer and count toward the image size; joined with `&&` in one `RUN`, the cleanup really removes them.

The price is a coarser build cache: when any part of the joined `RUN` changes, all of it runs again.

rules.description: Reports a `RUN` that calls `apt`; use `apt-get` or `apt-cache` instead.

example.input:
FROM alpine:3
RUN sudo make install
RUN cd /app && make
RUN service nginx start
RUN apt update
RUN wget https://example.com/f
RUN wget -q https://example.com/f
RUN ln -sf /bin/bash /bin/sh
RUN echo sudo cd ps
RUN make && \
    sudo make install
RUN v=$(sudo make) && echo "$(wget https://example.com/f)"
ONBUILD RUN sudo make
RUN ["sudo", "make"]

rules.why: `apt` is made for people at a terminal: its output and options may change between versions, and it prints a warning that it has no stable command line interface and should be used with caution in scripts. `apt-get` and `apt-cache` keep an interface that scripts can rely on.

rules.description: Reports a `COPY --from=stage / /`, which copies the whole file system of a stage to `/`. A copy of `/` into a folder (`/app/`) or of a folder is not reported.

example.input:
FROM alpine:latest
FROM --platform=linux/amd64 alpine:3
FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM alpine:3
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM alpine:3 AS scratch
FROM alpine:3@sha256:abc
WORKDIR app
WORKDIR /app
WORKDIR $HOME
EXPOSE 8080 70000
EXPOSE 80/tcp 443
CMD node server.js
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
ENTRYPOINT /run.sh
ONBUILD CMD echo hi
ONBUILD ONBUILD RUN x
ONBUILD MAINTAINER x
MAINTAINER a@b.c
COPY --from=0 / /
COPY a b /dest
COPY a b /dest/
COPY a /dest
ADD app.js /app/
ADD app.tar.gz /app/
ADD https://example.com/f /app/
USER app
USER 1000:1000
USER $UID
ENV DB_PASSWORD=x
ENV A=1 NPM_TOKEN=y
ARG GITHUB_TOKEN
ARG VERSION=1
ENV AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=x

It copies everything of the build stage: compilers, package caches, sources, and the stage's own `/etc` and `/usr` over the ones of the final image. The image becomes as large as the build stage, which defeats the purpose of a multi-stage build, and files of the base image are overwritten.

rules.description: Reports a `FROM` with a fixed `--platform`, such as `--platform=linux/amd64`. A value that contains `$BUILDPLATFORM` or `$TARGETPLATFORM` is not reported; other variables such as `$TARGETARCH` are.

example.input:
FROM alpine:latest
FROM --platform=linux/amd64 alpine:3
FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM alpine:3
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM alpine:3 AS scratch
FROM alpine:3@sha256:abc
WORKDIR app
WORKDIR /app
WORKDIR $HOME
EXPOSE 8080 70000
EXPOSE 80/tcp 443
CMD node server.js
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
ENTRYPOINT /run.sh
ONBUILD CMD echo hi
ONBUILD ONBUILD RUN x
ONBUILD MAINTAINER x
MAINTAINER a@b.c
COPY --from=0 / /
COPY a b /dest
COPY a b /dest/
COPY a /dest
ADD app.js /app/
ADD app.tar.gz /app/

rules.description: Reports a `RUN` that calls `ssh`, `vim`, `shutdown`, `service`, `ps`, `free`, `top`, `kill` or `mount`.

example.input:
FROM alpine:3
RUN sudo make install
RUN cd /app && make
RUN service nginx start
RUN apt update
RUN wget https://example.com/f
RUN wget -q https://example.com/f
RUN ln -sf /bin/bash /bin/sh
RUN echo sudo cd ps
RUN make && \

rules.description: Reports a `FROM` whose image has the tag `latest` (`alpine:latest`). A `latest` image with a digest (`alpine:latest@sha256:...`) is not reported; an image with no tag at all is the business of `untagged-base-image`.

example.input:
FROM alpine:latest
FROM --platform=linux/amd64 alpine:3
FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM alpine:3
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM alpine:3 AS scratch
FROM alpine:3@sha256:abc
WORKDIR app

WORKDIR $HOME
EXPOSE 8080 70000
EXPOSE 80/tcp 443

ENTRYPOINT /run.sh

COPY a b /dest
COPY a b /dest/

rules.description: Reports a `RUN` that replaces `/bin/sh`. That is an `ln` command with `/bin/sh` among its arguments (`ln -sf /bin/bash /bin/sh`).

example.input:
FROM alpine:3
RUN sudo make install
RUN cd /app && make
RUN service nginx start
RUN apt update
RUN wget https://example.com/f
RUN wget -q https://example.com/f
RUN ln -sf /bin/bash /bin/sh
RUN echo sudo cd ps
RUN make && \
    sudo make install
RUN v=$(sudo make) && echo "$(wget https://example.com/f)"
ONBUILD RUN sudo make
RUN ["sudo", "make"]

Replacing `/bin/sh` changes the shell that every script of the image, and of the packages you install, expects to be a POSIX `sh`. Scripts that start with `#!/bin/sh` then run under another shell than the one they were written for, and package scripts can fail in odd ways.

To use another shell for the build, the `SHELL` instruction (`SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-c"]`) changes only the shell of the later `RUN` instructions.

rules.description: Reports a `RUN` that calls `sudo`.

example.input:
FROM alpine:3
RUN sudo make install
RUN cd /app && make
RUN service nginx start
RUN apt update
RUN wget https://example.com/f
RUN wget -q https://example.com/f
RUN ln -sf /bin/bash /bin/sh
RUN echo sudo cd ps
RUN make && \
    sudo make install
RUN v=$(sudo make) && echo "$(wget https://example.com/f)"
ONBUILD RUN sudo make
RUN ["sudo", "make"]

rules.why:
A `RUN` already runs as the user of the last `USER` instruction, root by default, so `sudo` adds nothing. Most images do not have it installed, and where it exists it may ask for a password or reset the environment (`HOME`, `PATH`), so the command sees something else than the rest of the build.

For a step that needs root, put `USER root` before it and switch back after it; to drop privileges at start, use a tool such as `gosu` in the entrypoint.

rules.description: Reports an `npm install` (also `npm i` and `npm add`) of a package without a version: `express` instead of `express@4.18.2`, `@scope/name` instead of `@scope/name@1.2.0`. A path, a tarball (`.tgz`, `.tar.gz`) or a git URL with a `#ref` counts as pinned. The value of `--loglevel` or `--registry` is not taken for a package, and an `npm install` with no package (it reads `package.json`) is not reported.

example.input:

RUN pip install flask
RUN pip install flask==2.0 "requests>=2"
RUN pip3 install -r requirements.txt
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -i https://x/simple flask==1
RUN pip install .
RUN pip install git+https://github.com/a/b
RUN pip install git+https://github.com/a/b@v1
RUN npm install
RUN npm install express
RUN npm install express@4 @scope/pkg@1
RUN npm install --loglevel verbose express@4
RUN npm install ./local
RUN npm i express
RUN npm add express@4
RUN gem install rails
RUN gem install --no-document rails
RUN gem install --source https://rubygems.org rails:7.0
RUN gem install rails:7.0
RUN gem install rails -v 7.0

RUN go install example.com/x@v1
RUN go install example.com/x@latest

rules.why:
Without a version npm installs the latest release on the day of the build, so a new major version of the package can break the image and two builds of one Dockerfile differ.

Pin the version in the command, or keep it in `package.json` with a lock file and use `npm ci`.

rules.description: Reports a `USER` whose user is a name instead of a number (`USER app`, `USER app:1000`). `USER 1000`, `USER 1000:app` and a variable are not reported: only the user part is checked, the group may be a name.

example.input:

FROM --platform=linux/amd64 alpine:3
FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM alpine:3
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM alpine:3 AS scratch

WORKDIR $HOME

rules.why:

rules.description:
Reports a `pip install` (also `pip3`, `pip3.12`) of a package without a version. example.input:

An unpinned `pip install` takes the latest release of the package, and of the libraries it depends on, on the day of the build. A new major version can break the application, and two builds of one Dockerfile give different images.

rules.description: Reports a `RUN` with a pipe (`a | b`) in a stage whose `SHELL` does not set `pipefail`. No earlier `SHELL` instruction of the stage has a word that contains `pipefail` (`SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"]`). A `set -o pipefail` inside the `RUN` itself does not count. example.input:

RUN a
RUN b

RUN c
ENV A=1
RUN d

RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/x l

RUN apt-get update && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

rules.why:
The exit status of a pipe is the one of its last command. `curl -f https://example.com/x | tar xz` succeeds even when curl fails and tar gets nothing, so the build goes on with a missing or broken file and the error shows up much later. rules.description: Reports a `RUN` that calls `cd`, anywhere in its script (also in a subshell such as `(cd sub && make)`).

example.input:

RUN wget https://example.com/f

rules.description: Reports a `wget` call that does not limit its progress output. It has none of `--progress`, `-q` or `--quiet`, `-nv` or `--no-verbose`, `-o` or `--output-file`, `-a` or `--append-output`.

RUN cd /app && make

RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && yum clean all
RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && rm -rf /var/cache/yum/*
RUN yum install -y nginx-1.2 && yum clean all
RUN dnf install curl
RUN dnf install -y curl-7.0
RUN dnf install -y curl-7.0 && dnf clean all
RUN microdnf install -y curl-7.0
RUN dnf install -y ./a.rpm && dnf clean all
RUN zypper install curl
RUN zypper install -y curl=7.0 && zypper clean
RUN zypper install -y curl
RUN zypper dist-upgrade
RUN zypper -n in curl=1 && zypper cc

rules.why:
zypper asks for confirmation before it changes packages and, when there is a conflict, which solution to take. A build has no terminal to answer, so the command cannot continue and the `RUN` fails.

`--non-interactive` makes zypper take the default answer to every question.

rules.description: Reports a known EditorConfig or .NET property that has a value it does not accept (`indent_style = tabs`, `dotnet_diagnostic.CA1000.severity = high`). Values are case-insensitive, `unset` is always valid, and .NET code-style options may end in `:silent`, `:suggestion`, `:warning` or `:error`, which formatting options may not. A trailing `# comment` is ignored. Unknown properties are not checked.

example.input:
indent_style = tabs
indent_style = Tab
indent_size = four
indent_size = 4
indent_size = TAB
indent_size = 4 # four
indent_size = four ; words
indent_size = unset
tab_width =
max_line_length = off
charset = "utf-8-bom"
trim_trailing_whitespace = yes
end_of_line = LF
dotnet_diagnostic.CA1000.severity = high
dotnet_diagnostic.CA1000.severity = Warning
dotnet_style_qualification_for_field = maybe:suggestion
csharp_style_var_elsewhere = true:suggestoin
csharp_style_var_elsewhere = true:suggestion
csharp_new_line_before_open_brace = all
csharp_new_line_before_open_brace = methods, types
csharp_new_line_before_open_brace = methods, typs
csharp_new_line_before_else = true:suggestion
dotnet_naming_symbols.x.applicable_kinds = class, strukt
dotnet_code_quality.CA1822.api_surface = anything, goes
not_a_known_property = whatever

rules.why:
An editor ignores a value it does not know, so the setting silently has no effect (`indent_style = tabs` does not select tabs). The file looks right and the code is formatted another way.

To fix, use a value that the property accepts; the message names the closest one.

rules.description: Reports a `root` property inside a section. `root` stops the search for parent `.editorconfig` files only as a pair before the first `[section]`; inside a section editors ignore it. No fix: moving it into the preamble is the author's call.

example.input:
root = true

[*.cs]
indent_size = 4
Root = true
[*.vb]
rooted = true

rules.why:
The author meant to stop the search at this file, but it does nothing, so settings of the parent directories keep applying, and the files are formatted differently from what the file says.

To fix, put `root = true` above the first section.

rules.description: Reports a property name that is not an EditorConfig or .NET property (`dotnet_*`, `csharp_*`, `visual_basic_*`, naming rules, `dotnet_diagnostic.<ID>.severity`) but is one typo away from one. Names of other tools (`resharper_*`, `ij_*`) are not reported. The option `strict` also reports `dotnet_*`, `csharp_*` and `visual_basic_*` names that are close to no known property. The known names are in `crates/lang-editorconfig/data/properties.txt`.

example.input:
[*.cs]
indent_syle = space
INDENT_STYLE = space
dotnet_style_qualification_for_feild = false:suggestion
csharp_new_line_befor_open_brace = all
dotnet_diagnostic.CA1000.sevrity = none
dotnet_naming_rule.types.symbol = types
dotnet_diagnostic.CA1000.severity = none
dotnet_naming_style.pascal.capitalization = pascal_case
resharper_apply_auto_detected_rules = false
ij_formatter_enabled = true
dotnet_a_new_option_nothing_like_any = true

options.description: Also report `dotnet_*`, `csharp_*` and `visual_basic_*` names that are close to no known property (the list may lag behind new .NET options).
options.name: strict

rules.why:
A misspelled property is not an error to an editor, which ignores what it does not know, so the setting silently does nothing and a reader assumes it works.

To fix, correct the name; the message names the closest one.

rules.description: Reports a pattern with a backslash before a letter, digit, `_` or `-` (`build\out`), which is the pattern `buildout`. `\.` and `\#` are ordinary escapes and are not reported. No fix.

example.input:
build\out
\#file
foo\.bar

rules.why:
In a pattern file `\` escapes the next character, it does not separate paths as on Windows, so the pattern matches something other than the path the author wrote, and the files stay in version control or in the build context.

To fix, write `/`.

rules.description: Reports a pattern line with a ` #` after the pattern. Files of this syntax have no end-of-line comments: `*.log # logs` is a pattern for a file name with spaces and a `#`, which matches nothing. No fix.

example.input:
*.log # logs
# a # b
name#x
dist/

rules.why:
The line looks like a pattern with a comment, but the whole text is the pattern, so the files the author wants to ignore are not ignored.

To fix, put the comment on a line of its own above the pattern.

rules.description: Reports a `!` pattern for a path whose parent directory is excluded by an earlier pattern (`!a/b` after `a/`). Only literal paths are checked. In `.dockerignore`, where the later pattern wins, it is not reported.

example.input:
node_modules/
!node_modules/keep.js
/a/b
!/a/b/c
*.o
!/lib/a.o
vendor/
!vendor/
!vendor/x
src/gen
!other/src/gen/x

rules.why:
Git does not look inside an excluded directory, so it cannot re-include a file in it, and the negation does nothing. The file stays ignored although the file seems to say otherwise.

To fix, exclude the contents instead of the directory (`a/*`), then add the negation.

rules.description: Reports a pattern that appears twice with no opposite pattern (`!x` for `x`) between the two, on the second.

example.input:
*.log
build/
*.log
!keep.log
!keep.log
*.tmp
!*.tmp
*.tmp

rules.why:
The second pattern changes nothing. It is a copy and paste leftover that makes the file longer, and a reader looks for what it adds.

To fix, delete the second pattern.

rules.description: Reports a `foo/` or `/foo` pattern that follows a plain `foo`, with no `!` pattern between them: a name pattern already matches files and directories called `foo` at every level.

example.input:
build
/build/
out/
bin
!bin
bin/
dist/dir
/dist/dir/

rules.why:
The later pattern adds nothing, and a reader may think it is more specific than the first.

To fix, delete the later pattern.

rules.description: Reports an exported function, method, type, constant or variable whose doc comment does not start with its name. A type may start with `A`, `An`, `The` or `This` before the name. The comment of a group in parentheses is the comment of its types, and a constant or variable in a group whose comment has text is not checked. Directive lines (`//go:generate`) and a first line `Deprecated: ` are not text. A declaration with no comment is left to `missing-doc-comment`.

upstream.note: No stuttering check (a name that starts with the package name), no own-declaration check for `var a, B`; a method that is sortable through methods in another file of the package is reported

rules.why:
`go doc` and the package pages show the first sentence of a comment as the summary of the name, and search and lists read it as "Name does ...". A comment that starts with another word makes that sentence read wrong in the generated documentation.

To fix, start the comment with the name: `// Run does things.`

rules.description: A package-level `var` of one name made by `errors.New` or `fmt.Errorf` starts with `err`, or `Err` when exported.
rules.why: A package-level error variable is a sentinel that callers compare against with `errors.Is`, and it is read from other packages. The `err` and `Err` prefixes make such variables recognizable at the use site and keep the exported ones apart from other exported names. It is a Go convention; nothing breaks without it.

rules.description: The text of an error made with `fmt.Errorf`, `errors.New`, `errors.Errorf`, `errors.Wrap` and the like ends in `.`, `:`, `!` or a newline (a capital first letter is not reported). The text is the first argument, or the second of the functions that wrap an error (`errors.Wrap(err, "failed.")`).
rules.why: Error strings are joined into longer messages (`failed to open: ` plus the cause), so a full stop, colon, exclamation mark or newline at the end leaves a doubled or dangling mark in the result and in logs. The Go code review comments ask for messages without end punctuation.

rules.description: `errors.New(fmt.Sprintf(...))` is `fmt.Errorf(...)` (the `t.Error(fmt.Sprintf(...))` form on a `*testing.T` needs types and is not read).

example.input:
package a

func f() {
	_ = errors.New(fmt.Sprintf("x %d", 1))
	_ = errors.New(fmt.Sprint("x"), 1)
	_ = errors.New("x")
	_ = fmt.Errorf("x %d", 1)
	_ = errors.New(fmt.Sprintf("x") + "y")
}

rules.why:
`fmt.Errorf` formats and wraps (`%w`) in one call, and `go vet` knows its format string. `errors.New(fmt.Sprintf(...))` formats a string first and then wraps it in an error, which is longer and cannot wrap another error with `%w`.

To fix, call `fmt.Errorf` with the same format and arguments.

rules.description: `x += 1` and `x -= 1`, where `x++` and `x--` say the same. Only the literal `1` counts. Left out of a language that has no `++`.
rules.why: `x++` and `x--` are the short forms of `x += 1` and `x -= 1` and are what readers look for in a loop or a counter. Using one form everywhere makes counters easy to find. The rule is off by default because the long form is a valid style in some codebases.

rules.description: An `else` block after an `if` block that ends in `return`: the code of the `else` can follow the `if`. An `else if` is left alone.
rules.why:
When the `if` block ends in `return`, the `else` only adds a level of indentation to the code that follows. Without it the normal path stays at the left edge and the early return reads as a guard, which is the Go way of handling errors first. Removing the `else` does not change what the function does.

To fix, delete `else` and move its block after the `if`.

rules.description: Reports a package that has no comment right above the `package` clause in any file of its directory. The report is made once per directory, at the `package` keyword of the first file by name (a test file too). A test file or a file with a detached comment counts for the comment where it has one, and never causes the report. The files of the directory are read even when only some are linted; the rule is silent when one of them does not parse.

example.input:
package a

func F() {}

upstream.note: 52 findings are missed where a generated or build-excluded sibling that revive does not load holds the first file name or the only comment

rules.why:
The package comment is the first thing `go doc` and the package index show, and it tells a reader what the package is for. A package without one is listed with no description.

To fix, add a comment of the form `// Package name does ...` right above the `package` clause of one file.

rules.description: Reports a package comment whose first line does not start with `Package` and the name of the package. A comment of the right form with a blank line before the `package` clause is reported as detached. A file of package `main` is not checked.

example.input:
// Does things.
package a

upstream.note: 52 findings are missed where a generated or build-excluded sibling that revive does not load holds the first file name or the only comment

rules.why:
Documentation tools read the first sentence of the package comment as the package's summary, and a fixed form makes the summaries of all packages read the same. A blank line between the comment and the `package` clause makes the comment a plain comment, not the package's documentation.

To fix, start with `Package name` and remove the blank line.

rules.description: `for k, _ := range x`: the second value is the blank identifier, so `for k := range x` says the same.
rules.why: `for k, _ := range x` and `for k := range x` do the same; the blank identifier is noise that suggests the second value matters. The short form is what `gofmt -s` produces, so code that uses it needs no later cleanup.

rules.description: The methods of a type declared in one file name their receiver the same. The first method sets the name; `_`, `this` and `self` are left to `receiver-naming`.
rules.why: A method set reads as one unit. When one method calls its receiver `s` and the next `srv`, a reader has to check each body to know that both mean the same value, and a copied body keeps the wrong name. The Go code review comments ask for one receiver name per type.

rules.description: The name of a method's receiver is `_`, `this` or `self`: a receiver is named by a short form of its type, and left out when the method does not use it.

options.description: A regular expression the receiver name must match; one that starts with `!` is one it must not match. Empty: not checked.
options.name: receivers

rules.why: `this` and `self` carry the habits of other languages into Go, where a receiver is an ordinary parameter named after its type (`s` for `Server`). A `_` receiver is the same as no name, so leaving the name out says the method does not use the value. The Go code review comments ask for short names taken from the type.

rules.description: Reports a variable, constant, function, parameter, named result or type parameter that has the name of a predeclared identifier (`len`, `new`, `string`, `nil`, `max`, ...); a name on the left of an assignment counts too. A method and a receiver are not reported. The options `allow`, `kinds`, `except_parents` and `assigned_by` change what is checked.

options.description: Names that may be declared.
options.name: allow

options.description: The declarations that are checked (empty: all).
options.name: kinds

options.description: Grammar kinds whose direct declarations are left out (a receiver).
options.name: except_parents

options.description: Grammar kinds of statements whose left-side names are reported too (`len = 1`, `max += 1`).
options.name: assigned_by

rules.why:
The name hides the built-in in that scope, so a later `len(x)` or `string(b)` calls the new thing or fails to compile far from the declaration. The code works until somebody needs the built-in in the same scope, and then the error is hard to understand.

To fix, rename the declaration.

rules.description: An `else` block after an `if` block that ends in `break`, `continue` or `goto`: the code of the `else` can follow the `if`. An `else if` is left alone.
rules.why:
When the `if` block ends in `break`, `continue` or `goto`, control never reaches the `else`, so the `else` only indents the code that follows. Without it the code reads as a guard followed by the main path. Removing the `else` does not change what the loop does.

To fix, delete `else` and move its block after the `if`.

rules.description: Reports a parameter of a function with a body (a declaration or a literal) that its body never mentions. A name that matches `ignore_pattern` and the blank identifier are not checked; the receiver and the named results are not parameters; an assignment to a parameter counts as a use.

options.description: Which parameters are checked: those after the last one that is read, all of them, or none.
options.name: args

options.description: A regex for the names that are not checked (revive's `allowRegex`).
options.name: ignore_pattern

upstream.note: the options keep their defaults; `/*exported*/` and `/*global*/` comments are not read; a JSX tag counts as a use

A read in a block inside the function counts; the module counts only reads in the function itself and in `ForEach-Object` and `Where-Object` blocks. Parameters written after the function name (`function f($a)`) are not checked.
the options keep their defaults; `.d.ts` files and `declare module` blocks are not treated as used

rules.why:
A parameter that nothing reads is either dead weight in the signature or a sign that the body ignores a value it should use (a typo in a name often shows this way).

To fix, remove the parameter, or use it.

rules.description: Reports a name that is not spelled in Go style: it has an underscore, it is a constant in ALL_CAPS, or it writes a common initialism (`Id`, `Http`, `Url`) in mixed case. Checked are functions and methods with their parameters and results, the methods of interfaces (their parameters and results, not their names), constants, variables, types, the names of `:=` and the fields of structs. Receivers, function literals and function types are not checked. The options `initialisms` and `ignore_pattern` change the words and names.

options.description: The convention of the names: `words` or `off`.
options.name: names

options.description: The words (in capitals) that are written in capitals inside a name.
options.name: initialisms

options.description: A regex for the names that are not checked.
options.name: ignore_pattern

rules.why:
Go code is read with the conventions of the standard library, where `userID` and `ServeHTTP` are written the same everywhere. A name that follows another style stands out and makes grep and completion less predictable.

To fix, rename to mixed caps with initialisms in capitals: `userID`, not `user_id` or `userId`.

rules.description: Reports a name that does not follow the style set for what it names: operations, fragments, variables, fields, arguments, types, enum values and directives. `PascalCase` and `camelCase` allow letters and digits only, `snake_case` and `UPPER_CASE` forbid the other case; leading underscores are ignored. No fix: renaming changes the schema or the queries that use it.

options.description: Style of operation names.
options.name: operations

options.description: Style of fragment names.
options.name: fragments

options.description: Style of variable names.
options.name: variables

options.description: Style of field and input field names in definitions.
options.name: fields

options.description: Style of argument names in definitions.
options.name: arguments

options.description: Style of type names.
options.name: types

options.description: Style of enum values.
options.name: enum_values

options.description: Style of directive names.
options.name: directives

upstream.note: Google's camel segments and `@Test` method names are patterns of the options `methods` and `test_methods`.
The member pattern of Google's name rule.
A `static final` field or an interface field; no exceptions list.
No separate pattern for `for` variables.

Leading and trailing underscores are `no-name-underscore`. No forbiddenPrefixes, forbiddenSuffixes, requiredPrefixes, requiredSuffixes or ignorePattern; no per-kind styles for the root types, interfaces versus objects, or inputs versus objects; `PascalCase` and `camelCase` accept runs of capitals (`HTTPServer`) that change-case rewrites.
One format for every kind of block (tflint sets one per kind) and no custom regular expression.

rules.why:
Names that follow one convention are predictable: a reader can guess the name of a thing, tell a type from a variable at a glance and search for them. A name in another style stands out as a mistake or as code from another project. The convention itself is a choice of the project, which is why the expression is an option.

To fix, rename the declaration and its uses.

rules.description: Reports an operation without a name (`{ a }`, `query { a }`).
rules.why:
Servers, logs, traces and caches identify an operation by its name. An anonymous one shows up as nothing in the query log, so it cannot be told from the others when something is slow or fails, and a persisted-query store has nothing to key it on.

To fix, name the operation: `query GetA { a }`.

rules.description: Reports a name that starts or ends with an underscore: a type, field, argument, enum value, directive, operation, fragment or alias, and every reference to one. A field selected in a query is not reported (`__typename`).

upstream.note: Leading and trailing underscores are `no-name-underscore`. No forbiddenPrefixes, forbiddenSuffixes, requiredPrefixes, requiredSuffixes or ignorePattern; no per-kind styles for the root types, interfaces versus objects, or inputs versus objects; `PascalCase` and `camelCase` accept runs of capitals (`HTTPServer`) that change-case rewrites.

rules.why:
Names that begin with two underscores are reserved for introspection, and one underscore is a mark that style guides use for private or generated names, which GraphQL has no concept of. A schema that avoids them has names that clients can use in generated code without escaping.

To fix, rename without the underscore.

rules.description: Reports a field of an object or interface type that starts with the name of the type (`type User { userId: ID }`); case is ignored. No fix: renaming a field changes the schema.
rules.why:
The field is always read as `user.userId`, so the type name is said twice. It gets worse when a query is written with aliases or a field moves to another type.

To fix, drop the prefix (`id`).

rules.description: Reports an operation or fragment that nests selection sets deeper than the `max` option allows. Fragments that are spread are not followed.

example.config:
selection-set-depth:
  level: warn
  options:
    max: 2
example.input:
query Q { a { b { c } } }
fragment F on T { a { b } }

options.description: The deepest allowed nesting; the operation's own selection set is level 1.
options.name: max

upstream.note: Fragment spreads are not followed (upstream adds the depth of the spread fragments); no ignore option.

rules.why:
The cost of a query grows with its depth: each level can multiply the number of objects the server has to load. A depth limit is a cheap protection against queries that are expensive by accident or on purpose.

To fix, flatten the query, or split it into several requests.

rules.description: Reports two fragments of a document with the same name, within one file.

upstream.note: Not checked across files.

rules.why:
A spread names the fragment it means, and with two of one name the tool cannot tell which, so it takes one or fails depending on the order. Code generators write one type per fragment name and collide.

To fix, rename one of them.

rules.description: Reports two operations of a document with the same name, within one file.

upstream.note: Not checked across files.

rules.why:
A server cannot tell which operation a request with that name runs, and tools that key on the name (caches, persisted queries, generated code) collide.

To fix, rename one of them.

rules.description: Reports a `//` comment where `#` is the convention. The fix writes `#`.

example.fixed:
# old style
# fine
x = 1 # trailing
/* block */

rules.why: Both forms are valid in the language, but the style that the Terraform documentation and the formatter use is `#`. Comments in one style are easy to search for and look the same in every module.

rules.description: Reports a list item read with the legacy dot syntax, `a.0`. The fix writes `a[0]`.

example.fixed:
resource "a" "b" {
  name = var.name
  tags = [var.a, "x-${var.b}", "${var.c}${var.d}"]
  id   = var.e
  raw  = "${~ var.f ~}"
  id2  = aws_instance.web[0].id
  all  = aws_instance.web[0].id
  ids  = aws_instance.web.*.id
  num  = local.versions[1][2]
  key  = { (var.k) = 1 }
  sum  = 1 + "${var.n}"
}
example.input:
resource "a" "b" {
  name = "${var.name}"
  tags = ["${var.a}", "x-${var.b}", "${var.c}${var.d}"]
  id   = "${ var.e }"
  raw  = "${~ var.f ~}"
  id2  = aws_instance.web.0.id
  all  = aws_instance.web[0].id
  ids  = aws_instance.web.*.id
  num  = local.versions.1.2
  key  = { "${var.k}" = 1 }
  sum  = 1 + "${var.n}"
}

rules.why: The dot form is a deprecated spelling of the index. Newer versions of the language reject it or treat it differently, and the bracket form works with every expression.

rules.description: Reports a string that is one interpolation, `"${var.a}"`, where the expression alone does. The fix writes the expression. It is not reported in Nomad job files (`.nomad`, `.nomad.hcl`), whose agent fills those in at run time.

example.fixed:
resource "a" "b" {
  name = var.name
  tags = [var.a, "x-${var.b}", "${var.c}${var.d}"]
  id   = var.e
  raw  = "${~ var.f ~}"
  id2  = aws_instance.web[0].id
  all  = aws_instance.web[0].id
  ids  = aws_instance.web.*.id
  num  = local.versions[1][2]
  key  = { (var.k) = 1 }
  sum  = 1 + "${var.n}"
}
example.input:
resource "a" "b" {
  name = "${var.name}"
  tags = ["${var.a}", "x-${var.b}", "${var.c}${var.d}"]
  id   = "${ var.e }"
  raw  = "${~ var.f ~}"
  id2  = aws_instance.web.0.id
  all  = aws_instance.web[0].id
  ids  = aws_instance.web.*.id
  num  = local.versions.1.2
  key  = { "${var.k}" = 1 }
  sum  = 1 + "${var.n}"
}

options.description: Kinds of the parent (for example `Tuple`) whose strings are left alone. `Tuple`: only a string that is a whole argument is reported and unwrapped, as `terraform fmt` does.
options.name: except_in

rules.why: Since Terraform 0.12 an expression can stand alone, and wrapping it in a string turns the value into a string, which loses its type (a list or a number becomes text) and adds noise.

rules.description: Reports an `output` block with no `description` argument.
rules.why:
The description is what a user of the module reads in the registry and in generated documentation. An output without one has to be understood from the name and the expression.

To fix, add `description`.

rules.description: Reports a `variable` block with no `description` argument.
rules.why:
The description is what the person who uses the module reads to know what to put in the variable. Without it, they have to read the code that uses it.

To fix, add `description`.

rules.description: Reports a comparison with an empty list, `x == []` or `x != []`. It is false for an empty set or a tuple of another type.

example.input:
a = var.l == []
b = var.l != []
c = [] == var.l
d = length(var.l) == 0
e = var.l == [] && var.m
f = var.l == [1]

rules.why:
`[]` is a tuple, and Terraform compares values of different types as not equal, so the comparison is false for an empty set or an empty list of another type, and the condition silently does the wrong thing.

To fix, compare the length: `length(x) == 0`.

rules.description: Reports a provider that a `resource`, `data` or `provider` block uses and that no `required_providers` entry of the module names, on the last such block of the provider, and a `required_providers` entry without a `version`. The built-in `terraform` provider is exempt, and override files do not count.

upstream.note: Does not check each provider used for a `source` and a `version`, which needs the resources of the other files of the module.

rules.why:
Without the declaration Terraform picks the source of the provider by the default for its name, and without a version it takes the newest, so two runs of the same code can use different providers and a new major version can break the module with no change in the code.

To fix, add the provider to `required_providers` with a `source` and a version constraint.

rules.description: Reports a module none of whose `terraform` blocks sets `required_version`, on the `terraform` block, or on the start of `main.tf` when the module has no such block. Override files do not count.

upstream.note: A module with no `terraform` block at all is not reported (it needs the other files of the module).

rules.why:
Terraform language features and the state format change between versions, and a state file written by a newer version cannot be used by an older one. A constraint makes an incompatible version fail at the start with a clear message instead of in the middle of an apply.

To fix, set `required_version` in a `terraform` block.

rules.description: Reports a `variable` block with no `type` argument.
rules.why:
Without a type any value is accepted and converted when it is used, so a wrong value (a string where a list was meant) is found late, with an error far from the variable. A type checks the value when it is given and documents what is expected.

To fix, add `type`.

rules.description: Reports a variable, local value, data source or provider alias that no file of the module (the `.tf` files of the directory) refers to. Override files declare nothing of their own. A module with `.tf.json` files, a file that does not parse or one that cannot be read is not judged.

upstream.note: Reads one file: a declaration used only by another file of the module is reported.

rules.why:
An unused declaration is left over from a change. A variable that nothing reads misleads the user of the module, who sets it and sees no effect, and an unused data source still makes a request on each plan.

To fix, delete it.

rules.description: Reports a `[section]` header with no settings under it. Comments do not count as settings.

example.input:
[core]
bare = false

[empty]

[comment-only]
; nothing here

[user]
name = a

rules.why:
It usually is what is left when the last setting of a section was removed. A reader of the file wonders if the section matters, and some programs treat an empty section differently from a missing one.

To fix, delete the header, or add the setting.

rules.description: Reports a name with two or more capital letters in a row (`XMLParser`), for type, method, parameter, field and local variable names that match the `names` option. Names that match `ignored` (constants and overridden methods by default) are not reported. With an empty `names` the rule checks nothing.

options.description: Regular expression a type, method, parameter, field or local variable name must match; empty: not checked.
options.name: names

options.description: Regular expression matched for the names that are left out (constants, overridden methods): every name by default.
options.name: ignored

upstream.note: Only more than one capital in a row; no allowed length or ignore options.

rules.why:
A run of capitals hides where one word ends and the next starts: `XMLHTTPRequest` does not show if it is XML HTTP or XMLH TTP, and tools that split names into words get it wrong. Treating an abbreviation as a word (`XmlHttpRequest`) keeps the name readable and its camel case regular.

To fix, write the abbreviation as a word: `XmlParser`.

rules.description: Reports an array creation in which the `{` of the initializer follows the `]` right away (`new int[]{1}`).

upstream.note: Only the `{` of an array creation right after the `]`.

rules.why:
The space between the brackets and the braces is the convention of the Java code style guides, and it separates the type from the initializer so that `new int[] {1}` reads as two parts.

To fix, put a space between `]` and `{`.

rules.description: Reports a variable or parameter that puts the array brackets after the name (`int a[]`).
rules.why:
In Java the brackets are part of the type, and `int[] a` says it at the start. The C form is allowed for compatibility and makes the type hard to read, and `int[] a, b[]` declares two different types in one line.

To fix, write the brackets after the type: `int[] a`.

rules.description: Reports a string or character literal that writes a visible character as a `\uXXXX` escape when the line has no trailing comment. Escapes of control, space and format characters are not reported.

upstream.note: Printable-escape rule with control characters and tail comments allowed; no options.

rules.why:
The escape hides the character: the reader has to decode `é` to know it is an `é`, and cannot see a typo in the code. The source file is UTF-8, so the character itself is safe. An escape stays useful when a comment explains it, which is why a comment on the line allows it.

To fix, write the character itself, or add a trailing comment that says what it is.

rules.description: Reports a line of a Javadoc comment, after the first, that does not start with an asterisk. Empty lines are not reported.
rules.why:
Javadoc strips the leading `*` of each line, so a line without one is kept with its indentation, and the comment renders differently from how it reads in the source. The asterisks also show where the comment ends.

To fix, start the line with `*`.

rules.description:
Reports Javadoc paragraphs that do not use `

` in the usual way: a `

` must stand right before the first word of its paragraph (no space after it) and after an empty line, an empty line between paragraphs must be followed by `

`, and the comment must not start with `

`. Text inside `

`, `
    ` and the like, and after the first block tag, is not checked.

example.input:
/** * Good. * *

Fine paragraph. * *

Space after. * * Missing tag. *

Not after an empty line. * *

    *
  • item *
* * {@snippet : * code(); * * more(); * } * * 
 *
 * kept
 *
* * @param x text * * after the tags */ class A { /**

First thing. */ void f() {} }

upstream.note:
`

` and empty-line placement; not `allowNewlineParagraph`.

rules.why:
Javadoc ignores empty lines, so paragraphs not marked with `

` run together in the generated page. A `

` that is misplaced adds an empty paragraph or starts a paragraph in the wrong place. To fix, put `

` directly before the first word of each paragraph after the first.

rules.description: Reports a Javadoc comment that does not start with a summary: the first sentence must end with a period followed by a blank or the end of the text, and must not start with a fragment that matches the `forbidden_fragments` option. A comment that is `{@inheritDoc}` or `{@return ...}` needs no summary.

options.description: Regular expression a summary must not match at its start; empty: no check.
options.name: forbidden_fragments

upstream.note: Period and forbidden fragments; the summary is read from the lines of the comment, not from parsed HTML.

rules.why:
The first sentence is what the generated index and the IDE hover show, so a comment that does not start with a complete sentence gives a poor summary or one cut at the wrong place.

To fix, begin the comment with a sentence that ends with a period.

rules.description: Reports a line that continues a block tag (`@param x`) and is indented by fewer than `indent` blanks after the asterisk (5 by default). Lines that start HTML and lines inside `<pre>` and the like are not reported.

example.input:
/** * Summary. * * @param a first * continued with one blank * @param b first * continued with five blanks * @param c first * four blanks are not enough * @return x * 
 *   html is left alone
 *
*/ class A {}

options.description: Blanks after the asterisk that a continuation line needs.
options.name: indent

rules.why:
The indent shows that a line belongs to the tag above it: without it a long `@param` description reads as a paragraph of the comment.

To fix, indent the continuation lines.

rules.description: Reports a lone `;` that is the body of an `if` or a loop, such as `while (x);`, on the `;`.

upstream.note: Only the body of an `if` or a loop.

rules.why:
The semicolon ends the statement, so the code that follows on the next line is not the body of the loop, whatever its indentation says. It is a typical typo, and the loop either does nothing or never ends.

To fix, delete the `;`, or write `{}` if an empty body is meant.

rules.description: Reports a class that declares `boolean equals(Object)` and does not declare `hashCode()`.

upstream.note: Only `equals` without `hashCode`, not the reverse.

rules.why:
Objects that are equal must have the same hash code. Without an own `hashCode` the one of `Object` is used, so two equal objects land in different buckets and a `HashMap` or `HashSet` does not find them.

To fix, declare `hashCode()` from the same fields as `equals`.

rules.description: Reports a string or character literal that writes a backspace, tab, line feed, form feed, carriage return, quote or backslash as an octal or unicode escape (`\u0009`).

upstream.note: Only the special-escape message of the Google config.

rules.why:
These characters have their own escapes (`\b`, `\t`, `\n`, `\f`, `\r`, `\"`, `\'`, `\\`) which every reader knows. A unicode escape for a line feed is even translated before the lexer runs, so `\u000a` in a string ends the line and does not compile.

To fix, use the special escape.

rules.description: Reports a `switch` statement that has no `default` label.
rules.why:
Without `default`, a value that no `case` names is ignored without notice, so a new enum constant or an unexpected input falls through the switch and the program goes on with the wrong state.

To fix, add a `default` that handles the case or throws.

rules.description: Reports a `case` whose statements can reach the next `case` or `default`, and an empty one that is followed by a blank line, without a comment that says `falls through` before the next one (or at the end of its block). Cases that stack with no statement between them (`case 1: case 2: b();`) are not reported.
rules.why:
Execution that runs on from one case into the next is easily a forgotten `break`: the reader cannot tell it from an error, and the code of the second case then runs for the first value too.

To fix, end the case with `break` or `return`; if the fall-through is meant, write a `// falls through` comment.

rules.description: Reports an assignment to a parameter of a method. No fix.
rules.why:
A reassigned parameter means two things in one method: the value the caller passed, and the later one. A reader who sees the name expects the argument, and a later edit that reads the parameter gets the wrong value.

To fix, put the new value in a local variable.

rules.description: Reports `==` or `!=` with a string literal as an operand.
rules.why:
`==` on strings compares references, not text. It works for two literals because they are interned and fails for a string that was built or read, so the code passes its tests and breaks on real data.

To fix, use `equals`: `"a".equals(s)`.

rules.description: Reports a line of a comment that starts with `todo` in any other case, or with `TODO` and no colon. Javadoc comments are not read.

upstream.note: The Google format only, no option.
The check id of the Google TodoComment instance.

rules.why:
A fixed form (`TODO:`) lets people and tools find the open items by one search. A variant spelled differently is not found.

To fix, write `TODO:`.

rules.description: Reports an import whose name the file does not use. Imports with `*` are not checked, and a name in a doc comment counts as a use where the language has doc comments. No fix: removing an import can change which declaration a name means.

upstream.note: Names in Javadoc count as used; no option to turn that off.

rules.why:
An import that nothing uses is dead code. It misleads the reader about what the file depends on, and where an import runs the module, as in Python, it still costs the time to load it and fails where the module is not installed.

To fix, remove the import.

rules.description: Reports a local variable that is declared, and perhaps assigned, but never read. No fix.

upstream.note: not an assignment that is overwritten before any read

rules.why:
A variable that is assigned and never read is dead code. It is a leftover of an earlier version, or a sign that the code was meant to use it (a misspelled name, a result that is forgotten), and it misleads the reader about what the code computes.

To fix, remove the variable, or use it.

rules.description: Reports an integer literal that ends in a lower case `l` (`10l`).
rules.why:
A lower case `l` looks like the digit `1`, so `10l` reads as `101`. The upper case suffix cannot be mistaken.

To fix, write `10L`.

rules.description: Reports an overload (a signature or function with the same name as an earlier one) with another member between it and the earlier overloads. It checks interface and class members, call and construct signatures, and function declarations.
rules.why:
Overloads are read together as one declaration with several shapes. When another member sits between them, a reader can miss one shape or take a later signature for an unrelated member.

To fix, move the overloads next to each other.

rules.description: Reports `Array<T>`, `ReadonlyArray<T>` and `Readonly<T[]>` written as generic types, each level of a nested one (`Array<Array<number>>` is two reports). The bare `Array` is not reported.

upstream.note: only the default `array` style (`default` and `readonly` options); a local type named `Array` is still reported

rules.why:
Two spellings of one type make code harder to scan and search; the bracket form `T[]` is shorter and reads left to right.

To fix, write `T[]` and `readonly T[]`.

rules.description: Reports a `@ts-ignore` comment, a `@ts-nocheck` comment before the first statement, and a `@ts-expect-error` comment whose description is shorter than three characters (`// @ts-expect-error: the API types are wrong` is fine). Line and block comments are read. `@ts-check` is not reported.

upstream.note: the options (`minimumDescriptionLength`, per-directive settings, `descriptionFormat`) keep their defaults

rules.why:
`@ts-ignore` hides every type error on the next line and keeps hiding them after the code changes, so a later, real error on that line is never shown. `@ts-nocheck` turns checking off for the whole file. `@ts-expect-error` is safer, because the compiler complains when the error is gone, but without a reason nobody knows when it is safe to remove.

To fix, remove the error with a proper type, or use `@ts-expect-error` with a short reason.

rules.description: Reports a type alias of an object type (`type T = { a: 1 }`, also `{}` and an index signature type). A union, an intersection or any other type in an alias is not reported.

upstream.note: only the default `interface` style

rules.why:
An `interface` and an object type alias describe the same shape, but interfaces can be extended and merged, and the compiler reports their errors with the name of the interface instead of the expanded type. One form in a code base is easier to search.

To fix, write `interface T { a: 1 }`.

rules.description: Reports an import in a TypeScript file whose names are all used only as types (also in `typeof` of a type) and is not written `import type`, a mixed import with such a name (the value names stay in an `import`), and the type form `import("a").B`. A name that is not used at all is not reported.

upstream.note: the options keep their defaults (`prefer` type-imports, `fixStyle` separate-type-imports); `emitDecoratorMetadata` is not known, so a file with decorators is checked

rules.why:
An import used only for types is erased when the file is compiled, but the compiler cannot always know that, so a plain `import` may stay as a real load with side effects, and a cycle between files can appear that the types did not need. `import type` states it, so the import is always removed.

To fix, write `import type { T } from 'x'` or `import { type T } from 'x'`.

rules.description: Reports a getter written with `get name() {}` (in a class or an object literal) that does not return a value on every path: an empty body, a `return;` without a value, or an `if` without `else` that returns only in one branch. A getter that always throws is not reported, and neither is a `get` function given to `Object.defineProperty`.

upstream.note: the getters of Object.defineProperty and Reflect.defineProperty descriptors are not checked

rules.why:
A property read calls the getter and takes its result, so a path without a value makes the property `undefined`, usually by a forgotten `return` rather than by intent.

To fix, return a value on every path.

rules.description: Reports `new Promise(async ...)`: an `async` function (or arrow function) as the executor, with or without a second argument.
rules.why:
The `Promise` constructor ignores what its executor returns. An error thrown in an `async` executor rejects the promise the executor returned, which nobody holds, so the new promise never settles and the caller waits forever; the error shows up only as an unhandled rejection, if at all.

To fix, give the executor as a normal function and call `resolve` and `reject` yourself, or drop `new Promise` and write an `async` function that returns the value.

rules.description: Reports a `let`, `const`, `using`, function or class declared directly in a `case` or `default` clause. A declaration inside a block in the clause (`case 1: { let a; }`) is not reported, and neither is `var`.
rules.why:
A lexical declaration in a `case` clause is scoped to the whole `switch` block, not to the clause, so the other clauses can see the name and, when execution jumps over the declaration, reading it throws a `ReferenceError`. The code reads as if each clause had its own scope, and it does not.

To fix, put the body of the clause in braces: `case 1: { let b = 1; break; }`.

rules.description: Reports an assignment to a class that is declared by name (`class K {} K = 1;`).
rules.why:
A class declaration creates a binding, and replacing it means the name stops standing for the class: later code that uses the name (`new K()`) gets something else, and the class is no longer reachable by that name.

To fix, assign to another variable, or declare the class with `let K = class {}` where reassigning is intended.

rules.description: Reports a comparison with `-0` on either side of `==`, `!=`, `===`, `!==`, `<`, `<=`, `>` or `>=`. `Object.is(x, -0)` and a comparison with `+0` are not reported.
rules.why:
`-0` and `0` are different values but compare as equal: `0 === -0` is `true`. So `x === -0` is also true for plain zero, and the check does not do what it reads like.

To fix, use `Object.is(x, -0)`, which tells them apart.

rules.description: Reports a write to a `const` variable after its declaration: an assignment, `++` or `--`, or a destructuring target (`[c] = [1]`). The initializer is not a write.
rules.why:
Assigning to a `const` throws a `TypeError` when the line runs, so the program fails where the change was meant.

To fix, declare the variable with `let`, or stop reassigning it.

rules.description: Reports a statement or a call that stops the program in a debugger: a `debugger;` statement, a call of one of the `calls` of the language (Python `breakpoint()`, `pdb.set_trace()`), or an import matching the option `imports`. A language lists its calls in its grammar's `rule` row.

options.description: Calls that start a debugger
options.name: calls

options.description: An import of a debugger module
options.name: imports

rules.why:
A debugger call left in the code stops the program for whoever runs it, and in production it hangs a request or a process. It is always a leftover.

To fix, delete the statement.

rules.description: Reports `delete` applied to a plain variable name, also in parentheses (`delete x`, `delete (x)`). `delete x.y` and `delete x[0]` remove a property and are not reported.
rules.why:
`delete` removes object properties, not variables. On a variable it does nothing in sloppy mode (the expression is `false`) and is a syntax error in strict mode and in modules, so the code either has no effect or does not run.

To fix, assign `undefined` to the variable or leave the scope, or delete the property of an object instead.

rules.description: Reports a class member whose name is already used by another member of the class: two methods, two fields, a field and a method, two getters. A getter with its setter may share a name, and so may a `static` and an instance member.
rules.why:
When two members have one name, the later one silently replaces the earlier, so the first body is dead code. It is usually a copy-paste mistake where the second member was meant to have another name.

To fix, rename one of them or delete the one that is not used.

rules.description: Reports an `else if` whose condition cannot be true at that point: it repeats a condition of an earlier branch of the chain (`if (a) {} else if (a) {}`), or each operand of its `||` is a whole earlier condition or an operand of an earlier `||` (`if (a || b) {} else if (a) {}`). A condition that is only implied by an earlier one (`a && b` after `a`) is not found.
rules.why:
If an earlier condition was true its branch ran, and if it was false the same condition is false again, so the later branch never runs. This is nearly always a copy-paste slip where the condition was not changed, and the code the author meant to run is the dead one.

To fix, correct the condition or remove the branch.

rules.description: Reports an enum member initialised with a string or number that an earlier member of the same enum already has (`A = 0, B = 0`). Computed values (`1 + 1`) are not compared.
rules.why:
Two names for one value make a value to name lookup (the reverse mapping of a numeric enum) answer with the later one, and the second member is usually a copy-paste mistake with the value not changed.

To fix, give the member its own value.

rules.description: Reports an `else` when the `if` and every `else if` before it end in `return` (what the `else` itself holds does not matter). An `else if` is not reported, and neither is a chain in which one of the earlier branches can fall through.

upstream.note: the allowElseIf option and the skip for an else that declares names are not supported; one extra report in the three.js corpus (98 matched)

rules.why:
When every earlier branch returns, the code in the `else` can follow the `if` without the `else`, which removes one level of nesting and makes the early return plain.

To fix, delete the `else` and de-indent its body.

rules.description: Reports `[]` in a regex literal. `[^]` (any character) and a `[]` in the string given to `new RegExp` are not reported.
rules.why:
A character class with no members can match nothing, so a regex that contains it never matches. It is nearly always an escape that was forgotten (`\[\]` meant) or a class whose content was deleted.

To fix, add the characters, or escape the brackets.

rules.description: Reports the type `{}` (also in `type T = {}`) and an interface with no members that extends at most one type. `{}` in an intersection (`{} & X`) and an interface that extends two types are not reported.
