upstream.note: the options (`allowInterfaces`, `allowObjectTypes`, `allowWithName`) keep their defaults

rules.why:
`{}` does not mean an empty object: it accepts every value except `null` and `undefined`, numbers and strings included. An empty interface that only extends one type is the same as that type.

To fix, write `object` for any non-primitive, `unknown` for any value, `Record<string, never>` for an empty object, or the type itself.

rules.description: Reports a destructuring pattern with nothing in it: `{}` or `[]` in a declaration, a parameter, an assignment target or nested in another pattern (`var {a: {}} = x`). A default value in a pattern (`{a = {}}`) is not an empty pattern.
rules.why:
An empty pattern binds no name, so the statement does nothing but check that the value is not `null` or `undefined`. It is usually a mistake for a default value: `function f({a: {}}) {}` was meant to be `function f({a = {}}) {}`, and the parameter stays without a default.

To fix, write the names to bind, or the default with `=`.

rules.description: Reports the `any` type wherever a type is written (`let a: any`, `any[]`, a constraint such as `T extends any`).

upstream.note: the options (`ignoreRestArgs`, `fixToUnknown`) keep their defaults

rules.why:
`any` turns off type checking for everything that touches the value, and the value spreads: a call result, a property and an assignment of an `any` are `any` too, so one hole hides errors far from where it is written.

To fix, use `unknown` (it must be checked before use) or a real type.

rules.description: Reports `!!x` and `Boolean(x)` in a place that already converts the value to a boolean: the test of `if`, `while`, `do ... while`, `for` and `?:`, the operand of `!`, and the argument of `Boolean(...)`. `const b = !!x`, a call argument (`f(!!x)`) and `!!(x)` are not reported.

upstream.note: the `enforceForLogicalOperands` option is not supported

rules.why:
The cast changes nothing where the language already tests for truthiness, so it only adds noise and can suggest that the plain value is not allowed there. Where the real boolean is needed (an assignment, an argument), the cast does a job and is left alone.

To fix, remove the `!!` or the `Boolean(...)` call.

rules.description: Reports a second non-null assertion in a row (`a!!.b`) and a `!` right before an optional chain (`a!?.b`, `a!?.()`).
rules.why:
The second `!` of `a!!` changes nothing. In `a!?.b` the `!` says the value is not `null` while `?.` says it may be, so one of the two is wrong and the reader cannot tell which.

To fix, remove the extra `!`, or the `?.` if the value cannot be null.

rules.description: Reports an assignment to a function that is declared by name (`function f() {} f = 0;`), also `f++`.
rules.why:
A function declaration is hoisted, so calls above the assignment run the original and calls below run the new value. The name then means two things in one scope, and the declaration reads as the only definition.

To fix, assign to another variable, or declare the function with `let f = function () {}` where reassigning is intended.

rules.description: Reports a write to an imported name (`import a from 'a'; a = 1`, `bb = 2`), and a write to a member of a namespace import (`ns.x = 1`), a `delete ns.y` and `Object.assign(ns, {})`.
rules.why:
Imports are read-only live views of the exporting module. Assigning to one throws a `TypeError` in module code, and the namespace object of `import * as ns` cannot be changed either.

To fix, keep the value in a local variable, or let the exporting module offer a function that changes it.

rules.description: Reports a type annotation on a variable, parameter or class property whose initial value already gives that type (`const a: number = 5`, `s: string = 'x'`, `b: boolean = true`, `n: bigint = 1n`). A value from a call, a `readonly` property and an optional property are not reported.

example.input:
let a: "a" = "a", b: "a" = 'a', c: 1 = 1, d: string = "a";
class C { p: "a" = "a"; q = 1 as 1; r = <"a">"a"; s = "a" as "b"; }

upstream.note: the options (`ignoreParameters`, `ignoreProperties`) keep their defaults

rules.why:
The compiler infers the same type from the value, so the annotation only adds a second place to keep in sync.

To fix, drop the annotation.

rules.description: Reports unusual whitespace characters: vertical tab, form feed, no-break space (U+00A0), the spaces and zero-width characters U+2000 to U+200B, line and paragraph separators, narrow no-break space, medium mathematical space, ideographic space, and a byte order mark that is not at the start of the file. A string literal is not checked (the character is data there); comments, template literals and regex literals are. A run of them is one report.
rules.why:
These characters look like a space (or like nothing) but are different characters: a search for a space does not find them, a diff shows no change, and in code outside a string or comment some of them make the file fail to parse. They usually arrive by copying text from a web page or a document.

To fix, replace them with an ordinary space, or write the character as an escape (`\u00a0`) where it is wanted.

rules.description: Reports an `if` that is the only statement of an `else` block (`else { if (b) { ... } }`), also when that `if` has its own `else`. An `else` block with other statements, and an `if` inside an `else if`, are not reported.
rules.why:
`else { if (b) ... }` is the same as `else if (b) ...` and has one more level of nesting and braces for the reader to follow.

To fix, write `else if`.

rules.description: Reports a number literal that the 64-bit double it becomes does not hold exactly: `9007199254740993` (above 2^53), `0x20000000000001`, a value that is too large (`1e400`, becomes `Infinity`) or too small (`2e-400`, becomes `0`). `9007199254740992`, `0.1`, a number that has an exact double (`1e20`) and BigInt literals (`123n`) are not reported.
rules.why:
JavaScript rounds such a literal when the file is read, so the program computes with another number than the one written, with no error. Integers above 2^53 lose their last digits, which breaks ids and counters.

To fix, use a BigInt literal (`9007199254740993n`), keep the value in a string, or write the number the double really holds.

rules.description: Reports `new` and `constructor` declarations that do not describe a constructor: a class method signature `new(): C;` without a body that returns the class itself, an interface signature `new (): I` that returns the interface itself, and an interface member named `constructor()`. A class method named `new` with a body is not reported.
rules.why:
An interface cannot be constructed, so `new (): I` inside `interface I` describes a constructor that does not exist, and an interface member `constructor()` is only a method with that name, not a constructor. The code reads as a constructor but is not one.

To fix, declare the constructor in the class (`constructor()`), or put the `new` signature on a separate interface that types the constructor.

rules.description: Reports a `namespace N {}` or `module N {}` declaration, also a dotted `namespace A.B {}`. `declare module "x"`, `declare global`, and any namespace in a `.d.ts` file are not reported.

upstream.note: the option `allowDeclarations` keeps its default

rules.why:
A TypeScript namespace is an older way to group code that does not exist in JavaScript: it compiles to an object built by a function, cannot be tree-shaken well and is not understood by tools that only strip types. ES modules do the same grouping and are the standard.

To fix, move the members to a module file and `export` them.

rules.description: Reports a non-null assertion on the end of an optional chain: `a?.b!` and `(a?.b)!`. `a?.b!.c` is not reported.
rules.why:
An optional chain returns `undefined` when `a` is missing, so asserting its result is not `undefined` contradicts the chain, and the program will fail at run time when the assumption is wrong.

To fix, handle the missing value, or drop `?.` if `a` cannot be null.

rules.description: Reports a non-null assertion (`a!`, `a!.b`) in a TypeScript file.
rules.why:
`a!` tells the compiler the value is not `null` or `undefined` without checking it. When the assumption is wrong the program fails at run time with a `TypeError`, in the place the type system was meant to protect.

To fix, check the value (`if (a)`) or use optional chaining (`a?.b`) and handle the missing case.

rules.description: Reports a number literal that starts with `0` followed by another digit, such as `017` or `08`. `0`, `0.5` and the modern forms `0o17`, `0x1F` and `0b11` are not reported.
rules.why:
A leading zero makes a legacy octal literal: `017` is 15, not 17. A literal such as `08` or `09` has a digit that is not octal, so it is read as the decimal 8 or 9, which hides the mistake. Both forms are syntax errors in strict mode and in modules.

To fix, drop the leading zero for a decimal number or write `0o17` for an octal one.

rules.description: Reports a call of `hasOwnProperty`, `isPrototypeOf` or `propertyIsEnumerable` made on an object itself: `obj.hasOwnProperty(k)`, `obj?.hasOwnProperty(k)` and `obj['hasOwnProperty'](k)`. Reading the property without a call, and `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(obj, k)`, are not reported.
rules.why:
The method comes from the prototype chain, and the object may not have it. `Object.create(null)` objects have no `hasOwnProperty`, so the call throws, and data from outside (a parsed JSON with a key `"hasOwnProperty"`) can replace the method with its own value.

To fix, call it from the prototype: `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(obj, k)`, or use `Object.hasOwn(obj, k)` where the target supports it.

rules.description: Reports a call of the global `require(...)` and an `import x = require(...)`. A `require` that the file declares itself (a parameter, for example) is not reported.

upstream.note: the options (`allow`, `allowAsImport`) keep their defaults; a `require` the file declares itself is not reported

rules.why:
`require` is the CommonJS loader and is not typed like an import: the result is `any` unless a type is added, and bundlers and the compiler cannot always follow it. An `import` is checked by the type system and understood by tools.

To fix, use `import`.

rules.description: Reports a variable, function, class, parameter or function-expression name that is `NaN`, `Infinity`, `eval`, `arguments` or `undefined`. `var undefined;` without a value is not reported.

upstream.note: without scope analysis `var undefined;` is accepted whatever is assigned to it later

rules.why:
These names are read as the global values everywhere else in the program. A local called `undefined` or `NaN` changes what a test such as `x === undefined` means inside its scope, and a variable named `eval` or `arguments` is a syntax error in strict mode.

To fix, rename the variable.

rules.description: Reports a hole in an array literal, at the extra comma: `[1, , 2]` and `[, 1]`. A single trailing comma (`[1, ]`) is not a hole.
rules.why:
A hole is an index with no element. `[1, , 2]` has the length 3, and methods such as `forEach` and `map` skip the hole while `for` loops and spread read it as `undefined`, so the same array behaves differently depending on how it is read. It is nearly always a typo for a single comma.

To fix, remove the extra comma, or write `undefined` (or `null`) where a value is meant.

rules.description: Reports `const self = this`, `let self = this` and `self = this`: a variable that holds `this`. Destructuring `this` (`const { x } = this`) is not reported.

upstream.note: the options (`allowDestructuring`, `allowedNames`) keep their defaults

rules.why:
The alias is a leftover of code that needed `this` inside a function that has its own `this`. An arrow function takes the `this` of the surrounding code without it, and the alias lets a reader take `self` for something other than `this`.

To fix, use an arrow function, or `bind`.

rules.description: Reports a line that begins with `(`, `[` or a template literal right after a line that ends an expression, where the two lines are one expression: `var d = a` followed by `(b);` calls `a(b)`. A line that begins with `/`, `+` or another operator is not reported.

example.input:
const a = b
  (c || d).e();

rules.why:
Automatic semicolon insertion does not insert a semicolon before `(`, `[` or a template, so the new line continues the expression above: `a` followed by `(b)` is a call and followed by `[b]` is a property access, and the program runs with a different meaning than the layout shows.

To fix, end the statement with a semicolon, or join the lines on purpose.

rules.description: Reports a type parameter constrained to `any` or `unknown` (`<T extends unknown>`, also with a default).
rules.why:
Every type parameter already accepts any type, so `extends unknown` and `extends any` restrict nothing and add noise (`extends any` also lets a reader think the check is turned off by choice).

To fix, remove the constraint.

rules.description: Reports a conditional expression whose two arms are both boolean literals: `a ? true : false` (the same as `!!a`), `a ? false : true` (`!a`), and `a ? true : true`. A conditional with one non-boolean arm is not reported.

upstream.note: the `defaultAssignment` option is not supported

rules.why:
The condition is already the boolean value, or its negation, so the conditional only restates it in a longer form.

To fix, write the condition (or `!` of it); use `Boolean(a)` where a real boolean is needed from a value that is not one.

rules.description: Reports `return`, `throw`, and a `break` or `continue` that leaves the `finally` block, written in a `finally`. A `break` or `continue` of a loop inside the block, and a `return` in a function declared in the block, are not reported.
rules.why:
A jump out of `finally` replaces how the `try` ended: a `return` there discards the value returned by the `try` and swallows an exception that was being thrown, so errors disappear without a trace.

To fix, move the jump out of `finally` (after the `try` statement), or handle the error in a `catch`.

rules.description: Reports the global type `Function` used as a type, as an `interface ... extends` target and as an `implements` target. A class that `extends Function` (a value) is not reported.
rules.why:
`Function` accepts any callable value, and calling one takes any arguments and returns `any`, so the compiler no longer checks the call.

To fix, write the signature (`(x: number) => string`), or `(...args: never[]) => unknown` for any function without losing the check.

rules.description: Reports `!a in b` and `!a instanceof B`, where the `!` is written without parentheses on the left operand. `!(a in b)` and `(!a) in b` are not reported.

upstream.note: the `enforceForOrderingRelations` option is not supported

rules.why:
The `!` binds tighter than `in` and `instanceof`, so `!a in b` tests whether the key `false` (the negation of `a`) is in `b`, and `!a instanceof B` is always `false` for a boolean. The test the author meant, the negation of the whole expression, is never made.

To fix, write `!(a in b)` or `!(a instanceof B)`.

rules.description: Reports a `catch` clause whose only statement is `throw` of the caught error, as in `catch (e) { throw e; }`. It is also reported when the `try` has a `finally`. A `catch` that does more, or that throws something else, is not reported.
rules.why:
A catch that only rethrows has the same effect as no catch: the error goes on up with its stack, so the clause is noise that makes a reader look for handling that is not there.

To fix, delete the `catch` (keep the `finally`, if there is one) or handle the error there.

rules.description: Reports a backslash before a character that needs no escape, in a string (`'\d'`), a template literal or a regex literal (`/\-/`, `/\_/`). Valid escapes (`\n`, `\t`, `\\`, `\'`, `\"`, `\x41`, `\u0041`, `\0`, a line continuation) are not reported, and neither are a `\-` in the middle of a character class (`/[a\-z]/`), `\^` at the start of one and `\/` in a regex literal.

upstream.note: regex `v` flag classes are read like `u` classes
`\/` counts as useless, as the plugin reports it

rules.why:
In a string the useless backslash is dropped, so `'\d'` is the letter `d`, which is not what a reader who knows regex expects. In a regex it hides the characters that matter.

To fix, remove the backslash, or write the escape that is meant (`\\d`).

rules.description: Reports an expression statement whose value is thrown away and that has no effect of its own: a name, a literal, a member access or an operator expression (`x + y;`, `x.y;`, `-x;`, `x ? y : z;`). Calls, assignments, `delete` and `void` are not reported; a directive such as `"use strict"` is, as it is a string. What counts as pure is the `#pure` tag of the language's grammar: Python's table has names, literals, member accesses and list, set and dict displays, so `x + 1`, `x == 2` and `-x` are not reported there. Off by default.

upstream.note: the options keep their defaults
the options keep their defaults

rules.why:
The statement is evaluated and dropped, so it does nothing. It is typically a line that was meant to be a call (a missing `()`), a comparison written where an assignment was meant, or what is left of a deleted line.

To fix, delete it, or write the call or the assignment it was meant to be.

rules.description: Reports a `var` declaration (also `declare var` in TypeScript). `let` and `const` are not reported.
rules.why:
A `var` belongs to the whole function, not to the block, and is hoisted: it can be read before its line (as `undefined`) and declared twice in one scope without an error. `let` and `const` are limited to their block, a second declaration is an error, and `const` states that the binding does not change.

To fix, use `const` where the variable is not assigned again, otherwise `let`.

rules.description: Reports a `with` statement.
rules.why:
Inside `with (obj) { ... }` every name may be a property of `obj` or a variable, and which one it is depends on `obj` at run time, so neither a reader nor a tool can tell what `b` in `with (a) { b }` refers to. The statement is a syntax error in strict mode and in ES modules, so a file that uses it cannot be turned into a module later.

To fix, name the object in each access (`a.b`) or copy the properties you need into variables before the block.

rules.description: Reports the global types `BigInt`, `Boolean`, `Number`, `Object`, `String` and `Symbol` used as type names. The lower-case primitives are not reported.
rules.why:
`String` and the like are the types of the wrapper objects (`new String('a')`), not of the primitive values, and a primitive is assignable to them only by accident of the language. `Object` accepts every value except `null` and `undefined`, numbers and strings included.

To fix, write `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `bigint` or `symbol`; for any non-primitive value write `object`.

rules.description: Reports a literal type that only repeats the literal it is given: `let a: 'a' = 'a'`, `'a' as 'a'` and `<'a'>'a'`. A type that differs from the value (`let a: 'a' = 'b'` is a type error, not reported) and `as const` are not reported.

example.input:
let a: "a" = "a", b: "a" = 'a', c: 1 = 1, d: string = "a";
class C { p: "a" = "a"; q = 1 as 1; r = <"a">"a"; s = "a" as "b"; }

rules.why:
The literal is written twice and the two copies can drift apart when one is edited. `as const` says it once and keeps the literal type.

To fix, write `let a = 'a' as const`.

rules.description: Reports a `let` variable that is assigned once and could be a `const`: the single write is its initializer, a `for-in` or `for-of` head, or the first assignment statement in the same block as the declaration. A variable written in a nested block or function, a `let` of a `for (;;)` head, and a destructuring that assigns members or outer names are not reported.

upstream.note: the options keep their defaults (`destructuring: any`, `ignoreReadBeforeAssign: false`)

rules.why:
A `let` says the variable changes. When it never does, the keyword misleads the reader into looking for the later assignment, and `const` lets the compiler stop one.

To fix, write `const`.

rules.description: Reports `arguments` used in an ordinary function, except as the object of a member read by name (`arguments.length`). `arguments[0]` and passing `arguments` on are reported; an arrow function has no `arguments` of its own and is not checked.
rules.why:
`arguments` is an array-like object, not an array, and is tied to the function in ways that disable some optimizations, so `arguments.map(...)` fails. A rest parameter (`...args`) is a real array and shows in the parameter list.

To fix, declare `...args`.

rules.description: Reports `f.apply(undefined, args)`, `f.apply(null, args)`, `o.m.apply(o, args)` and `o['m'].apply(o, args)`, where the first argument is `null`, `undefined`, or the same object that the method is read from. `f.apply(this, args)`, `o.m.apply(p, args)` with another object, and an array literal or a spread (`...args`) as the arguments are not reported.
rules.why:
When the call keeps the same `this`, `apply` only spreads an array into arguments, which the spread syntax says directly: `f(...args)` and `o.m(...args)`. The `apply` form needs the reader to know the first argument is ignored.

To fix, write the call with `...args`.

rules.description: Reports a name declared again in the same scope (`var` twice, a `var` and a parameter, two functions). In TypeScript files declaration merging (interfaces, namespaces, a class with an interface) is allowed. Built-in globals are not checked.

upstream.note: the `builtinGlobals` option and `/*global*/` comments are not supported (the files are modules, whose top scope is not the global scope)
`builtinGlobals` and `/*global*/` comments are not supported; `ignoreDeclarationMerge` keeps its default

rules.why:
The second declaration replaces or merges with the first, so the earlier one is dead, and which of the two a use reaches depends on the order. It is usually a copy that should have had another name.

To fix, remove the repeat, or rename one of them.

rules.description: Reports a generator (`function*`, a generator method, `async function*`) that has statements but no `yield`. An empty generator is not reported.
rules.why:
A generator that never yields produces no values: iterating it runs the body once and ends at once. That is the mistake of a `function*` that was meant to be a normal function, or of a `yield` that was left out.

To fix, add the `yield`, or drop the `*`.

rules.description: Reports a variable, parameter or function with the name of one declared in a scope around it. A function declared later in the outer scope still counts (it is hoisted), a variable declared later does not, and `var a = function a() {}` is not a shadow. In TypeScript files a type and a value of one name, and the parameters of function types, are not reported.

options.description: Names that may shadow.
options.name: allow

options.description: The declarations that are checked for shadowing something (empty: all).
options.name: kinds

upstream.note: the options keep their defaults (`builtinGlobals` off, `hoist` functions, `allow` empty, `ignoreOnInitialization` off)
the options keep their defaults

rules.why:
The inner name hides the outer one for the rest of its scope, so the same word means two things, and a change that was meant for the outer variable lands on the inner one or the reverse.

To fix, rename the inner variable.

rules.description: Reports a `/// <reference path="x" />` or `/// <reference types="x" />` before the first statement of the file; for `types` only when the file also imports that module. A directive after the first statement is not reported.

upstream.note: the options (`lib`, `path`, `types`) keep their defaults

rules.why:
Triple-slash references are the older way to include files and types before modules. An `import` states the dependency where it is used, is followed by bundlers and other tools, and does not depend on the order of directives.

To fix, replace the reference with an `import` (an `import type` where only types are needed).

rules.description: Reports a name that no scope declares, that is not a global of ES2026 (or, in a `.cjs` file, `require`, `module`, `exports` and `global`) and that is not in the option `globals`. `typeof x` and JSX tags are not reported.

example.input:
<?php

function f(int $a, $b = 1) {
    $x = $a + $b;
    [$p, $q] = g();
    foreach ($arr as $k => $v) {
        echo $k . $v . $p . $q . $x;
    }
    try {
        h($m);
    } catch (Exception $e) {
        echo $e;
    }
    $r = function () use ($x) {
        return $x + $undefined;
    };
    $s = fn($z) => $z + $x;
    global $gg;
    static $st = 0;
    $x++;
    preg_match('/a/', $a, $m2);
    $list[] = 1;
    echo $gg . $st . $m2 . $list . Foo::$bar . $this->z . $_GET['a'];
    echo isset($maybe) ? "$x {$y}" : '';
    return $s;
}

function g() {
    return $top;
}

function h() {
    extract($data);
    return $name;
}

$top = 1;
echo $top . $nowhere;

options.description: Names the environment declares (ESLint's `languageOptions.globals`), such as `window` or `console`.
options.name: globals

upstream.note: the `typeof` option keeps its default; `languageOptions.globals` is the rule's `globals` option, and `/*global*/` comments are not read; JSX tags are not references

Only a variable that nothing in its function assigns (PHPStan's level 0 reports exactly those); a variable passed to a call counts as assigned, and a function with `extract`, `parse_str`, `include` or `$$x` is not checked.

rules.why:
An undeclared name fails with a ReferenceError when the line runs, or it silently creates a global when it is assigned. A typo in a name is the usual cause.

To fix, declare the name, import it, or add it to `globals` if the environment provides it.

rules.description: Reports a reference that comes before the declaration of what it names in the source (function declarations included), or that runs while the variable is being initialized. References in types are not reported.

options.description: Check function declarations.
options.name: functions

options.description: Check class declarations.
options.name: classes

options.description: Check `var`, `let` and `const` variables.
options.name: variables

upstream.note: the options keep their defaults; JSX tags are not references
the options keep their defaults

rules.why:
A `let`, `const` or class read before its declaration fails at run time, and a `var` is `undefined` until then. Even where it works (a hoisted function), a reader meets the use before the definition.

To fix, move the declaration above its first use.

rules.description: Reports a comparison with `NaN` (`NaN` or `Number.NaN` on either side of `==`, `!=`, `===`, `!==`, `<`, `>`...), and `NaN` as the `switch` discriminant or as a `case` test. `isNaN(a)` and `Number.isNaN(a)` are not reported.

upstream.note: the `enforceForIndexOf` option is not supported; a local `NaN` is not told from the global

rules.why:
`NaN` is not equal to any value, itself included, so `a === NaN` is always `false` and `a !== NaN` is always `true`; a `switch` on `NaN` never matches a case, because it compares with `===`. The check never does what it reads like.

To fix, use `Number.isNaN(a)`, which is true only for `NaN`; the global `isNaN` first converts its argument to a number.

rules.description: Reports a `typeof` comparison whose other side is a string that `typeof` never returns (a typo such as `'strnig'`, or `'null'`), or the identifier `undefined` instead of the string `'undefined'`. A string template, a variable and a valid type name are not reported.

upstream.note: the `requireStringLiterals` option is not supported

rules.why:
`typeof` returns one of `"undefined"`, `"object"`, `"boolean"`, `"number"`, `"bigint"`, `"string"`, `"symbol"` or `"function"`. A comparison with any other string is always false, and a typo then silently turns a type check into dead code. `typeof a === undefined` compares a string with the value `undefined`, which is never true either (and `typeof null` is `"object"`, not `"null"`).

To fix, use one of the eight names, as a string.

rules.description: Reports an argument list of a call that the Kotlin formatter would wrap or join differently: the arguments on one line when they fit, one per line when they do not.
rules.why:
A call whose arguments are wrapped in a mixed way (two on the first line, the rest below, aligned to the bracket) is hard to scan and makes a diff show a change on every line when one argument is renamed. One layout for all lists lets the formatter apply it and keeps the diffs small.

To fix, run the formatter, which lays the list out.

rules.description: Reports a declaration (function, property, class, object, typealias) with a blank line before it that the formatter would add or remove. Declarations with comments or annotations before them are included.
rules.why:
Blank lines show where one declaration ends and the next one begins. A file that is consistent shows the structure at a glance, and a formatter that keeps the same spacing does not turn up as a diff on each save.

To fix, run the formatter.

rules.description: Reports a `when` entry with a blank line before it that the formatter would add or remove.
rules.why:
Blank lines between the entries of a `when` are laid out by one rule, so the spacing does not depend on the author and is not changed by hand.

To fix, run the formatter.

rules.description: Reports a call chain (`a.b().c()`, with `?.` too) whose line breaks differ from what the formatter writes.
rules.why:
A chain that is broken in some places and not in others hides which calls belong together, and a later edit adds or moves breaks. One layout for all chains makes each step visible and keeps the diff small.

To fix, run the formatter.

rules.description: Reports a class, interface or object whose name starts with a lowercase letter or an underscore.

example.input:
class my_class
class Good
interface other
object lower
object Fine
class `a name`

upstream.note: Names in backticks are accepted; no test-file exceptions.

rules.why:
Kotlin follows the convention that types are in PascalCase, so a lowercase name reads as a variable or a function and is mistaken for one at the call site.

To fix, rename the class to PascalCase.

rules.description: Reports a class header (name, constructor, supertypes) that the formatter would lay out differently.
rules.why:
A long class header is laid out by fixed rules, so that all classes of a project look the same and a change to one parameter is one line in the diff.

To fix, run the formatter.

rules.description: Reports an enum entry whose name is neither PascalCase nor UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (`a` in `enum class E { a, B }`).

example.input:
enum class E { a, B, C_D, _e, FooBar }
enum class F { `1x flows`, G_1, _2BIG }

rules.why:
Enum entries are constants, and the conventions for constants are `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` or, since Kotlin reads them as objects, `PascalCase`. A lowercase entry reads as a property.

To fix, rename the entry in one of the two styles.

rules.description: Reports a `.kt` file whose name, up to its first dot, is not in PascalCase. The check that a file with a single class is named after it is not made.

example.input: package a

options.description: Regular expression the file name up to its first dot must match; empty: not checked.
options.name: pattern

upstream.note: A file with a single class is not checked against the class name

rules.why:
Kotlin files that hold a class are named after it, and the convention for all files is PascalCase. A file named `my-file.kt` has a name that cannot be the name of a class in it, and tools that match file and class names do not find it.

To fix, rename the file (`MyFile.kt`).

rules.description: Reports a function with a block body that is only a `return`, which the formatter would write as an expression body (`fun f(): Int { return 1 }` is `fun f(): Int = 1`).
rules.why:
A function with a single `return` as its body is clearer as an expression: the type is inferred and a line of braces goes away. One style makes functions of that kind look the same.

To fix, run the formatter, or write the expression body.

rules.description: Reports a function whose name does not match the expression set for its kind: camel case; a function with a declared return type may also be a factory named in Pascal case. A function that is an `override` or `@Composable` is not reported.

options.description: Regular expression the name of a `@Composable` function must match.
options.name: composables

options.description: Regular expression the name of an `override` function must match.
options.name: overridden

options.description: Regular expression the name of a function with a declared return type must match.
options.name: factories

options.description: Regular expression the name of any other function must match.
options.name: functions

upstream.note: `@Composable`, `override` and backtick names are left alone; a factory function is a capitalised name with a declared return type

rules.why:
Kotlin code reads functions in camel case, and a name in another case reads as a class or a constant. Factory functions that look like constructors (`Foo()`) and Compose functions are an exception by convention.

To fix, rename the function to camel case.

rules.description: Reports a function whose signature (everything up to the body) the formatter would lay out differently: the parameters on one line or one per line, the return type, and where the body starts.
rules.why:
A signature that is laid out the same way in the whole project is quick to scan, and when a parameter is added only one line changes.

To fix, run the formatter.

rules.description: Reports an import list that the formatter would reorder or rewrite.
rules.why:
Imports in a fixed order make it easy to find one, and two developers who add an import in the same place do not conflict.

To fix, run the formatter.

rules.description: Reports an expression that spans lines and starts after code on its line: the value of a property or a function body after `=`, or an argument.
rules.why:
An expression that begins after `val a = ` and goes on over several lines has its first line far from the left edge and the rest below, so the shape of the block is hard to read. A new line before it gives it a place of its own.

To fix, start the expression on the next line.

rules.description: Reports an `if` whose line breaks the formatter would change.
rules.why:
An `if` and `else` that are split over lines in an arbitrary way are hard to read, and a line added to a branch that has no braces is not part of it. One layout for every `if` avoids both.

To fix, run the formatter.

rules.description: Reports a bracket, comma or arrow where the formatter would break the line, or add a trailing comma.
rules.why:
A list that wraps in one place and not in another has a layout that depends on who wrote it. One rule for the line breaks, and the trailing comma of a wrapped list, makes it independent of the author.

To fix, run the formatter.

rules.description: Reports a class or interface with `{ }` and nothing in it (`class A {}`).

upstream.note: Comments inside the braces do not count as content.

rules.why:
An empty body adds two characters and says nothing. Kotlin does not need the braces for a class without members.

To fix, delete the braces: `class A`.

rules.description: Reports a `.kt` file with nothing in it but a package, imports and comments.

example.input:
package a

import b.C

rules.why:
A file without a declaration is a leftover of a deleted class, or one that was never filled, and it still compiles and shows up in the project.

To fix, delete the file, or add the declaration.

rules.description: Reports a function with a block body that declares `: Unit` as its return type.
rules.why:
`Unit` is what a function returns by default, so writing it repeats the language and distracts a reader who looks for a type that matters.

To fix, delete `: Unit`.

rules.description: Reports a package whose name has an uppercase letter or an underscore.

example.input:
package a.My_pkg

val x = 1

rules.why:
Package names in Kotlin and Java are in lowercase, joined without underscores, so a name with capitals looks like a class and does not match the directory on file systems that ignore case.

To fix, write the name in lowercase.

rules.description: Reports a parameter list that the formatter would wrap or join differently.
rules.why:
A function with a long parameter list is laid out by a fixed rule, so that the layout does not depend on the author and a new parameter is one line in the diff.

To fix, run the formatter.

rules.description: Reports a property whose name does not match the expression set for its kind: a `const val` is in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE; top-level and object properties may also be written as constants; a backing property may start with `_`; an `override` is not reported.

options.description: Regular expression the name of a `const val` must match; empty: not checked.
options.name: constants

options.description: Regular expression the name of an `override` property must match.
options.name: overridden

options.description: Regular expression the name of a property of an object must match.
options.name: singleton_members

options.description: Regular expression the name of a top-level property must match.
options.name: top_level

options.description: Regular expression the name of any other property (a member of a class, a local) must match.
options.name: members

upstream.note: `override` properties are left alone; `_name` backing properties are not matched to a property

rules.why:
The case of a name tells a reader if it is a constant or a variable. A `const val` in camel case reads as a variable that can change, and a mutable property in capitals reads as a constant.

To fix, rename the property to the style of its kind.

rules.description: Reports a block whose line breaks the formatter would change, such as several statements on one line (`{ a(); b() }`).
rules.why:
One statement to a line is the layout every Kotlin reader expects, and a second statement after a `;` is easily missed. It also makes a diff show a change to the statement and not to its neighbour.

To fix, run the formatter.

rules.description: Reports the last argument of a multi-line call that has a trailing comma the formatter would add or remove.
rules.why:
With a trailing comma, adding an argument at the end changes one line instead of two, and moving arguments does not need the comma moved. A project that chooses one form gets the same diff everywhere.

To fix, run the formatter.

rules.description: Reports the last parameter of a multi-line declaration that has a trailing comma the formatter would add or remove.
rules.why:
With a trailing comma, adding a parameter at the end changes one line instead of two, and reordering parameters does not need the comma moved.

To fix, run the formatter.

rules.description: Reports a `when` entry whose first line the formatter would change.
rules.why:
Entries of one `when` that are written in different ways (some with braces, some without, in different line layouts) look as if the difference meant something. One layout for all entries makes a real difference stand out.

To fix, run the formatter.

rules.description: Reports a rule whose recipe has more lines than the `max` option. Every physical line counts, a continued command and a tab-indented comment included.

example.input:
build:
	echo 1
	echo 2
	echo 3
	echo 4
	echo 5
	echo 6
fine:
	echo 1


blank-before:
	echo 1
	echo 2
	echo 3
	echo 4
	echo 5
	echo 6

options.description: The most lines a recipe may have.
options.name: max

upstream.note: checkmake ends a recipe at a blank line, a comment line without a tab or a conditional; Sudsy follows make, where they belong to the recipe.

rules.why:
A long recipe is a script that lives in a Makefile, where it is run by `make` through the shell line by line, cannot be tested by itself and is hard to read. A limit moves it to a script file.

To fix, move the commands to a script and call it.

rules.description: Reports a target of the `required` option (default `all`, `clean` and `test`) that is not declared `.PHONY`, on the last `.PHONY` line, or on the last rule when there is none.

example.config:
min-phony:
  level: warn
  options:
    required: [all, build]
example.input:
.PHONY: all test
all:
test:

options.description: The targets every Makefile must declare `.PHONY`.
options.name: required

rules.why:
Conventional targets (`all`, `clean`, `test`) do not name files. If a file with that name appears, `make` considers the target up to date and does nothing.

To fix, add the target to `.PHONY`.

rules.description: Reports a target with no recipe that is not declared `.PHONY`. Targets that start with a `.` are special and are not reported.

example.input:
.PHONY: all clean
all: build
clean:
build:
	echo
.DEFAULT: ;
empty: all
both one two:
$(OBJS): ;

rules.why:
A target without a recipe that is not a file only groups other targets. If a file of that name appears, `make` stops running it, so the behaviour of the Makefile depends on what is in the directory.

To fix, add the target to `.PHONY`.

rules.description: Reports a variable whose value runs `date` and that is not simply expanded (`:=`, `::=`): every use runs `date` again and the values differ within one build.

example.input:
A = $(shell date +%s)
B := $(shell date +%s)
C ?= a date
D = date
E += $(shell date)
F ::= $(shell date)
G != date
foo: H = $(shell date)

rules.why:
A recursively expanded variable (`=`) runs its text each time it is used, so a build that uses `TS = $(shell date)` twice gets two different times, and file names built from it do not match.

To fix, write `TS := $(shell date +%s)`, which runs once.

rules.description: Reports a target defined by more than one rule, which merges prerequisites and overrides recipes. Double-colon rules, `.PHONY` and the targets of the `ignore` option are not reported.

example.input:
a:
	echo
a:
	echo
b::
b::
.PHONY: a
.PHONY: b
c d:
d:

options.description: Targets that may be defined more than once.
options.name: ignore

rules.why:
Several rules for one target add their prerequisites and only one of them may have a recipe; `make` uses the last and warns about the override. The recipe that runs depends on the order of the rules.

To fix, merge the rules, or rename a target.

rules.description: Reports a fenced code block in which every non-blank line starts with `$ `, so it shows commands without their output. A block that has any line without the prompt, such as an output line, is not reported.

example.input:
```sh
$ npm install
$ npm test
```

```sh
$ npm test
all passed
```

```sh
npm test
```

upstream.note: Reported once on the block, markdownlint reports every command line (so no parity fixture); indented code blocks are not checked.

rules.why:
A reader who selects and copies the block gets the `$ ` with each command, and the shell then fails on the first character. Blocks that mix commands and output need the prompt to tell them apart, which is why they are left alone.

To fix, delete the `$ ` prompts, or show the output below the commands.

rules.description: Reports a link whose text is `click here`, `here`, `link` or `more` (in any case) and nothing else.

example.input: [here](https://example.com), [Click here](https://example.com) and [the guide](https://example.com).

upstream.note: No `prohibited_texts` option.

rules.why:
Screen reader users often move from link to link and hear the texts without the text around them, and search engines read the text as a description of the target. `here` says neither where the link goes nor why, and the reader has to read the sentence to find out.

To fix, write the text so that it names the destination: `[the install guide](...)`.

rules.description: Reports a fenced code block that has no info string after the opening fence.

example.input:
```
no language
```

```rust
fn main() {}
```

upstream.note: No `allowed_languages` or `language_only` options.

rules.why:
Renderers use the language to highlight the code, and tools use it to pick a formatter or to run a check on the block. Without it a block of JSON looks like any text, and tools skip it.

To fix, name the language after the fence (```` ```json ````), or `text` when the block is not code.

rules.description: Reports a heading that is more than one level deeper than the heading before it (an `h4` right after an `h2`). Going back up by any number of levels is not reported.

example.input:
# One

### Three

## Two

#### Four

rules.why:
Headings make the outline of the page that screen readers and tables of contents are built from. A skipped level leaves a hole in that outline: a reader who jumps by level finds an `h4` with no `h3` above it.

To fix, use the missing level, or give the heading the level it has in the outline.

rules.description: Reports an image whose alternate text is empty (`![](url)`).

example.input: ![](logo.png) and ![Logo](logo.png).

upstream.note: An HTML `` is not an image here.

rules.why:
The alternate text is what a screen reader reads, what shows when the image fails to load, and what a search engine indexes. An image without it is invisible to all of them.

To fix, describe the image in the brackets. An image that is only decoration can keep an empty text on purpose, and then the rule should be turned off for that file.

rules.description: Reports a URL (`http://` or `https://`) written in a paragraph that is neither a link nor an autolink, on the URL. It is found when it follows whitespace or starts the paragraph; headings are not checked.

example.input:
https://example.com is bare.

<https://example.com> and [site](https://example.com) are not.

upstream.note: Reported on the paragraph; a URL right after `(` or `[` is not found.

rules.why:
Markdown flavours differ in whether a bare URL becomes a link: some leave it as plain text, and one that includes the trailing punctuation breaks the link. Marking it with `<...>` or a link makes the intent explicit and the same everywhere.

To fix, write `<https://example.com>` or `[text](https://example.com)`.

rules.description: Reports a heading whose text is the same as an earlier heading in the document, on the later one, with the first as the related location.

example.input:
# Usage

## Install

## Usage

Setext
------

Setext
======

upstream.note: No `siblings_only` option.

rules.why:
Headings that have the same text get the same anchor (the renderer adds a number to the second), so a link to `#usage` goes to the first one and a reader of the table of contents cannot tell the two apart.

To fix, make the headings different, for example by adding the name of the section they belong to.

rules.description: Reports a paragraph of one line that is only emphasized text (`**Overview**`) with no closing punctuation, outside a heading.

example.input:
**Overview**

*Notes*

**A sentence.**

Text with **bold** inside.

upstream.note: No `punctuation` option.

rules.why:
Bold text is not a heading to tools: it is missing from the outline, from the table of contents and from the navigation of a screen reader, and it cannot be linked to. A short bold line that works as a title belongs in a heading.

To fix, use a heading (`## Overview`). Text that ends with punctuation (`**Note.**`) is a sentence and is not reported.

rules.description: Reports a link whose destination is empty or only `#` (`[docs]()`, `[docs](#)`).

example.input: A [docs]() and [anchor](#) and [ok](#top) link.

rules.why:
A link with no target does nothing or reloads the page, and it usually marks a link that was never filled in or lost its URL while editing.

To fix, add the destination, or write plain text.

rules.description: Reports raw HTML in a document, on each tag of inline HTML and on each HTML block. Comments are not reported.

example.input:
Text with bold HTML and .
block

upstream.note: No `allowed_elements` option; an HTML block is one report, not one per tag.

rules.why:
Markdown is meant to be read as it is and to be rendered in many places. HTML is dropped, escaped or restyled by some renderers (a README on a package page, a chat message), and a document that depends on it renders differently in each.

To fix, use the Markdown form (`**bold**`, a link or an image). Where HTML is needed, turn the rule off for that file.

rules.description: Reports a paragraph that starts with one to six `#` and no space after them (`#Heading`).

example.input:
#Heading

## Fine

###Also missing

Text with #hash inside.

rules.why:
To a reader this is a heading, but CommonMark needs a space after the `#`, so it is plain text with a `#` in front. The heading is missing from the outline and from the table of contents.

To fix, add a space: `# Heading`. A deliberate hash tag at the start of a line can be escaped with `\#`.

rules.description: Reports link syntax written the wrong way round (`(text)[url]`), at the start of a paragraph or after whitespace, on the whole paragraph. No fix, because `(text)[url]` may be meant literally.

example.input:
(Docs)[https://example.com] is reversed, [Docs](https://example.com) is not.

Text (with parentheses) and [brackets] stay.

upstream.note: Reported on the paragraph, not the link; a link followed by a reference `[a](b)[c]` is not told apart.

rules.why:
Markdown reads `[text](url)` as a link; with the brackets and parentheses swapped the text is shown as it is, with both pairs in it, and the link does not exist.

To fix, swap them: `[text](url)`.

rules.description: Reports a code span that starts or ends with a space (`` ` code ` ``). A span whose content starts or ends with a backtick and is padded on both sides to separate it is not reported.

example.input: A ` code` and `code ` and `code` span.

rules.why:
A renderer strips one space from each end only when both ends have one, so the spaces are lost or shown depending on the renderer. In code that shows the exact text (a command with a leading space) the difference matters, and elsewhere the spaces are noise.

To fix, delete the spaces inside the backticks.

rules.description: Reports link text that starts or ends with a space (`[ docs ](url)`).

example.input: A [ docs](https://example.com) and [docs ](https://example.com) and [docs](https://example.com).

rules.why:
The spaces become part of the link, so the underlined, clickable text has blanks at its ends and the link looks off.

To fix, move the spaces out of the brackets.

rules.description: Reports a heading that ends with `.`, `,`, `;`, `:` or `!` (or the full-width forms). A `?` at the end is not reported.

example.input:
# Introduction.

## Why?

## Setup:

Overview!
---------

upstream.note: No `punctuation` option; reported on the heading, not at the punctuation.

rules.why:
A heading is a title, not a sentence, and the punctuation at its end is carried into the table of contents and the anchor. A heading that ends with `?` is a question title and is accepted.

To fix, delete the punctuation.

rules.description: Reports a second or later top-level heading (`# Title`) in a document.

example.input:
# One

## Sub

# Two

Three
=====

upstream.note: No `level` option, and a `title:` in the front matter does not count as a title.

rules.why:
A document has one title: the top-level heading is what tools use as the page title, so a second one makes the title ambiguous, and the outline then has several roots.

To fix, make the later headings second-level, or split the document.

rules.description: Reports a parameter with a type that does not allow `null` and a `null` default (`int $a = null`).

example.input:
<?php
function a(int $a = null, ?int $b = null, int|null $c = null, $d = null, mixed $e = null) {}
class P { function __construct(public $x = null, public string $y = null) {} }

upstream.note: A typed parameter with a `null` default and no `?` or `null` in its type.

rules.why:
The parameter is nullable only through the default, which is deprecated since PHP 8.4 and a notice to code that runs there. The type says one thing and the default another.

To fix, write the nullable type: `?int $a = null`.

rules.description: Reports a function or method whose native return type or `@return` tag is not `void` or `never` and whose end can be reached without a `return` or `throw`, on the last statement that reaches the end. Generators are not reported, and a call that never returns (`exit`, `die`, a `@return never` function) is not seen.

example.input:
<?php
function a($x): int { if ($x) { return 1; } }
function b($x): int { if ($x) { return 1; } elseif ($x > 1) { return 2; } else { return 3; } }
function c($x): int { if ($x): return 1; else: throw new E(); endif; }
function d($x): int { if ($x) { return 1; } exit; }
function d2($x): int { if ($x) { return 1; } die(1); }
function e($x): void { if ($x) { return; } }
function f($x): iterable { if ($x) { yield 1; } }
/** @return int */
function g($x) { if ($x) { return 1; } }
/** @return int|null */
function h($x) { if ($x) { return 1; } }
class K { function __construct() { } }

upstream.note: A native or `@return` type that is not void, never, mixed or null and a reachable end of the body; `exit` and `die` end a path; a call of a `@return never` function in another file (`bail()`, `abort()`), a type narrowed to every case, and a loop with an inner `break` are not seen (27 extra against 19 covered, so the rule is not in the preset).

rules.why:
The function runs off its end and returns `null`, which breaks the declared type: a native type gives a `TypeError` at run time, and a documented type gives the caller a `null` where it expects a value.

To fix, return a value on every path, or throw.

rules.description: Reports a `function name() {}` statement in the body of a function, method or closure.

example.input:
<?php
function a() { function b() {} }
function c() { $f = function () {}; }
class D { function m() { function n() {} } }
function e() {}

upstream.note: A named function declared in a function, method or closure.

rules.why:
The inner function is declared when the outer one runs, so it does not exist before the first call, and a second call of the outer function fails with an error that the function is already declared.

To fix, declare the function at the top level, or use a closure.

rules.description: Reports `unset($this->name)` of a property the class declares when a subclass could give the property a hook (PHP 8.4): the class is not final and the property is not private, final, static or readonly.

example.input:
<?php
class A { public $a; private $b; public readonly int $c;
    function f() { unset($this->a); unset($this->b); unset($this->c); unset($this->z); }
}
final class B { public $a; function f() { unset($this->a); } }

upstream.note: `unset($this->p)` of a property the class declares; a property declared in a parent in another file is not seen.

rules.why:
A property with a hook cannot be unset, so the call fails with an error in the subclass that overrides the property, while it works in the class that wrote it.

To fix, set the property to `null` instead, or make the class or the property final.

rules.description: Reports `new static` in a class that is not final and has no final or abstract constructor of its own. A constructor or a final parent in another file cannot be seen; the `@phpstan-consistent-constructor` tag of the class itself is.

example.input:
<?php
class A { function make() { return new static(); } }
final class B { function make() { return new static(); } }
class C { final public function __construct() {} function make() { return new static(); } }
trait T { function make() { return new static; } }
class D { function make() { return new self(); } }
/** @phpstan-consistent-constructor */
class E { function make() { return new static(); } }

upstream.note: A class without a final class or final or abstract constructor of its own; a constructor or final parent in another file, and a `@phpstan-ignore` comment, cannot be seen (about 17 findings of the 317).

rules.why:
`new static` builds the class of the caller, so a subclass can be built with its own constructor with other parameters, and the call in the parent fails with a missing argument.

To fix, make the class or the constructor final, or call `new self`.

rules.description: Reports a function named `Verb-Noun` whose verb is not one that `Get-Verb` returns. A name without a dash is not checked.

upstream.note: Names without a dash are not checked; the verb list is fixed and cannot follow the host.

rules.why:
PowerShell users find commands by verb (`Get-Command -Verb Get`) and expect a verb to mean the same in every module. An unapproved verb such as `Make-` or `Delete-` also makes `Import-Module` print a warning about the module's names.

To fix, rename the function with an approved verb (`New-`, `Remove-`).

rules.description: Reports a call of a cmdlet that gives none of the parameters that every parameter set requires, by name or by position. A `-name` takes the element after it as its value, so `Write-Verbose -Verbose "text"` leaves `-Message` unbound. A command behind a pipe or with a splatted argument is left alone.

example.input:
Write-Verbose -Verbose "text"
Write-Verbose "text"
Write-Verbose -Message "text" -Verbose
Write-Verbose -ErrorAction Stop "text"
Write-Verbose -Verbose:$true "text"
Write-Verbose
Write-Verbose @args
"text" | Write-Verbose
Join-Path -Path a
Join-Path -Resolve a
Join-Path a -Resolve

upstream.note: Reads a table of the cmdlets that have a parameter mandatory in every parameter set (generated by `scripts/gen_powershell_commands.ps1` from the built-in modules of PowerShell 7.7); the module asks the commands of its host, user functions included. A `-name` takes the next element as its value, which is how the module reads `Write-Verbose -Verbose "x"`.

rules.why:
PowerShell asks for a missing mandatory parameter at run time and waits for input. In a script or on a server that hangs the run, or fails with an error when there is no host to ask.

To fix, give the parameter by name.

rules.description: Reports an assignment to an automatic variable, a parameter or a `foreach` variable that has the name of one (`$Error`, `$Event`, `$input`, `$PSItem`, `$_`, `$PWD`, `$Host`, `$this`, `$true` and so on). `$null = ...` is not reported.

upstream.note: The report is at the start of the parameter (its attributes included), the module's at the variable, so a parameter with attributes on earlier lines differs in the line.

rules.why:
Automatic variables are set by PowerShell, so an assignment is overwritten or is refused, and a parameter with the same name hides the value that other code expects (`$input`, `$Host`). The code reads as if it set something that it does not.

To fix, use another name.

rules.description: Reports a command written with one of the default aliases of Windows PowerShell and PowerShell 7 (`gci`, `ls`, `%`, `?`, `iex` and so on). The table is the one of a Windows host.

upstream.note: The table is fixed (a Windows host's); PSScriptAnalyzer reads the aliases of the host it runs on, so on Linux `ls` and `cat` are not aliases there, and user-defined aliases are not known. No fix that expands the alias. `& ls` is reported at the `&`.

rules.why:
Aliases are for typing at a prompt. In a script they are less readable (`%` and `?` are not words), may be absent or mean another command on a platform (`ls` is the native command on Linux), and users can redefine them.

To fix, write the full name of the cmdlet.

rules.description: Reports a `[switch]` parameter with the default value `$true`.

upstream.note: Other values that evaluate to true (`= 1`) are not reported.

rules.why:
A switch is present or absent, and the caller turns it on by naming it. A switch that is on by default can be turned off only with the odd form `-Name:$false`.

To fix, invert the meaning, with a name for the opposite (`-NoLog` for `-Log`).

rules.description: Reports a call of one of the `calls` that run a string as code, on the call. Each language lists its calls in its grammar's `rule` row.

options.description: Calls that run a string as code
options.name: calls

rules.why:
Code that is built from a string runs with all the rights of the program, so any part of the string that comes from outside is a way to run commands on the machine. It is also hard to read and not checked by the tools that analyse the program.

To fix, use a parser for the data (`json.loads`), a lookup table, or a function.

rules.description: Reports a variable in the `global:` scope, other than the special variables that PowerShell and its tools use (`$global:LASTEXITCODE`, `$global:ErrorActionPreference`, `$global:PSDefaultParameterValues` and so on).

upstream.note: Variables inside strings, and `Get-Variable -Scope Global`, are not looked at.

rules.why:
A global variable is shared by everything in the session, including other modules and the user's own commands. Two scripts that use the same name change each other's state, and the value is hard to trace to where it was set.

To fix, pass values as parameters, or use a `script:` variable.

rules.description: Reports a backtick that is followed by blanks before the end of the line.

example.input:
Get-ChildItem `  
    -Force `
    -Name
$x = 1 + `	
    2

rules.why:
The backtick continues a line only when it is the last character. With a space after it, the backtick escapes the space, the line is not continued, and the next line runs as a separate command. The space is invisible in an editor.

To fix, remove the blanks after the backtick, or avoid the backtick with splatting or a bracketed expression.

rules.description: Reports a `[string]` parameter whose name contains `password`, `passphrase` or `cred`.

upstream.note: `SuppressMessageAttribute` is not honored (see the scope).

rules.why:
A `[string]` stays in memory as clear text and is easy to log or to show in history and transcripts. `[SecureString]` and `[PSCredential]` keep the secret protected and make the cmdlet fit with the credential handling of other commands.

To fix, take a `[SecureString]` or a `[PSCredential]`.

rules.description: Reports a call of `ConvertTo-SecureString` with `-AsPlainText`.
rules.why:
It turns a clear-text string into a `SecureString`, and the clear text is in the script, the history and the logs already. The protection is only in name.

To fix, read the secret as a `SecureString` (`Read-Host -AsSecureString`, a vault or `Get-Credential`).

rules.description: Reports a call of one of the `calls` that write to the console, unless an argument matching `redirect` sends the output elsewhere and none matching `console` sends it back to the console. Each language lists its calls and the two patterns in its grammar's `rule` row.

options.description: Calls that print
options.name: calls

options.description: An argument that sends the output elsewhere
options.name: redirect

options.description: An argument that sends the output to the console
options.name: console

rules.why:
A print call is usually debugging that was left in. It cannot be turned off by configuration, has no level or timestamp and ends up on the wrong stream in a service, where a logger is configured and read.

To fix, use the project's logger, or delete the call.

rules.description: Reports a call of `Get-WmiObject`, `Invoke-WmiMethod`, `Register-WmiEvent`, `Remove-WmiObject` or `Set-WmiInstance`.
rules.why:
The WMI cmdlets are not in PowerShell 7 and later. The CIM cmdlets (`Get-CimInstance`, `Invoke-CimMethod`) do the same work on Windows, use the newer remoting protocol, and are in both editions.

To fix, use the CIM cmdlet of the same job.

rules.description: Reports a `-eq` or `-ne` comparison (or a case variant, as `-ceq`) with `$null` on the right.

upstream.note: The module does not report a left operand it knows to be a scalar (a parameter or variable of a non-array type); Sudsy has no types, so `[string]$a` ... `$a -eq $null` is reported. A comparison whose expression also holds `-and`, `-or` or `-xor` at the same level is skipped (the expression is not split). No fix that swaps the operands.

rules.why:
When the left side is an array, `-eq` and `-ne` filter it and return the elements: `@(1, 2) -eq $null` is an empty array and `@(1, 2) -ne $null` is the whole array. The test does not say whether the value itself is `$null`.

To fix, write `$null` on the left: `$null -eq $x`.

rules.description: Reports a function or script block with a parameter that has `ValueFromPipeline` or `ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName` and no `process` block. A `filter` counts as having one.

upstream.note: A `process` block anywhere in the function text counts, a nested one too.

rules.why:
Without a `process` block the body runs once, after the pipeline has finished, and sees only the last object that came in. The others are lost.

To fix, put the work in `process { }`.

rules.description: Reports a function named `Verb-Nouns` whose noun ends in `s`. A noun that ends in `ss`, `us`, `is` or `as` (`Status`, `Address`, `Analysis`, `Alias`) is not reported.

upstream.note: The module asks an English pluralizer; Sudsy takes a noun ending in `s` as plural unless it ends in `ss`, `us`, `is`, `as` or is `News`, `Series`, `Species`, `Data`.

rules.why:
The Microsoft guidelines name the noun in the singular, even when the command returns many objects, so that users can guess names and the names look the same in every module.

To fix, use the singular noun.

rules.description: Reports a function whose name has the verb `New`, `Set`, `Remove`, `Start`, `Stop`, `Restart`, `Reset` or `Update` and whose text has no `SupportsShouldProcess`, or has `SupportsShouldProcess = $false`.

upstream.note: The verbs are the module's (`New`, `Set`, `Remove`, `Start`, `Stop`, `Restart`, `Reset`, `Update`); the attribute is looked for in the whole text of the function, nested functions included.

rules.why:
A command that changes something is expected to accept `-WhatIf` and `-Confirm`, so a user can see what it would do first. Without `SupportsShouldProcess`, they are not available and the user must run it to find out.

To fix, add `[CmdletBinding(SupportsShouldProcess)]` and call `$PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess(...)` before the change.

rules.description: Reports an enum whose first value is not 0. Proto3 and editions with open enums require it; proto2 files (also those with no `syntax`) are checked only with the `proto2` option.

options.description: Check proto2 files too, as buf does.
options.name: proto2

rules.why:
In proto3 the default of an enum field is the first value, and the value that a reader sees when the field is not set. It has to be 0, and a first value that means something real (`ACTIVE = 1` and a hidden 0) makes unset data look valid.

To fix, make the first value 0 and name it for "not set".

rules.description: Reports `option allow_alias = true;` in an enum.
rules.why:
Aliases give two names to one number. A value read from the wire becomes one of the names, which one depends on the generator, so the name in the code is not stable, and JSON output shows one of them.

To fix, give each value its own number, and remove the option.

rules.description: Reports an enum name that is not PascalCase.
rules.why:
The Protobuf style guide names types in PascalCase, and the generated code of most languages uses the name as a type name, where another form reads as something else.

To fix, rename to PascalCase.

rules.description: Reports an enum value that does not start with the name of the enum in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE and an underscore (`COLOR_RED` in `Color`).
rules.why:
Enum values are scoped to the enclosing message or file, not to the enum, as in C++. Two enums in one scope with a value `RED` collide, and the prefix prevents it.

To fix, add the prefix to the value.

rules.description: Reports an enum value name that is not UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.
rules.why:
The Protobuf style guide writes enum values in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, as the generated code of many languages writes constants.

To fix, rename the value.

rules.description: Reports an enum value numbered 0 whose name does not end in `_UNSPECIFIED`.

upstream.note: The suffix is not configurable.

rules.why:
The zero value is what a field has when it is not set, so its name should say "nothing chosen". A zero value named `ACTIVE` makes missing data look like a real choice.

To fix, name it `<ENUM>_UNSPECIFIED`.

rules.description: Reports a field name that is not lower_snake_case.
rules.why:
The Protobuf style guide writes fields in lower_snake_case. Generators convert the name to camel case or leave it as it is, and the JSON mapping is derived from it, so a field that is written in another form maps to an unexpected name.

To fix, rename the field.

rules.description: Reports a proto2 `required` field.
rules.why:
A required field can never be removed or made optional without breaking every reader and writer that was built before the change: an old reader rejects messages without it. Protobuf's own advice is to avoid `required`.

To fix, make it `optional` and check for it in the code.

rules.description: Reports a file whose name (without `.proto`) is not lower_snake_case.

options.description: Regular expression the file name without its extension must match; empty: not checked.
options.name: pattern

rules.why:
The Protobuf style guide names files in lower_snake_case, and generated file names and import paths derive from it. A different style gives different names in each language.

To fix, rename the file and update the imports.

rules.description: Reports `import public`.
rules.why:
A public import makes the imported file's names visible to every file that imports this one. The dependency spreads without being written down, and a change in the imported file breaks files that never mention it.

To fix, import the files where their names are used.

rules.description: Reports a message name that is not PascalCase.
rules.why:
The Protobuf style guide names messages in PascalCase, and the name becomes a class or type name in the generated code.

To fix, rename the message.

rules.description: Reports a oneof name that is not lower_snake_case.
rules.why:
The Protobuf style guide writes oneof names as it does fields, in lower_snake_case, since the generators turn it into a property.

To fix, rename the oneof.

rules.description: Reports a file without a `package` statement.
rules.why:
Without a package every name is global, so two files from different projects that define `Order` collide, and the generated code puts the types in the default namespace.

To fix, add a `package` statement.

rules.description: Reports a package whose components are not lower_snake_case.
rules.why:
The Protobuf style guide writes packages in lower_snake_case, dot separated. Generators turn the package into namespaces or modules, and another form reads as something else there.

To fix, rename the package.

rules.description: Reports a package whose last component is not `v1`, `v1test...`, `v1alpha1`, `v1beta1` or `v1p1alpha1` (`v1beta` too).
rules.why:
A version in the package lets an incompatible API live next to the old one under another name (`api.v2`) instead of breaking its users. Without it a breaking change has to be made in place.

To fix, add a version component, for example `acme.orders.v1`.

rules.description: Reports an rpc name that is not PascalCase.
rules.why:
The Protobuf style guide names rpcs in PascalCase, and the name becomes a method name in the generated client and server code.

To fix, rename the rpc.

rules.description: Reports an rpc whose request type is not named `<Rpc>Request` or `<Service><Rpc>Request`.
rules.why:
A request type with the name of its rpc is not reused for another rpc. A shared type couples the two calls, and a change for one changes the other.

To fix, give each rpc its own request message with that name.

rules.description: Reports an rpc whose response type is not named `<Rpc>Response` or `<Service><Rpc>Response`.
rules.why:
A response type with the name of its rpc is not reused for another rpc. A shared type couples the two calls, and a change for one changes the other.

To fix, give each rpc its own response message with that name.

rules.description: Reports a service name that is not PascalCase.
rules.why:
The Protobuf style guide names services in PascalCase, and the name becomes a class name in the generated code.

To fix, rename the service.

rules.description: Reports a service whose name does not end in `Service`.

upstream.note: The suffix is not configurable.

rules.why:
The suffix tells a reader of the generated code, which has clients and servers of the service, that the name is a service. It also keeps the service from clashing with the message of the same name.

To fix, rename it `OrdersService`.

rules.description: Reports a file without `syntax = ...;` or `edition = ...;`, which makes it proto2.
rules.why:
A file without the statement is proto2 by default. New files almost always mean proto3 or an edition, and with the default they get required fields and other rules that differ.

To fix, add `syntax = "proto3";` or an `edition`.

rules.description: Reports a class named `l`, `O` or `I`.
rules.why:
In many fonts `l` (lower case L), `I` (upper case i) and the digit `1` look alike, and so do `O` and `0`. A class with one of these names is hard to tell from a number or another name in `x = O()`.

To fix, give the class a name that says what it is.

rules.description: Reports a function or method named `l`, `O` or `I`.
rules.why:
In many fonts `l` (lower case L), `I` (upper case i) and the digit `1` look alike, and so do `O` and `0`. A call such as `l(x)` or `O(x)` is easy to misread as an expression with a number.

To fix, give the function a name that says what it does.

rules.description: Reports a variable, parameter or `global` name that is `l`, `O` or `I`.
rules.why:
In many fonts `l` (lower case L), `I` (upper case i) and the digit `1` look alike, and so do `O` and `0`. In `l = O + 1` a reader cannot tell the names from the numbers.

To fix, rename the variable.

rules.description: Reports an `__eq__` or `__ne__` method whose second parameter is annotated `Any`.

example.input:
from typing import Union
x: Union[int, str]

from typing import Optional
x: Optional[int]

from typing import List
x: List[int]

from typing import Generator
x: Generator[int, None, None]

def f(x: "int"):
    pass

from typing import TypeAlias
X: TypeAlias = int

from typing import Generic, TypeVar
T = TypeVar("T")
class A(Generic[T]):
    pass

from typing import TypeVar
T = TypeVar("T")
def f(x: T) -> T:
    return x

def g() -> T:
    pass

import datetime
x = datetime.timezone.utc

from typing_extensions import Self

import sys
if sys.version_info >= (3, 8):
    pass

from typing import TypeVar
T = TypeVar("T")
class A:
    def f(self: T) -> T:
        return self

from typing import Any
class A:
    def __eq__(self, other: Any) -> bool:
        return True

from typing import TypeVar
T = TypeVar("T", covariant=True)

rules.why:
Python calls `__eq__` with any object on the right, so the accurate type is `object`. With `Any` a type checker accepts `other.value` without a check and the method fails at run time on a value of another type.

To fix, annotate `other: object` and check its type before using it.

rules.description: Reports an `assert` whose test is the literal `False`, with or without a message.

example.input:
import collections
from typing import Sequence

x = a = b = 1


def f(a=[], b={}, c=set(), d=list(), e=collections.deque(), g=[x for x in a]):
    pass


def immutable(a: Sequence[int] = [], b: tuple = (), c=(), d=frozenset(), e=bytearray()):
    pass


assert False
assert False, "message"
assert 0
getattr(x, "name")
getattr(x, "__private")
getattr(x, "class")
getattr(x, "name", None)
setattr(x, "name", 1)
y = setattr(x, "name", 1)
setattr(x, "class", 1)
zip(a, b)
zip(a)
zip(a, b, strict=True)
try:
    pass
except (ValueError,):
    pass
except (ValueError, TypeError):
    pass

rules.why:
`assert` statements are removed when Python runs with `-O`, so an `assert False` that is meant to stop the program does nothing there and execution goes on past the line.

To fix, write `raise AssertionError(...)`, which always runs.

rules.description: Reports an `assert` whose test is a tuple, usually the condition and the message written inside the parentheses.

example.input:
x = 1
assert (x, "message")
assert x, "message"
assert (x)
assert ()

rules.why:
A tuple with elements is always true, so `assert (x > 0, "x must be positive")` never fails, and the check looks like it is there. Python warns about it when the file is compiled.

To fix, write the message after a comma outside the parentheses: `assert x > 0, "x must be positive"`.

rules.description: Reports a `raise` with no exception in code that no `except` clause of its function contains.

example.input:
raise NotImplemented
raise NotImplemented("a")
raise NotImplementedError
raise

rules.why:
A bare `raise` re-raises the exception being handled. With no `except` around it, it fails with `RuntimeError: No active exception to reraise`, unless the function is only ever called from a handler, which nothing in the file shows.

To fix, raise a named exception, or move the `raise` into the `except` clause.

rules.description: Reports a `break` that no loop of its function or class contains.
rules.why:
Python rejects the file with `SyntaxError: 'break' outside loop`, so no code in it runs.

To fix, remove the `break`, or put the statement in the loop it is meant for. In a function, `return` leaves it.

rules.description: Reports a method decorated with `functools.lru_cache` or `functools.cache`. Static methods are not reported.

example.input:
def f():
    a, b = g()
    return a

class A:
    x = []

import os as os

def f(a):
    with g() as a:
        pass

x = ["a" "b", "c"]

__all__ = ["b", "a"]

class A:
    __slots__ = ("b", "a")

import sys
import os

import functools
class A:
    @functools.cache
    def f(self):
        pass

def f(x=list()):
    pass

import subprocess
subprocess.run(["ls"])

a = b = "x"
x = ", ".join([a, b])

x = "%s" % y

x = "{}".format(y)

import re
x = re.compile("a", re.I)

rules.why:
The cache belongs to the function and is shared by all instances. It stores `self` as part of each key, so an instance that called the method stays alive until its entry is evicted, and with no size limit (`functools.cache`, `maxsize=None`) for as long as the cache does.

To fix, keep the cache per instance (create it in `__init__`), use `functools.cached_property`, or move the work to a function that takes only the values it needs.

rules.description: Reports an `if` whose only statement is another `if`, when neither has an `elif` or `else`.
rules.why:
The two tests are one condition, `if a and b:`. The nesting adds an indent level and makes the reader check that nothing else happens between the tests.

To fix, join the tests with `and`.

rules.description: Reports a `continue` that no loop of its function or class contains.
rules.why:
Python rejects the file with `SyntaxError: 'continue' not properly in loop`, so no code in it runs.

To fix, remove the `continue`, or put the statement in the loop it is meant for.
