@if (a == 1) { } @for (x of xs) { } @for (x of xs; track x.id) { }

rules.why:
Angular needs the expression to tell the items of the list apart, and it stops the build without it. With a good key it moves the elements when the list changes instead of rebuilding them.

To fix, add `; track item.id` (a unique value of the item) to the `@for`.

rules.description: Reports an `<li>` whose parent is not a list (`<ul>`, `<ol>` or `<menu>`).

example.input:
a
a

  • a
  • b

rules.why:
An `<li>` outside a list is not a list item, so a screen reader announces no list, and the browser draws no marker.

To fix, put the item in a list.

rules.description: Reports a prop in the array form (`defineProps(['a'])`), and an object with no `type` or `validator`.

example.input:
<script>
export default {
  props: {
    a: String,
    b: { type: String, default: '' },
    c: { required: true, type: Number },
    d: Boolean,
    e: [String, Number],
    f: {},
    g: Object,
  },
  data() {
    return { a: 1, h: 2 }
  },
  computed: {
    h() { return 1 },
    get k() { return 1 },
    set k(v) {},
  },
  methods: { go() {} },
}
</script>

<script setup>
defineProps(['x', 'y'])
const ok = 1
const model = defineModel()
</script>

upstream.note: a type it cannot resolve in the file is skipped, a component object only at the top level as for `no-dupe-keys`

rules.why:
A prop with no type accepts anything, so a wrong value is shown only as a failure far from the cause, and the component has no documentation of what it takes.

To fix, write the prop as an object with a `type`.

rules.description: Reports a `<script src>` and a `<link rel="stylesheet" href>` with no `integrity` attribute.

example.input:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<title>x</title>
<script src="https://cdn.example/a.js"></script>
<script src="https://cdn.example/b.js" integrity="sha384-x" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
<script src="a.js"></script>
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.example/a.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="a.css">
<link rel="icon" href="https://cdn.example/a.png">

upstream.note: no target, include and exclude options

rules.why:
A file loaded from a CDN or another server can change after the page was written, and the page then runs or applies the changed file without noticing.

To fix, add `integrity` with the hash of the file and `crossorigin="anonymous"`.

rules.description: Reports a `<script>` whose `type` is a JavaScript MIME type (`text/javascript`, `application/javascript`, ...) or empty. `type="module"` and other types are not reported.

upstream.note: the JavaScript MIME types and an empty type; the allowed module and importmap types are not special

rules.why:
The browser assumes that type, so the attribute says nothing and is only more text.

To fix, remove the `type`.

rules.description: Reports `name={name}` where the shorthand `{name}` would do. The fix writes the shorthand.

example.fixed:
t {#snippet children()}hi{/snippet} {#snippet children(x)}{x}{/snippet}

{"text"} {'it'} {`tpl`} {`a${b}`} {"a'b"} {text}

{{ a: 1 }} {[1]} {function () {}} {text}

x x x x
example.input:
t {#snippet children()}hi{/snippet} {#snippet children(x)}{x}{/snippet}

{"text"} {'it'} {`tpl`} {`a${b}`} {"a'b"} {text}

{{ a: 1 }} {[1]} {function () {}} {text}

x x x x

rules.why:
The name is written twice for nothing, and one form keeps the components uniform.

To fix, write `{name}`; the fix does it.

rules.description: Reports `bind:name={name}`, `class:name={name}` and `style:name={name}` where the shorthand (`bind:name`) would do. The fix writes the shorthand.

example.fixed:
t {#snippet children()}hi{/snippet} {#snippet children(x)}{x}{/snippet}

{"text"} {'it'} {`tpl`} {`a${b}`} {"a'b"} {text}

{{ a: 1 }} {[1]} {function () {}} {text}

x x x x
example.input:
t {#snippet children()}hi{/snippet} {#snippet children(x)}{x}{/snippet}

{"text"} {'it'} {`tpl`} {`a${b}`} {"a'b"} {text}

{{ a: 1 }} {[1]} {function () {}} {text}

x x x x

rules.why:
The name is written twice for nothing, and one form keeps the components uniform.

To fix, write `bind:name`; the fix does it.

rules.description: Reports an HTML comment with no space after `<!--` or before `-->` (`<!--text-->`).

example.fixed:
t {#snippet children()}hi{/snippet} {#snippet children(x)}{x}{/snippet}

{"text"} {'it'} {`tpl`} {`a${b}`} {"a'b"} {text}

{{ a: 1 }} {[1]} {function () {}} {text}

x x x x
example.input:
t {#snippet children()}hi{/snippet} {#snippet children(x)}{x}{/snippet}

{"text"} {'it'} {`tpl`} {`a${b}`} {"a'b"} {text}

{{ a: 1 }} {[1]} {function () {}} {text}

x x x x

rules.why:
A space keeps the text apart from the marker and reads as text, not as commented-out code.

To fix, write `<!-- text -->`.

rules.description: Reports an `<svg>` that has no `focusable` attribute.

example.input:
y
y y y
x

rules.why:
Internet Explorer 11 and old Edge make every `<svg>` a stop of the Tab key unless it says `focusable="false"`.

To fix, add `focusable="false"`.

rules.description: Reports a `<button>` with no name: no text (an `<svg>` counts by the text inside it, such as its `<title>`), no image with a non-empty `alt` and no `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`. A `title` does not count.

example.input:
y
y y y
x

upstream.note: button only

rules.why:
A button with no name is announced as just "button", and the user cannot tell what it does.

To fix, put text in the button or add `aria-label`.

rules.description: Reports landmarks of the same kind (`<nav>`, `<aside>`, or elements with the same landmark `role`) that a screen reader user cannot tell apart: with several of them, each needs an `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` that no other has.

example.input:
y
y y y
x

upstream.note: header, footer, section and form landmarks are not checked

rules.why:
A list of landmarks that holds "navigation, navigation, navigation" gives no way to pick the right one.

To fix, give each landmark a label that tells it from the others.

rules.description: Reports a named character reference in text (`&name;`) that HTML does not define. Numeric references and references in attribute values are not checked.

example.input: &foo; & © {

upstream.note: named references in text only
named references in text only; a missing semicolon, ignoreCase and references in attribute values are not checked

rules.why:
The browser shows the text as written, `&foo;`, which was not meant; it is usually a typo of an entity.

To fix, correct the name, or write `&` before it if the text is meant.

rules.description: Reports an element, an attribute or an attribute value that not all major browsers support (`<geolocation>`, `popover="hint"`, `rel="manifest"` on `<link>`), by the baseline data of web-features. A name the data does not list is not reported; custom elements are skipped, and so are `is` and `slot` in Vue, Svelte and Angular templates, where the framework owns them. The option `available` sets how widely a feature must be available.

example.input:
x

x

x

options.description: How widely a feature must be available: `widely` (in all major browsers for 30 months), `newly` (in all of them), or a year (baseline since that year or before).
options.name: available

upstream.note: not the `sms:` links (a value prefix)

rules.why:
A feature that only some browsers have works for part of the users and does nothing or breaks for the rest, and the author sees it only in the browser they test with.

To fix, use a feature with wider support, or provide a fallback and turn the rule off for it.

rules.description: Reports `v-bind:` where the shorthand `:` would do (`v-bind:href`). The fix writes `:`.

example.fixed:
<template>
  <MyCard :title="t" @click="go" :cardTitle="c" cardSub="s" my-prop="p"
    :ok="1"
    :cardOther="o">
    <template #head>h</template>
    <template v-slot="p">d</template>
  </MyCard>
  <svg :viewBox="v"></svg>
</template>
example.input:
<template>
  <MyCard v-bind:title="t" v-on:click="go" :cardTitle="c" cardSub="s" my-prop="p"
    :ok="1"
    :cardOther="o">
    <template v-slot:head>h</template>
    <template v-slot="p">d</template>
  </MyCard>
  <svg :viewBox="v"></svg>
</template>

rules.why:
One form keeps the templates uniform and shorter; the long form reads as a different thing from the short one though they mean the same.

To fix, write `:`; the fix does it.

rules.description: Reports a `v-for` with no `:key` (or `v-bind:key`). On a `<template>` or `<slot>` the key goes on the child elements; components are left to `valid-v-for`.

example.input:
• a
  • b
  • c

rules.why:
Without a key Vue patches the elements in place when the list changes, which keeps stale state in inputs and components and breaks transitions.

To fix, add a `:key` with a value that is unique to each item.

rules.description: Reports an event of a component that is written in camelCase (`@cardOpen`). A component is a tag in PascalCase or with a hyphen; HTML and SVG elements are not checked. Only in `.vue` files.

upstream.note: `always` only, no `ignore` list

rules.why:
Event names in a template are read in lowercase by the HTML parser, so kebab-case is the one form that works in every kind of template, and the component emits it in the same style.

To fix, write the event in kebab-case (`@card-open`).

rules.description: Reports `v-on:` where the shorthand `@` would do (`v-on:click`). The fix writes `@`.

example.fixed:
<template>
  <MyCard :title="t" @click="go" :cardTitle="c" cardSub="s" my-prop="p"
    :ok="1"
    :cardOther="o">
    <template #head>h</template>
    <template v-slot="p">d</template>
  </MyCard>
  <svg :viewBox="v"></svg>
</template>
example.input:
<template>
  <MyCard v-bind:title="t" v-on:click="go" :cardTitle="c" cardSub="s" my-prop="p"
    :ok="1"
    :cardOther="o">
    <template v-slot:head>h</template>
    <template v-slot="p">d</template>
  </MyCard>
  <svg :viewBox="v"></svg>
</template>

rules.why:
One form keeps the templates uniform and shorter.

To fix, write `@`; the fix does it.

rules.description: Reports `v-slot:` where the shorthand `#` would do (`v-slot:head`). The fix writes `#`.

example.fixed:
<template>
  <MyCard :title="t" @click="go" :cardTitle="c" cardSub="s" my-prop="p"
    :ok="1"
    :cardOther="o">
    <template #head>h</template>
    <template v-slot="p">d</template>
  </MyCard>
  <svg :viewBox="v"></svg>
</template>
example.input:
<template>
  <MyCard v-bind:title="t" v-on:click="go" :cardTitle="c" cardSub="s" my-prop="p"
    :ok="1"
    :cardOther="o">
    <template v-slot:head>h</template>
    <template v-slot="p">d</template>
  </MyCard>
  <svg :viewBox="v"></svg>
</template>

rules.why:
One form keeps the templates uniform and shorter.

To fix, write `#`; the fix does it.

rules.description: Reports an `id` that is empty, has white space, begins with a digit or has characters other than letters, digits, `-` and `_`.

upstream.note: the strict form only, without the relaxed option

rules.why:
Such an id is valid HTML5, but it must be escaped in CSS selectors (`#1a` does not select it) and some scripts and older tools fail on it.

To fix, rename the id.

rules.description: Reports a `v-bind` that has no expression (`:name` alone is the shorthand for `:name="name"`, a bare `v-bind` is not) or a modifier other than `camel`, `prop`, `attr` and `sync`.
rules.why:
A binding with no value, or with a modifier Vue does not know, is ignored or fails to compile, and the attribute is missing from the element.

To fix, give the binding an expression and use the modifiers of the list.

rules.description: Reports a `v-cloak` that has an expression, an argument or a modifier.
rules.why:
The directive takes no value; a value is ignored, so the author believes there is a condition that does not exist.

To fix, write `v-cloak` alone.

rules.description: Reports a `v-else` that has an expression, an argument or a modifier, shares an element with `v-if` or `v-else-if`, or is not on the element right after one with `v-if` or `v-else-if`. Only comments and blank space may sit between the elements of a chain.
rules.why:
A `v-else` that does not continue a chain is a compile error, and an expression on it is ignored, so the author believes there is a second condition.

To fix, write a bare `v-else` right after the `v-if` or `v-else-if` element.

rules.description: Reports a `v-else-if` that has no expression, has an argument or a modifier, shares an element with `v-if` or `v-else`, or is not on the element right after one with `v-if` or `v-else-if`. Only comments and blank space may sit between the elements of a chain.
rules.why:
A `v-else-if` that does not continue a chain is a compile error, or it is ignored and the element is always rendered.

To fix, write `v-else-if="condition"` right after the `v-if` or `v-else-if` element.

rules.description: Reports a `v-for` whose value is not `item in items` (or `of`), or that has an argument or a modifier. A missing `:key` is `v-for-key`.
rules.why:
A `v-for` that does not parse is a compile error, or it loops over nothing.

To fix, write `v-for="item in items"`.

rules.description: Reports a `v-html` that has no expression, an argument or a modifier.
rules.why:
Without an expression the directive fails to compile or inserts nothing.

To fix, write `v-html="body"`.

rules.description: Reports a `v-if` that has no expression, has an argument or a modifier, or is on the same element as `v-else` or `v-else-if`.
rules.why:
A `v-if` without an expression fails to compile or always hides the element, and an argument or a modifier is ignored.

To fix, write `v-if="condition"` and put `v-else` on the next element.

rules.description: Reports a `v-is` that has no expression, an argument or a modifier.
rules.why:
Without an expression the directive fails to compile.

To fix, write `v-is="name"`.

rules.description: Reports a `v-memo` that has no expression, an argument or a modifier.
rules.why:
Without a list of values the directive fails to compile and the subtree is never cached.

To fix, write `v-memo="[a, b]"`.

rules.description: Reports a `v-model` that has no expression, and a `v-model` on a file input.
rules.why:
A file input has no value that Vue can set, so the binding fails; a `v-model` with no expression binds nothing.

To fix, write `v-model="name"`, and listen to `@change` on a file input.

rules.description: Reports a `v-on` with no handler and no modifier (`@click`). `@click.prevent` alone is not reported.
rules.why:
A listener with no handler does nothing, so the click, or the key, has no effect.

To fix, write `@click="go"`.

rules.description: Reports a `v-once` that has an expression, an argument or a modifier.
rules.why:
The directive takes no value; a value is ignored, so the author believes there is a condition that does not exist.

To fix, write `v-once` alone.

rules.description: Reports a `v-pre` that has an expression, an argument or a modifier.
rules.why:
The directive takes no value; a value is ignored, so the author believes there is a condition that does not exist.

To fix, write `v-pre` alone.

rules.description: Reports a `v-show` that has no expression, an argument or a modifier.
rules.why:
Without an expression the directive fails to compile or never changes the element.

To fix, write `v-show="open"`.

rules.description: Reports a `v-slot` with a modifier, and a `v-slot` on a plain HTML element (`<div #item>`). It goes on a `<template>` or a component. Only in `.vue` files.
rules.why:
Only a component can receive a slot, so the content on a plain element is lost.

To fix, put the `v-slot` on a `<template>` (`<template #name="props">`) or on the component.

rules.description: Reports a `v-text` that has no expression, an argument or a modifier.
rules.why:
Without an expression the directive fails to compile or shows nothing.

To fix, write `v-text="msg"`.

rules.description:
Reports a `/` at the end of a void element (`
`, ``).

example.input:
x

t

ok

ok

upstream.note: the omit style only, without the style option

rules.why:
A void element has no end tag and the slash is ignored, so it adds nothing; it only suggests the tag is closed like XML, which can mislead a reader about other elements such as `
`. To fix, write `
`.

rules.description: Reports a property or event whose accessors are in the wrong order: `get` goes before `set` or `init`, and `add` before `remove`. The fix swaps the two accessors; it is not offered when a comment stands between them or inside them.
rules.why: Readers expect to meet the reading accessor first and the writing one second. One order in all properties makes a file quick to scan and makes the odd one out stand out.

rules.description: Reports an `async` method that returns `Task` or `ValueTask` and whose name does not end in `Async`. Overrides, explicit interface implementations and `Main` are not reported, because their names are not the method's to choose. Renaming needs the binding layer, so there is no fix.
rules.why:
The suffix tells the caller that the method returns a task that has to be awaited. A call that forgets `await` on `Load()` compiles and runs on without waiting, but `LoadAsync()` calls for it. It also leaves room for a synchronous `Load()` next to it.

To fix, rename the method to end in `Async`.

rules.description: Reports a comparison with the constant on the left: `null == x` is `x == null`, `1 < x` is `x > 1`. Without the type layer a constant is a literal, `nameof`, a member such as `int.MaxValue`, or an expression made of those; a named constant on the left is not recognised.
rules.why:
"Yoda" conditions came from C, where `x = null` by mistake compiled. In C# an assignment in a condition does not compile for a non-boolean, so the form has no protection to give, and it reads backwards: `x == null` says what is tested first.

To fix, swap the sides and mirror the operator. The fix is safe and does it.

rules.description: Reports the summary of a constructor that does not start with the standard sentence: "Initializes a new instance of the `<see cref="T"/>` class" (or "struct"), "Initializes static members of the ..." for a static constructor. A private constructor may say "Prevents a default instance of the ... from being created". The `<see>` is compared with the name of the type. The fix puts the standard sentence before the text and is unsafe.

upstream.note: the `<see cref>` is compared with the name of the type by spelling, not resolved (a cref through a using alias or a different qualification of the same type is not recognized); other cultures' texts are not available

rules.why: A constructor needs no description of what it does that every constructor does not already say; the standard sentence gives the same first line to all of them, and the text after it adds what is special about this one. Many documentation conventions require it.

rules.description: Reports a `Debug.Assert` call without a message, or with a message that is a constant blank string. With the type layer the call is checked against `System.Diagnostics.Debug`; without it any call written `Debug.Assert` is. No fix.
rules.why:
When an assertion fails in a debug build the message is all that is shown. Without it the developer has the line number and the condition, and a long sequence of asserts in a function does not tell which one broke or why it matters.

To fix, add a message that says what is wrong when the condition is false.

rules.description: Reports a `Debug.Fail` call with a constant blank message. With the type layer the call is checked against `System.Diagnostics.Debug`; without it any call written `Debug.Fail` is. No fix.
rules.why:
`Debug.Fail` is reached only when something is wrong, and the message is the only information about what. An empty message leaves the reader of the failure with a stack trace and no idea of the cause.

To fix, say what went wrong.

rules.description: Reports the summary of a finalizer that does not start with "Finalizes an instance of the `<see cref="T"/>` class." The `<see>` is compared with the name of the type. The fix puts the standard sentence before the text and is unsafe.

upstream.note: the `<see cref>` is compared with the name of the type by spelling, not resolved; other cultures' texts are not available

rules.why: A finalizer is called by the runtime and not by code, so there is nothing to say about how it is used. The standard sentence gives every finalizer the same first line, and the text after it adds what the finalizer cleans up.

rules.description: Reports a preprocessor directive that has a space between `#` and its keyword (`# if`). The fix removes the space.
rules.why: The convention writes the directive as one word, `#if`, `#region`, so a search for it finds all of them and the directives look alike.

rules.description: Reports a documentation line (`///`) that does not start with a single space. More spaces are allowed to indent continuation lines, but not on the first line of the comment; a tab or no space is always reported. The fix writes the single space.
rules.why: The space after the slashes separates the marker from the text, so the text of a comment reads the same as a line of prose. A comment that starts at the slashes (`///<summary>`) is hard to read and differs from the rest of the file.

rules.description: Reports a `<param>` in a documentation comment that has no `name` attribute, or an empty one. No fix.
rules.why:
The `name` is how the tools connect the text to a parameter. A `<param>` without it is documentation that tells the IDE nothing and is shown nowhere.

To fix, add `name="value"` with the name of the parameter.

rules.description: Reports a `<param>` without text. A comment with `<inheritdoc />` is not reported. No fix.
rules.why:
An empty `<param name="x"></param>` looks like documentation and says nothing, and it stops the compiler from warning about the missing parameter.

To fix, describe the parameter.

rules.description: Reports a parameter of a documented, non-private method, constructor, delegate, operator or indexer that has no `<param name="...">` in its `///` comment. A comment with `<inheritdoc />` or `<include>` is not reported, and neither is a declaration without a comment. No fix.
rules.why:
The comment is what the IDE shows when the method is called and what the generated reference lists. A parameter that is not described leaves the caller to guess what it means, its unit, whether it may be null or empty, and what the method does with it.

To fix, add the tag that documents the parameter.

rules.description: Reports a partial type or method without a documentation comment, or with an empty one. Each part is checked on its own: accepting one documented part would need all the other parts of the project. Which elements need documentation follows the default of private members being left out.

upstream.note: a partial type or method is reported when this part is undocumented even if another part is documented (needs the other parts)

rules.why:
A partial type is built from several files, and the documentation tools take the comment from one of them. A part without a comment leaves the reader of that file with nothing to read at the declaration.

To fix, document the part.

rules.description: Reports a documentation comment of a partial type or method that has no `<summary>` or `<content>` (and no `<inheritdoc />`). Each part is checked on its own. No fix.

upstream.note: each part of a partial type or method needs its own summary here; StyleCop reads the same per-part comment, but SA1601's cross-part acceptance is not available (see SA1601)

rules.why:
The summary is the part of the comment that tools show in a list or a hover. A comment of a partial type without it is shown with no description.

To fix, add a `<summary>`.

rules.description: Reports a partial type or method whose `<summary>` (or `<content>`) has no text. Each part is checked on its own. No fix.

upstream.note: each part is checked on its own; StyleCop's partial rules also read the other parts through the project

rules.why:
An empty summary is shown in a list or a hover as no description, and it hides that nobody wrote one.

To fix, write the summary.

rules.description: Reports a documented partial generic type (one that has a `<summary>`) that has no `<typeparam>` for one of its type parameters, on the parameter. Each part is checked on its own. No fix.

upstream.note: each part of a partial generic type is checked on its own

rules.why:
Without the tag a reader of the documentation sees `T` and has to read the code to learn what it stands for.

To fix, add `<typeparam name="T">` with the meaning of `T`.

rules.description: Reports a `<returns>` without text. A comment with `<inheritdoc />` is not reported. No fix.
rules.why:
An empty `<returns></returns>` looks like documentation and tells the reader nothing about the value, and it keeps tools from reporting that the result is not described.

To fix, describe what the method returns.

rules.description: Reports a documented method or delegate that does not return `void` and has no `<returns>` (and no `<inheritdoc />`). Private members are not reported. No fix.
rules.why:
The summary says what a method does, and `<returns>` says what comes back, which a caller needs to use it right: units, meaning of `null`, which failure value.

To fix, add a `<returns>` that describes the value.

rules.description: Reports a documentation comment without `<summary>` (and without `<inheritdoc />`) on a type, member or field that needs documentation: everything but private members. Partial types and methods belong to `doc-partial-summary-required`. No fix.
rules.why:
The summary is what tools show in lists, in hovers and in the generated reference. A comment without it appears without a description, however much the other tags say.

To fix, add a `<summary>`.

rules.description: Reports a `<summary>` without text (`<summary></summary>`; `<summary />` is not reported). Partial types and methods belong to `doc-partial-summary-text`. No fix.
rules.why:
An empty summary is a placeholder that was never filled in: it satisfies a check that a summary exists and tells the reader nothing.

To fix, write the summary.

rules.description: Reports the last text of an element of a documentation comment that does not end with a period (`.` or `.)`). Each paragraph of `<para>` and `<note>` is checked. A paragraph that ends in a colon (except the last), `-or-` and `<seealso>` are not reported, and an inline element (`<see />`, `<c>`, ...) at the end counts as not ending with a period. The fix adds the period, or replaces a trailing comma or semicolon with it.
rules.why: Documentation is read as sentences in the generated reference, where the elements are shown one below the other. Text with and without the final period looks uneven, and the missing period is the first thing that shows that a sentence was not finished.

rules.description: Reports a `<remarks>`, `<example>`, `<exception>` or `<permission>` element without text, written `<remarks></remarks>` or `<remarks />`. No fix.
rules.why:
An empty element is shown as a heading with nothing below it in the generated documentation, so it adds noise and hides that the text was never written.

To fix, write the text or delete the element.

rules.description: Reports a `<typeparam>` without a `name` attribute, or with an empty one, in the documentation of a generic class, struct, interface, method or delegate. No fix.
rules.why:
The `name` connects the text to a type parameter. Without it the tag is not shown with its parameter.

To fix, add `name="T"`.

rules.description: Reports a `<typeparam>` without text (`<typeparam name="T" />` counts as without text), in the documentation of a generic class, struct, interface, method or delegate. No fix.
rules.why:
A type parameter with an empty description looks documented and says nothing about what `T` is for, and it stops tools from reporting the missing text.

To fix, describe the type parameter.

rules.description: Reports a property's `<value>` without text (`<value></value>`; `<value />` is not reported). A comment with `<inheritdoc />` is not reported. No fix.
rules.why:
An empty `<value>` is a placeholder: it satisfies a check that the tag exists and gives the reader nothing about what the property holds.

To fix, describe the value.

rules.description: Reports a field whose name begins with an underscore. The option `fields` is the expression a field name must match.

options.description: Regular expression the name of a field must match; empty: not checked.
options.name: fields

rules.why:
The convention of many style guides names fields in camel case without a prefix and tells them from locals by writing `this.`. A leading underscore is the other convention; a project picks one, and the rule enforces it.

To fix, rename the field.

rules.description: Reports a file whose name, up to its first dot and ignoring case, is not the name of the first type in the file; a generic type may also be written `Name{T,U}`. Not checked when that type is partial. No fix.

example.input: class Orders { }

rules.why:
A file named after its type is found by the name from the file tree, from a stack trace and from a search. A file whose name says something else sends the reader to the wrong place.

To fix, rename the file or the type.

rules.description: Reports `<inheritdoc />` without `cref` on a type that has no base list, or on a member that neither overrides nor implements anything. A constructor whose signature matches a base constructor is not reported. No fix.
rules.why:
`inheritdoc` takes the documentation from what the member inherits. If it inherits nothing, the tool has no text to copy, and the member is shown without documentation although the comment looks complete.

To fix, write the documentation, or name the source with `cref`.

rules.description: Reports a member that is out of order compared with the member before it, in the order of the `element_order` option: the kind (fields, constructors, finalizers, delegates, events, enums, interfaces, properties, indexers, operators, methods, structs, classes; in a namespace or file: namespaces, delegates, enums, interfaces, structs, classes), the access (public, internal, protected internal, protected, private protected, private), constants before other fields, static before instance members, readonly fields before the others. A trait counts only between members that agree on the traits listed before it. No fix: moving members would have to take their comments and directives along.

options.description: The traits that decide the order, most important first. A trait that is left out is not checked.
options.name: element_order

rules.why:
A fixed order lets a reader find a member without reading the class: fields at the top, constructors next, then the rest by visibility. Different files of a project then look the same.

To fix, move the member to its place.

rules.description: Reports a type, member, field or enum item that needs documentation and has no `///` comment before it: public, protected or internal ones, in types that are too. Members of an interface, explicit interface implementations and enum items count as public. Partial declarations are not reported, and private members are not either. No fix.

upstream.note: Only methods and constructors, no minimum line count.
Only types, no scope option.
No stuttering check (a name that starts with the package name), no own-declaration check for `var a, B`; a method that is sortable through methods in another file of the package is reported

rules.why:
Documentation of the public interface is what the users of a library read, in the IDE and in the generated reference. An element without a comment shows only its name and signature, and the caller has to read the code to learn what it does and what it expects.

To fix, add a comment that says what the element is for.

rules.description: Reports a comment between the head of an `if`, `else`, `while`, `do`, `for`, `foreach`, `lock`, `try`, `catch`, `finally`, `switch`, `checked` or `unchecked` and its `{`.
rules.why:
A comment there is attached to neither the head nor the block, and a reader may take it for a part of the condition. It is also easy to separate from its statement when the code is moved.

To fix, put the comment inside the block or above the statement.

rules.description: Reports a control character (below U+0020) in the constant string given to `new Regex(...)` and the static methods of `Regex`, written raw or as an escape.
rules.why:
A control character in a pattern is almost never intended: it is invisible in the source, and the pattern then matches a character that the reader cannot see. It is usually the result of a pasted character or of an escape that was written for something else.

To fix, remove the character, or write the one that is meant (`\t`, `\n`, `\r`) with its letter escape.

rules.description: Reports a `<summary>` that starts with the text Visual Studio generates, "Summary description for ...". A comment with `<inheritdoc />` is not reported. No fix.
rules.why:
The text is a placeholder that the tool inserts. It stays in the generated documentation as a sentence that says nothing about the element.

To fix, write the real summary.

rules.description: Reports `new S()` of a value type that has an implicit parameterless constructor and no initializer: write `default(S)`, or the named constant where there is one (`Guid.Empty`, `CancellationToken.None`, `IntPtr.Zero`, the enum member with value 0). No fix for a target-typed `new()`.
rules.why:
`new S()` of such a struct is the zero value, the same as `default(S)`, but it reads as a call that does something. `default` states that the value is the zero value, and a named constant (`Guid.Empty`) says what that value means.

To fix, write `default(S)` or the constant.

rules.description: Reports a `<placeholder>` element in a documentation comment. No fix.
rules.why:
`<placeholder>` marks text that is to be filled in later, so a comment that has one is not finished.

To fix, write the text.

rules.description: Reports a `///` comment that holds only text and no XML element: a plain comment written with documentation slashes. The fix writes `//`, unless the comment documents a declaration (it would remove documentation).
rules.why:
Three slashes make the comment documentation, and the compiler and tools then read it as XML. A plain remark written that way is attached to the next declaration and shown in its hover, or reported as malformed.

To fix, write `//`.

rules.description: Reports two elements of one documentation comment with the same text (a `<param>` pasted twice, for example). Empty elements and "The parameter is not used." are not reported. No fix.
rules.why:
Two parameters described in the same words is almost always a copy and paste that was not edited, so one of the descriptions is wrong.

To fix, write the right text for each element.

rules.description: Reports an attribute with empty parentheses: `[Foo()]` is `[Foo]`. Parentheses with a comment in them are not reported. The fix removes the parentheses.
rules.why: The parentheses add two characters and no meaning: the attribute is constructed in both cases with its parameterless constructor.

rules.description: Reports an anonymous method with an empty parameter list: `delegate() { }` is `delegate { }`. Parentheses with a comment in them are not reported. The fix is unsafe: without a parameter list the method also converts to delegate types that have parameters, which can change which overload is chosen.
rules.why: `delegate { }` is the shorter spelling of the same body, and the empty parentheses add nothing to read. They are not always the same to the compiler: the form without a list also converts to delegate types that have parameters, which can change which overload is chosen, and that is why the fix is unsafe.

rules.description: Reports a lone `;` that does nothing. A statement labelled `label: ;` is not reported. The fix removes the statement (its whole line when it is alone on it), or turns an empty loop or `if` body into `{ }`; it is not offered for the only statement of a switch section. The compiler reports `if (x);` too.
rules.why:
A stray `;` is usually the result of a typo or an edit. After `if (x);` or `while (x);` it is the body of the statement, so the line that follows runs unconditionally, whatever its indentation says.

To fix, delete the `;`, or write `{ }` for a body that is meant to be empty.

rules.description: Reports a character class in the constant string given to `new Regex(...)` and the static methods of `Regex`, in which a combining mark follows another character.

upstream.note: the surrogate pair, emoji modifier, flag and joined-sequence checks are not made

rules.why:
A combining mark is a separate code point that attaches to the character before it. In a character class each code point is its own member, so the class matches the base letter or the mark alone and never the combined character the author sees.

To fix, write the combined character as a group outside the class, or as a single precomposed character.

rules.description: Reports two or more spaces outside a character class in the constant string given to `new Regex(...)` and the static methods of `Regex`.
rules.why:
Several spaces in a row are hard to count, and a pattern that has them is easily changed by an editor that collapses white space or by a reader who counts wrongly. The number of spaces is part of what the pattern matches.

To fix, write the number as a count (`a {3}b`).

rules.description: Reports a `#region` inside a block (a method, accessor or lambda body, or any block in one). Regions belong between members. No fix.
rules.why:
A region in a body splits one piece of logic with a fold that hides the middle of it. A body that needs sections is a body that should be split into methods.

To fix, extract the section into a method and delete the region.

rules.description: Reports every `#region` outside a block (a region inside a block is `no-region-in-body`'s), also in disabled `#if` branches. No fix, because removing a pair is a judgment call.
rules.why:
A region hides code behind a label, so a reader of a large class sees only the labels and not the size of what is behind them. Regions make a file longer without making it clearer, and are often a sign that the class should be split.

To fix, remove the region, or move its members to a class of their own.

rules.description: Reports a `<returns>` on a method or delegate that returns `void`. The fix removes the element with its line when it is alone on it.
rules.why: There is nothing to return, so the tag documents a value that does not exist and is shown in the reference as a result.

rules.description: Reports `base.M()` or `base[i]` where the type does not override the member, so `this` binds to the same one. The fix writes `this`.
rules.why: `base.` says that the call goes to the parent on purpose, and a reader looks for the override that makes this necessary. When there is none, `this.M()` is the same call, and the `base` is a misleading hint.

rules.description: Reports an import of every name of a package or module (`import a.b.*;` in Java and Kotlin, `from a import *` in Python, `import . "fmt"` in Go). A named import is not reported. Off by default.

example.input:
package a

import (
	. "fmt"
	"os"
	_ "embed"
	m "math"
)

import . "strings"

options.description: The aliases that bring in every name of the imported package
options.name: wildcard_aliases

upstream.note: No allow-list option.

rules.why:
A wildcard hides where a name comes from, and a name added to the package later can silently clash with one in the file or change which one a call reaches. Tools and readers cannot tell from the imports what the file uses.

To fix, import the names the file uses.

rules.description: Reports `Nullable<int>` or `System.Nullable<int>`, which is `int?`. The check is by name: a type of your own called `Nullable` is reported too. It is not reported in `using` aliases, in `nameof`, in `typeof(Nullable<>)`, and before a member access (`Nullable<int>.Equals`). The fix writes `int?`.
rules.why: `int?` is the form of the language and is shorter. One spelling makes the nullable types easy to find, and `Nullable<T>` stays for the places where the generic name is the point.

rules.description: Reports a member or element access on an expression that the nullable analysis says may be null. Only code under `#nullable enable` is checked. Off by default: the compiler reports the same thing.
rules.why:
Dereferencing a null reference throws `NullReferenceException` at run time, so the warning points at a crash that the code allows.

To fix, check for null before the access, or change the type if it cannot be null.

rules.description: Reports a property summary that does not start with "Gets", "Sets" or "Gets or sets" as the accessors that are reachable from outside the type say; for `bool` properties "Gets a value indicating whether" and the like. The type is read from the declaration (`bool`, `Boolean`, `System.Boolean`). The fix replaces the start of the text and lower-cases what follows, and is unsafe.

upstream.note: a property whose type is an alias of `System.Boolean` (using alias) is not recognized as `bool`

rules.why: A summary that says "Gets or sets" for a property that can only be read promises something the caller cannot do. The first words are a contract that tools and readers rely on.

rules.description: Reports a property summary that says "Gets or sets" while one of the accessors is not reachable from outside the type (`private set`, `internal get` on a public property). The fix replaces the start of the text with the one that matches the visible accessor and is unsafe.
rules.why: The documentation is for the callers of the property, and a caller outside the type cannot use the restricted accessor, so the summary should describe only what is possible.

rules.description: Reports a field, property, method or event of the containing type that is used by its simple name. The fix writes `this.` before it.
rules.why: With `this.` it is clear at a glance that the name is a member and not a local, a parameter or a static, so a reader does not scroll up to see where a name comes from. It is a style that some projects choose and others do not.

rules.description: Reports a `using` directive inside a namespace whose name is not written fully qualified, so that it resolves relative to the enclosing namespace. The fix writes the full name, unless it has type arguments.
rules.why:
A relative name resolves to different things when a namespace with that name is added anywhere in the enclosing namespaces, so a new file can change what a `using` means without touching it.

To fix, write the full name.

rules.description: Reports a `using` directive that nothing in the file needs. It is not reported in a file that has compiler errors or `#if` regions, because unresolved or inactive code could be the one using it. The fix removes the directive.
rules.why: An unused `using` adds noise at the top of the file, suggests a dependency that does not exist, and slows the compiler a little. Removing them keeps the list of what the file uses true.

rules.description: Reports an attribute list with several attributes: `[A, B]` is `[A]` and `[B]`. Lists on parameters and type parameters are not reported. The fix is not offered when the list has a comment in it.
rules.why: One attribute to a list gives each its own line, so a diff shows exactly the attribute that was added or removed and a comment can be put on one.

rules.description: Reports a declaration of several fields or events (`int a, b;`), which becomes `int a;` and `int b;`, each with the attributes, modifiers and type of the original. The fix is not offered when the declaration has a comment in it.
rules.why: One field to a declaration gives each its own line, so a change to one is one line in the diff and each can have its own comment and initializer.

rules.description: Reports a class or record that comes after the first one in a file: more parts of the first class (when it is partial) are not reported. Structs, interfaces, enums and delegates are not counted. No fix.
rules.why:
A file with one class is found by the name of the class, and a change to a class touches one file. A file with several is a place where a class has to be searched for.

To fix, move the class into a file of its own.

rules.description: Reports a namespace that comes after the first one in a file; nested namespaces are reported too. No fix.
rules.why:
A file with one namespace has one place where its names come from. Several namespaces in a file make the meaning of a name depend on where in the file it is read.

To fix, move the later namespaces into files of their own.

rules.description: Reports a `SuppressMessage` attribute whose `Justification` is missing, `null`, empty, blank, or `"<Pending>"`. The attribute is matched by name. No fix.
rules.why:
A suppression hides a warning for good, and the reason is the only information a later reader has to judge whether it still holds. The text generated by tools ("<Pending>") is a placeholder that stays forever.

To fix, write why the warning does not apply.

rules.description: Reports a tuple type in the signature of a method, constructor, property, indexer, conversion operator or delegate whose elements have no names. Overrides and implementations of interface members are not reported, since their names are not the member's to choose. No fix.
rules.why:
A caller sees `(int, int)` in the signature and `Item1` and `Item2` in the result, so it has to read the body to know which is which. Names (`(int Width, int Height)`) make the signature the documentation.

To fix, name the elements.

rules.description: Reports a value stored in a local variable that no path reads before it is overwritten or the variable goes out of scope (a dead store). Variables that are captured or whose address is taken are not checked. A variable that is never read at all is `unused-variable`'s.

example.input: class A { int F() { int n = 0; n = G(); return n; } int H() { int m = 0; m = 1; m = G(); return m; } int G() => 1; }

rules.why:
A dead store is a computation whose result is thrown away. It is often the sign of a bug: the value was meant to be used and a later line forgot it, or an earlier branch was changed.

To fix, use the value, or delete the assignment (keep the right side if it has a side effect).

rules.description: Reports a private field, method, property or event that no file of the project uses (needs `analysis: deep`). Members with attributes, overrides, interface implementations, `extern` and `partial` methods are not reported, and neither are the private methods named in `reflection_methods` of a type derived from one of `reflection_base_types` (a framework calls them by reflection; the `csharp/unity` preset lists Unity's).

options.description: Names of base classes whose derived types are called by a framework                           through reflection (with `reflection_methods`). A base is matched by its                           simple name anywhere up the inheritance chain, also when the project                           does not load its assembly.
options.name: reflection_base_types

options.description: Names of private methods that count as used in a type derived from                           one of `reflection_base_types`.
options.name: reflection_methods

rules.why:
A private member that nothing uses is dead code that readers have to understand, tests and refactorings have to keep, and the compiler has to compile.

To fix, delete it.

rules.description: Reports a local variable or catch variable that is never used, or that is only assigned constants and never read. Variables captured by lambdas or local functions count as used. The fix removes the declaration. Off by default, because the compiler already warns.

example.input:
function F {
    $unused = 1
    $read = 2
    "$read"
    $member = @{}
    $member.x = 1
    $list = @(1)
    $list[0] = 2
    $a, $b = 1, 2
    $script:s = 1
    $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
    $count = 1
    $count++
    $block = 1
    $f = { $block }
    & $f
    $Mixed = 1
    "$mixed"
    ${with space} = 1
    ${with space}
    $q = 1
    $script:t = $q
    $splat = @{}
    Get-Item @splat
    $u = 1
}

upstream.note: the options keep their defaults; `/*exported*/` and `/*global*/` comments are not read; a JSX tag counts as a use

The shared scope model, where a name is looked up through the blocks around it, so a read in an inner block of a name the inner block assigns itself counts for the outer one; the module counts by name inside each block. A scope that reads `$PSBoundParameters` is not checked (a documented difference).
A name the whole file assigns and never reads; the file is one scope, `local` is not told apart.
the options keep their defaults; `.d.ts` files and `declare module` blocks are not treated as used

rules.why:
A variable that is never read is a leftover of changed code, or a result that was meant to be used, so the logic that should have used it is missing.

To fix, remove the variable, or use its value.

rules.description: Reports an anonymous method (`delegate (x) { ... }`) where a lambda can be written. The fix is offered when the anonymous method has a parameter list and no comment before its body; `delegate { }` without a parameter list converts to delegate types with any parameters, so it has no fix.
rules.why: Lambdas are the short and usual form, and they bind the same way for the common cases. One form for all code avoids the extra keyword and makes the file read the same.

rules.description: Reports a numeric literal cast to `long`, `ulong`, `uint`, `float`, `double` or `decimal` when the literal's own type differs: `(long)1` is `1L`. Hexadecimal and binary literals cast to a floating-point type are not reported, since they have no suffix. The fix writes the suffix.
rules.why: The suffix gives the literal its type directly. A cast does the same at run time or as a constant, and it hides that the literal is a number of another type.

rules.description: Reports `""` (or `@""`) where `string.Empty` can be used. It is not reported where a constant is required: `const`, attribute arguments, default parameter values, `case` labels and patterns.

upstream.note: Only the `string.Empty` direction; no option for the opposite style (RCS1078) because no preset needs it

rules.why:
`string.Empty` states that the string is empty on purpose, while `""` can be a value that was forgotten. It is a convention that some projects choose and others do not.

To fix, write `string.Empty`.

rules.description: Reports `ValueTuple<int, int>` and `ValueTuple.Create(a, b)` where tuple syntax (`(int, int)` and `(a, b)`) can be used; not inside an expression tree. The fix is offered for types and `ValueTuple.Create` calls.
rules.why: The tuple syntax is the form of the language, short and the one that supports element names. `ValueTuple<...>` is the type it compiles to, so writing it out is noise.

rules.description: Reports `using` directives of a file or namespace that are out of order: `System` first (`system_first`), names in alphabetical order (`compare`), and, with the options `static_position` and `alias_position` set to `after`, `using static` directives after the plain ones and aliases after those, each group sorted. `global using` and `using unsafe` stay where they are, and a list restarts at a directive that has a preprocessor directive in front of it (the fix leaves such lists alone). Comments on lines of their own stay where they are; a comment after a directive moves with it.

options.description: Put `System` and `System.*` before the other namespaces.
options.name: system_first

options.description: `ordinal` compares code points; `culture` ignores case (and puts punctuation before digits before letters, a lower-case name before an upper-case one that is otherwise equal); `culture_ignore_case` leaves names that differ only in case in their order.
options.name: compare

options.description: `after`: `using static` directives come after the plain usings, sorted (System ones first with `system_first`); `keep`: they stay where they are.
options.name: static_position

options.description: `after`: alias directives come after all other usings, sorted by alias name; `keep`: they stay where they are.
options.name: alias_position

upstream.note: no blank-line group handling
no blank-line group handling
no blank-line group handling

rules.why: A sorted list is easy to scan for a namespace, and two developers who add a directive do not both put it at the end and conflict. The `System` first convention is that of the .NET libraries.

rules.description: Reports a `using` directive outside the namespace declaration in a file that has one. No fix: moving a directive changes how names are looked up.
rules.why: A `using` inside the namespace is resolved relative to it, and one outside is global to the file. Projects choose one place for all files, so that the lookup of names does not depend on which file a directive is in.
